days.guide: Teach body safety calmly: your body belongs to you; private parts are the parts covered by a swimsuit; no one should touch them or ask you to touch theirs except for health reasons with a parent present; never keep secrets about touching.

questions.q: If someone asks you to keep a secret about touching, what should you do?
questions.a: Never keep it; tell a trusted adult right away. You will not be in trouble.

questions.q: What is the difference between a surprise and a secret?
questions.a: A surprise is fun and will be told soon (like a birthday gift); an unsafe secret makes you feel bad and should be told.

days.guide: Role-play 3 refusal scenarios with you playing the other person.

questions.q: Show how you would say no with your body.
questions.a: Stand tall, feet planted, look the person in the eye, and say 'No!' in a loud, firm voice.

weeks.assessment_key: Refusal role-play rubric: across 3 scenarios the child 4 = says 'No' clearly with a firm voice, eye contact and strong posture, gets away, and names who they would tell; 3 = does all three steps but with a weak voice or hesitation; 2 = says no but doesn't leave or tell; 1 = goes along with the scenario.

weeks.prep: A computer or tablet. Look up guidance on passphrases. Prepare the family technology agreement template and the Unit 4 quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking people online are who they say they are. Anyone can pretend to be a kid online.
Thinking it's fine to share a password with a best friend. Passwords are shared only with parents.

days.guide: Sort info cards into okay to share online (favorite color, pet's type) and private (full name, address, school, phone, photos, birthday, passwords).

questions.q: Is it okay to post your school name online?
questions.a: No. It's private because it tells strangers where to find you.

questions.q: Name two things that are private online.
questions.a: Any two: full name, address, phone number, school, passwords, photos of yourself, birthday.

days.guide: Create a passphrase of 3–4 random words with a number or symbol. Explain only parents get to know it.

questions.q: Who should you share your password with?
questions.a: Only your parents or guardians.

questions.q: Which is stronger: 'max123' or 'purple-taco-river-7'?
questions.a: 'purple-taco-river-7', because it is longer and harder to guess.

days.guide: Discuss: if someone online asks personal questions, wants photos, asks to keep a secret or to meet, stop, don't reply, and tell a parent.

questions.q: Someone in a game asks where you live. What do you do?
questions.a: Don't answer, stop chatting, and tell a parent.

questions.q: Is it ever okay to meet an online friend in person alone?
questions.a: No. Never; always tell a parent.

days.guide: Write a family tech agreement together: times, allowed apps, where devices are used, what to do if something online is upsetting. Everyone signs.

questions.q: What should you do if you see something online that makes you uncomfortable?
questions.a: Close it or turn off the screen and tell a parent.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 quiz.

questions.q: What should you do if you hear the smoke alarm?
questions.a: Get out right away and go to the meeting place.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 quiz key: 1) Get out and stay out in a fire; crawl low under smoke. 2) Stop, drop and roll. 3) Test smoke alarms monthly. 4) Look left-right-left before crossing. 5) Helmet: eyes-ears-mouth test. 6) Escape a rip current by swimming parallel to shore. 7) Reach or throw, don't go. 8) Tell the 911 dispatcher your name, address and what happened. 9) Earthquake: drop, cover, hold on. 10) Never share your address, school or password online. Tech agreement proficient: includes screen time limits, allowed apps, what to do if something online feels wrong, and is signed. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Empty medicine boxes (pain reliever, cough medicine, vitamins); remove any pills. Store real medicine out of reach. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.
misconceptions: Thinking more medicine works faster or better. Taking more than the label says can be dangerous.
Thinking medicine prescribed for someone else is safe for you. Prescriptions are made for one person's body and illness only.
Thinking vitamins are candy. They're medicine-like and can make you sick in large amounts.

days.guide: Define: a drug is any substance that changes how the body or mind works; a medicine is a drug used to prevent or treat illness. Sort examples (cough syrup, caffeine, nicotine, antibiotics, alcohol).

questions.q: What is the difference between a medicine and a drug?
questions.a: All medicines are drugs, but a medicine is used to prevent or treat illness; some drugs (like nicotine and alcohol) are harmful and not medicine.

questions.q: Is nicotine a medicine?
questions.a: No, it is a harmful, addictive drug.

days.guide: Read a medicine box together: find the dose, the age or weight it's for, how often, and warnings.

questions.q: Why does a medicine label list ages?
questions.a: Doses are different for different ages and sizes; the wrong amount can be harmful.

questions.q: What is the difference between over-the-counter and prescription medicine?
questions.a: Over-the-counter can be bought without a doctor's order; prescription medicine requires a doctor's order and is for one specific person.

days.guide: Teach the rule: only take medicine from a parent or trusted adult, never alone.

questions.q: You find a pill on the floor. What do you do?
questions.a: Don't touch or take it; tell an adult.

questions.q: Your friend offers you some of her allergy medicine. What should you say?
questions.a: No thanks. Only take medicine from your own parent or trusted adult.

days.guide: Show pictures of medicine and candy that look alike. Ask the child to guess which is which and discuss why that's dangerous.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous that some medicines look like candy?
questions.a: Young children might eat them thinking they are candy and could get very sick.

questions.q: What number do you call if someone swallows medicine by accident?
questions.a: Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if they are not breathing or unconscious.

days.guide: The child writes 5 rules for a younger child, in simple words with pictures.

questions.q: What is the most important medicine rule?
questions.a: Only take medicine given by a parent or trusted adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Medicine safety rules key (5 rules for a younger child, any 5 accurate): 1) Only take medicine from a parent or trusted adult. 2) Never take someone else's medicine. 3) Medicine is not candy. 4) Follow the label or doctor's directions exactly. 5) Never take medicine you find. 6) Tell an adult if you feel sick after taking medicine. Rubric: 4 = 5 accurate rules in kid-friendly words; 3 = 4; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: Read the KidsHealth article on vaping (kidshealth.org) ahead. Find a healthy vs. smoker's lung image (CDC or American Lung Association). Parent note: the images can be upsetting; preview and keep the tone factual.
misconceptions: Thinking vapes are just harmless water vapor. Vape aerosol contains nicotine and other chemicals and tiny particles that harm the lungs.
Thinking you can try it once without problems. Nicotine is highly addictive, especially for young brains.
Thinking secondhand smoke only matters indoors for a long time. Any secondhand smoke is harmful; there's no safe level.

days.guide: Compare the healthy and smoker's lung images. The child lists effects on the lungs (damage, coughing, cancer, trouble breathing) and heart (faster heartbeat, heart disease).

questions.q: Name two effects of smoking on the body.
questions.a: Any two: lung damage, lung cancer, heart disease, coughing, shortness of breath, stained teeth, bad breath.

questions.q: What is the addictive drug in tobacco?
questions.a: Nicotine.

days.guide: Read the vaping article. The child highlights 3 facts.

questions.q: Is vape 'smoke' just water vapor?
questions.a: No. It's an aerosol with nicotine, flavoring chemicals and tiny particles that can harm the lungs.

questions.q: Why is nicotine especially harmful for kids?
questions.a: Their brains are still developing, so they can get addicted more easily, and it can affect attention and learning.

days.guide: Discuss secondhand smoke and how to avoid it (move away, ask to open a window, ask adults not to smoke in the car).

questions.q: What is secondhand smoke?
questions.a: Smoke breathed in by people near someone smoking.

questions.q: How can you avoid secondhand smoke?
questions.a: Move away from smokers, go to a smoke-free area, and ask adults politely not to smoke around you or in the car.

days.guide: Look at how vapes are marketed: candy flavors, bright packaging, social media, friends. Discuss why companies do this.

questions.q: Why do vapes come in candy or fruit flavors?
questions.a: To make them appealing to young people and hide the harsh taste, which is a trick to get new users.

days.guide: The child writes 5 facts about tobacco and vaping.

questions.q: What is the legal age to buy tobacco or vapes in California?

weeks.assessment_key: Tobacco facts key (any 5 accurate): cigarettes and vapes contain nicotine, which is addictive; smoking damages lungs and causes lung cancer and heart disease; smoking makes the heart beat faster and narrows blood vessels; vape aerosol is not just water vapor and contains harmful chemicals; secondhand smoke harms people nearby; the legal age to buy tobacco and vapes is 21; smoking stains teeth and causes bad breath and less stamina. Rubric: 4 = 5 accurate facts; 3 = 4; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: A simple brain diagram (cerebrum, cerebellum, brain stem). Clear space and an adult spotter for the spinning activity (soft surface, stop if the child feels sick). Parent note: if alcohol use is part of family life, explain that adults can choose to drink responsibly but it is harmful to kids.
misconceptions: Thinking alcohol is a stimulant that makes people more active. Alcohol is a depressant; it slows the brain and body.
Thinking a little alcohol is fine for kids. Growing brains are especially sensitive; it's illegal and harmful under 21.

days.guide: Explain that alcohol is a depressant drug that slows messages in the brain, affecting judgment, balance, speech and reaction time. Point to brain areas.

questions.q: Does alcohol speed up or slow down the brain?
questions.a: It slows it down; alcohol is a depressant.

questions.q: Name two things alcohol affects.
questions.a: Judgment, balance, coordination, speech, memory, reaction time.

days.guide: With an adult spotter, the child spins slowly 5 times then tries to walk a straight line. Discuss how alcohol similarly affects balance.

questions.q: Why was it hard to walk the line?
questions.a: Spinning confused the balance system; alcohol also impairs balance and coordination.

days.guide: Explain the brain keeps developing until the mid-20s and alcohol can harm it. The legal age is 21 to protect young people.

questions.q: Why is alcohol especially harmful for kids?
questions.a: Their brains and bodies are still growing, and alcohol can damage development and affect learning and memory.

questions.q: What is the legal drinking age in the U.S.?

days.guide: Look at ads or TV scenes showing alcohol. Discuss what message they send (fun, friends, relaxing) and what they leave out.

questions.q: What do alcohol ads usually leave out?
questions.a: The harmful effects: accidents, poor decisions, illness and addiction.

days.guide: Give the 6-question alcohol quiz.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to drink and drive?
questions.a: Alcohol slows reaction time and impairs judgment and coordination, causing crashes.

weeks.assessment_key: Alcohol quiz key: 1) Alcohol is a depressant; it slows the brain. 2) It harms judgment (decision making). 3) It harms balance and coordination. 4) It slows reaction time, which is why drinking and driving is dangerous. 5) The legal age to buy or drink alcohol in the U.S. is 21. 6) It is especially harmful to kids because their brains are still growing. Proficient: 5–6 correct.

weeks.prep: Scenario cards about being offered a vape or alcohol; poster board and markers. Prepare the Unit 5 quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking peer pressure is always bad. Positive peer pressure (friends encouraging you to try out for a team or study) can help.
Thinking you need a long excuse to refuse. A firm 'No thanks' is enough.

days.guide: Define peer pressure (influence from people your age). List positive examples and negative ones.

questions.q: Give an example of positive peer pressure.
questions.a: A friend encouraging you to join a team, study, try a new healthy food, or be kind to someone.

days.guide: Teach the 5 ways to say no; model each with a different voice and body language.

questions.q: Name the 5 refusal strategies.
questions.a: Say no firmly, give a reason, change the subject, walk away, suggest something else.

days.guide: Role-play 3 scenarios where an older kid offers a vape or alcohol. Coach a firm voice and leaving.

questions.q: An older kid offers you a vape and says 'Everyone does it.' What could you say?
questions.a: Example: 'No thanks, I don't want to get addicted. Let's go shoot hoops instead.' Then walk away and tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: The child designs a drug-free poster with a positive message.

questions.q: Why use a positive message on a poster?
questions.a: Positive messages show the benefits of healthy choices and are more inspiring than scare tactics.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 quiz.

questions.q: What is the addictive drug in vapes?
questions.a: Nicotine.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 quiz key: 1) A medicine treats or prevents illness; take only from a trusted adult. 2) Never take someone else's prescription. 3) Poison Control 1-800-222-1222. 4) Nicotine is the addictive drug in tobacco and vapes. 5) Vape aerosol is not harmless water vapor. 6) Secondhand smoke harms people nearby. 7) Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain. 8) Legal age for alcohol and tobacco: 21. 9) Five refusal strategies: say no firmly, give a reason, change the subject, walk away, suggest something else. 10) Peer pressure can be positive or negative. Poster proficient: clear positive message, accurate fact, eye-catching. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Glitter, lotion, soap, a spray bottle of water, large paper. Know the CDC 5 steps: wet, lather, scrub (at least 20 seconds), rinse, dry.
misconceptions: Thinking a quick rinse with water kills germs. Soap and 20 seconds of scrubbing are needed to remove germs.
Thinking antibiotics cure colds. Colds are viruses; antibiotics only work on bacteria.

days.guide: Explain that germs are tiny living things. Bacteria are single-celled living things (some helpful, some cause strep throat); viruses are much smaller and cause colds and flu. Germs spread by touch, droplets, food and water.

questions.q: What is the difference between bacteria and viruses?
questions.a: Bacteria are tiny one-celled organisms (some helpful, some cause illness like strep throat); viruses are much smaller and can only multiply inside living cells (they cause colds and flu).

questions.q: Name two ways germs spread.
questions.a: Touching hands or surfaces, coughs and sneezes, contaminated food or water.

days.guide: Put lotion and glitter on the child's hands, then shake hands with family members and touch a doorknob. Count how many people and objects have glitter.

questions.q: What did the glitter show?
questions.a: How easily germs spread from hands to other people and objects.

days.guide: Wash with the 5 steps for 20 seconds (hum 'Happy Birthday' twice). Then try with glitter: water only vs. soap and scrub.

questions.q: What are the 5 handwashing steps?
questions.a: Wet, lather, scrub for 20 seconds, rinse, dry.

questions.q: Name three times you should wash your hands.
questions.a: Before eating, after the bathroom, after coughing/sneezing, after touching animals, after being outside.

days.guide: Spray water at paper from a few feet to show droplet spread. Practice coughing or sneezing into the elbow.

questions.q: Why sneeze into your elbow rather than your hand?
questions.a: So germs don't get on your hands and then spread to things and people you touch.

days.guide: The child makes a handwashing sign for the bathroom.

questions.q: How long should you scrub?
questions.a: At least 20 seconds.

weeks.assessment_key: Handwashing sign key: the 5 CDC steps in order — 1) Wet hands with clean running water; 2) Lather with soap (backs, between fingers, under nails); 3) Scrub for at least 20 seconds (hum 'Happy Birthday' twice); 4) Rinse; 5) Dry with a clean towel or air dry. Rubric: 4 = all 5 steps in order, 20 seconds mentioned, pictures; 3 = 4 steps; 2 = steps out of order; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Toothbrush, floss, a hand mirror, two hard-boiled eggs (white shells), dark soda, water, two cups. Set up the egg experiment on Day 2 and check on Day 3. Find a Mouth Healthy Kids brushing video (mouthhealthykids.org, American Dental Association).
misconceptions: Thinking baby teeth don't matter because they fall out. They hold space for adult teeth and cavities in them can hurt and cause infections.
Brushing hard and fast. Use gentle small circles for 2 minutes.

days.guide: Use a mirror to find incisors (front, cutting), canines (pointed, tearing), premolars and molars (back, grinding). Name the parts: enamel (hard outer layer), dentin, pulp, root, gums.

questions.q: What do molars do?
questions.a: Grind and crush food.

questions.q: What is the hardest outer layer of a tooth called?
questions.a: Enamel.

days.guide: Place one egg in soda and one in water overnight. The child writes a prediction.

questions.q: Why use an egg?
questions.a: The shell is made of calcium like tooth enamel, so it models how drinks affect teeth.

days.guide: Remove the eggs and compare. Watch the brushing video, then brush for 2 minutes with a timer: small gentle circles, all surfaces, tongue too.

questions.q: What happened to the egg in soda and why?
questions.a: It got stained (and may be softer) because the soda's color and acid affect the calcium shell, like teeth.

questions.q: How long and how often should you brush?
questions.a: 2 minutes, twice a day, with fluoride toothpaste.

days.guide: Model flossing: about 18 inches of floss, wrap on middle fingers, slide gently between teeth and curve in a C shape around each tooth.

questions.q: Why floss?
questions.a: It removes food and plaque between teeth where the toothbrush can't reach.

questions.q: How often should you floss?
questions.a: Once a day.

days.guide: Start the 2-week brushing and flossing tracker and post it in the bathroom.

questions.q: Name two foods or drinks that are bad for teeth and one that's good.
questions.a: Bad: soda, candy, sticky sweets, juice. Good: water, milk, cheese, crunchy vegetables.

weeks.assessment_key: Egg experiment notes key: the egg in soda is stained brown and may feel rougher; the egg in water is unchanged. Conclusion: soda's color and acid can stain and weaken enamel, like teeth. Brushing tracker: proficient = brushing twice a day for 2 minutes and flossing once a day recorded for 14 days, with at least 12 days complete.

weeks.prep: Sleep log, sunscreen (SPF 30+), UV beads or dark construction paper. Know: AASM recommends 9–12 hours of sleep for ages 6–12.
misconceptions: Thinking sunscreen is only needed at the beach or on hot days. UV rays reach you on cloudy days and in winter.
Thinking sleep is wasted time. During sleep the brain stores memories and the body grows and repairs.

days.guide: Explain sleep needs (9–12 hours) and why: memory, growth, mood, fighting germs. The child lists 3 good bedtime habits.

questions.q: How many hours of sleep do kids your age need?
questions.a: 9 to 12 hours.

questions.q: Name two good bedtime habits.
questions.a: No screens an hour before bed, same bedtime every night, a quiet dark room, reading, a calm routine.

days.guide: The child records bedtime and wake time each night and calculates hours slept.

questions.q: You went to bed at 8:30 p.m. and woke at 6:30 a.m. How long did you sleep?
questions.a: 10 hours.

days.guide: Teach sun safety: SPF 30+ sunscreen, reapply every 2 hours, hats, shade from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Test sunscreen on UV beads (or cover half of dark paper with a sunscreen-coated plastic bag) in sunlight.

questions.q: What did sunscreen do to the UV beads (or paper)?
questions.a: The beads under sunscreen changed color less, showing sunscreen blocks UV rays.

questions.q: When is the sun strongest?
questions.a: About 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

days.guide: The child creates a morning and evening hygiene checklist.

questions.q: Why is daily bathing and wearing clean clothes important?
questions.a: It removes sweat, dirt and germs, prevents odor and skin problems, and helps you feel good.

days.guide: Analyze the 5-night log: find the average and set a bedtime goal.

questions.q: If you slept 9, 10, 8, 10 and 8 hours, what's the average?

weeks.assessment_key: Sleep log analysis and hygiene checklist key: analysis correctly computes hours slept each night (e.g., bedtime 9:00 p.m., wake 7:00 a.m. = 10 hours), finds the average, compares to 9–12 hours and sets a specific bedtime goal. Hygiene checklist proficient: morning (brush teeth, wash face, deodorant if needed, brush hair, clean clothes) and evening (bathe/shower, brush and floss, trim/clean nails weekly, lay out clean clothes). Rubric: 4 = all correct and complete; 3 = one math error or missing item; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Arrange a short phone or in-person interview with a health worker (relative who is a nurse, family dentist, etc.). Plan a pharmacy visit at a quiet time. Interview questions sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking pharmacists just hand out boxes. They check that medicines are safe together and the dose is right, and answer questions.
Thinking public health is only hospitals. Public health workers inspect restaurants, test water and track diseases.

days.guide: The child lists 6 health helpers and their jobs.

questions.q: What does an optometrist do?
questions.a: Examines eyes, checks vision, and prescribes glasses or contacts.

questions.q: What does a pharmacist do?
questions.a: Prepares and gives out medicines, checks that they are safe, and explains how to use them.

days.guide: The child interviews a health worker with 5 prepared questions and takes notes.

questions.q: Write one good interview question.
questions.a: Examples: 'What does a typical day look like?' 'What training did you need?' 'How do you help keep people healthy?'

days.guide: At the pharmacy counter, the child observes and asks (if appropriate) how pharmacists keep medicine safe.

questions.q: Name one way a pharmacist keeps medicine safe.
questions.a: Checks the dose, checks for harmful interactions with other medicines, labels clearly, and explains how to take it.

days.guide: Explain public health: inspectors check restaurant kitchens, water treatment plants clean water, and health departments track outbreaks and give vaccines.

questions.q: How do public health workers keep restaurants safe?
questions.a: They inspect kitchens to make sure food is stored, cooked and handled safely and the place is clean.

days.guide: The child completes the booklet.

questions.q: Who would you see for a toothache?
questions.a: A dentist.

weeks.assessment_key: Health helpers booklet rubric: 4 = at least 6 pages (doctor – checks health and treats illness; nurse – cares for patients, gives shots; dentist – cares for teeth; pharmacist – fills prescriptions and explains medicine; school nurse – first aid and health at school; optometrist – checks eyes and prescribes glasses) each with an accurate job and picture, plus the interview page; 3 = 4–5 pages accurate; 2 = 2–3 pages or errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: AirNow website (airnow.gov) bookmarked. Gloves, a bathroom scale or kitchen scale, 3 bins for trash audit. Know AQI levels: 0–50 green/good, 51–100 yellow/moderate, 101–150 orange/unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151–200 red/unhealthy, 201–300 purple/very unhealthy, 301+ maroon/hazardous.
misconceptions: Thinking pollution is only what you can see. Some air pollution (fine particles, ozone) is invisible.
Thinking recycling is the only answer. Reducing and reusing come first because they prevent waste.

days.guide: Explain how air pollution (car exhaust, smoke from wildfires, factories) can irritate lungs and trigger asthma, and how water pollution can make people sick.

questions.q: How can air pollution affect health?
questions.a: It can irritate the lungs, cause coughing and trouble breathing, and trigger asthma attacks.

questions.q: Name two sources of air pollution.
questions.a: Car exhaust, wildfire smoke, factories, power plants, burning trash.

days.guide: Each day, check AirNow for your ZIP code, record the AQI number and color, and decide if it's a good outdoor-play day.

questions.q: The AQI is 160 (red). Should you play hard outside?
questions.a: No. The air is unhealthy for everyone; stay inside or keep outdoor activity light and short.

questions.q: What AQI color is best?
questions.a: Green (0–50), good.

days.guide: With gloves, sort a day's trash into landfill, recycling and compost and weigh each.

questions.q: Which bin does a banana peel go in?
questions.a: Compost.

questions.q: Which bin does a clean plastic bottle go in?
questions.a: Recycling.

days.guide: The family chooses 3 items to reduce, reuse or recycle and writes a plan.

questions.q: What do reduce, reuse and recycle mean?
questions.a: Reduce: use less. Reuse: use things again. Recycle: turn used materials into new products.

days.guide: The child writes the paragraph on how a clean environment keeps people healthy.

questions.q: Why does clean water matter for health?
questions.a: Dirty water can carry germs and chemicals that make people sick.

weeks.assessment_key: AQI log and paragraph key: log has 7 days of AQI values with colors and a correct decision (play outside for green/yellow; limit hard outdoor play at orange for sensitive people; stay inside or keep play light at red or above). Paragraph rubric: 4 = topic sentence, at least 2 specific ways a clean environment protects health (clean air helps breathing/asthma, clean water prevents illness, less trash means fewer germs and pests), a concluding sentence; 3 = 1 specific way; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gloves, trash bags, a clipboard with a tally sheet, grabbers if possible. Choose a safe location. Safety rules: gloves on, don't touch sharp items or needles (tell an adult), stay away from traffic and water edges, wash hands after. Prepare Unit 6 quiz below.
misconceptions: Picking up sharp or dangerous items. Never touch glass shards, needles or chemicals; point them out to an adult.
Thinking one family's cleanup doesn't matter. Data and sharing results can inspire others.

days.guide: Choose a site, list supplies and write 4 safety rules together.

questions.q: What should you do if you find a needle or broken glass?
questions.a: Don't touch it; tell an adult right away.

days.guide: Do the cleanup for 1 hour, tallying items by type (wrappers, bottles, cans, cigarette butts, etc.).

questions.q: Why wear gloves during a cleanup?
questions.a: To protect your hands from germs and sharp objects.

days.guide: The child makes a bar graph of the tallies and identifies the most common item.

questions.q: What does the tallest bar on your graph tell you?
questions.a: The most common type of trash collected.

days.guide: The child writes a short letter or post sharing results and asking others to help.

questions.q: What should your letter include?
questions.a: What you did, what you found (data), why it matters for health, and a request for others to help.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 quiz.

questions.q: How many hours of sleep do kids need?
questions.a: 9–12 hours.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 quiz key: 1) Wash hands for 20 seconds with soap. 2) Sneeze into your elbow. 3) Bacteria vs. viruses: bacteria are single-celled; viruses are smaller and cause colds/flu. 4) Brush 2 minutes twice a day; floss once a day. 5) Kids need 9–12 hours of sleep. 6) Use SPF 30+ sunscreen. 7) A pharmacist prepares and explains medicine. 8) An AQI of 0–50 (green) is good. 9) Reduce, reuse, recycle. 10) Clean environments prevent illness. Graph proficient: bar graph with title, labeled axes, correct tallies, most common item identified. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Planning sheet with sections: topic, audience, message, 3 facts, materials. Have KidsHealth and MyPlate open for fact-checking.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad ('be healthy'). Narrow to one action, like 'wash your hands for 20 seconds.'
Writing facts from memory without checking. Every fact should come from a reliable source.

days.guide: The child reviews the year's topics and chooses one to promote, explaining why it matters.

questions.q: Why is your chosen topic important?
questions.a: Answer should give a health reason, e.g., 'Helmets prevent head injuries.'

days.guide: Choose an audience and list what they already know and need to know.

questions.q: How would a message for 5-year-olds differ from one for adults?
questions.a: Simpler words, more pictures, shorter sentences and fun elements for young children.

days.guide: Write a positive message (e.g., 'Wash for 20, beat the germs!') with 3 facts.

questions.q: What makes a health message 'positive'?
questions.a: It tells people what to do and the benefit, instead of only scaring them.

days.guide: Plan what goes on the poster, in the brochure and in the PSA.

questions.q: What is a PSA?
questions.a: A public service announcement: a short message to inform the public about something important for their health or safety.

days.guide: Share the plan with you; give 2 compliments and 1 suggestion; the child revises.

questions.q: Is your message clear in one sentence?
questions.a: Yes, it states one action and the benefit.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign plan rubric: 4 = names one specific health topic, a specific audience and what they need, a short positive message, 3 accurate facts with sources, and the 3 planned materials (poster, brochure, 1-minute PSA); revised after parent feedback; 3 = all parts but one fact weak or unsourced; 2 = missing 2 parts; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Poster board, markers, paper for a tri-fold brochure, a phone or tablet for recording.
misconceptions: Putting too much text on a poster. A poster needs a big slogan, a picture and only a few words.
Recording without practicing. Read the script aloud 2–3 times first.

days.guide: The child creates the poster with a catchy slogan and picture.

questions.q: What makes a slogan catchy?
questions.a: It is short, memorable and may rhyme or use rhythm, e.g., 'Buckle up, every trip!'

days.guide: Fold paper into thirds and make a brochure: cover, facts, tips and where to learn more.

questions.q: What goes on the cover of a brochure?
questions.a: The title, a picture and the main message.

days.guide: Write a PSA script: hook, problem, facts, action, slogan. Time it to about 1 minute.

questions.q: What is a 'call to action'?
questions.a: Telling the audience exactly what to do, like 'Wear your helmet every time you ride.'

days.guide: Record the PSA. Allow retakes.

questions.q: What helps a recording sound clear?
questions.a: A quiet room, speaking slowly and loudly, and practicing first.

days.guide: Check each fact against KidsHealth or MyPlate, fix errors, and practice presenting.

questions.q: Why check facts?
questions.a: So the campaign gives true information and people can trust it.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign materials rubric: 4 = poster has a readable slogan and picture; brochure is tri-fold with 3+ accurate facts and tips; PSA script is about 1 minute with a hook, facts and call to action; all facts checked against KidsHealth or MyPlate; 3 = all materials with a minor error; 2 = one material missing or several inaccuracies; 1 = mostly incomplete.

weeks.prep: Campaign materials, an audience (family, cousins, co-op). Prepare the final quiz below.
misconceptions: Thinking a presentation is finished once it's given. Asking for feedback shows whether the message worked.
Setting vague summer goals. Use SMART goals with numbers and times.

days.guide: The child presents the campaign to the chosen audience using the poster, brochure and PSA.

questions.q: What is the one action you want your audience to take?
questions.a: Answer states the campaign's call to action.

days.guide: The child asks the audience what they learned and one change they'll make, and records answers.

questions.q: Why ask for feedback?
questions.a: To find out whether the message was understood and how to improve it.

days.guide: Give the final quiz.

questions.q: How many food groups are on MyPlate?
questions.a: Five.

days.guide: The child sets 2 SMART summer health goals.

questions.q: Make 'sleep better' a SMART goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will be in bed by 8:30 p.m. at least 6 nights a week all summer.'

days.guide: The child writes a reflection on the healthiest change they made this year.

questions.q: What made the change possible?
questions.a: Answer names a strategy or support, such as a tracker, family help or a reminder.

weeks.assessment_key: Final quiz key (12 questions): 1) Five food groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy. 2) Kids need 60 minutes of activity a day. 3) On labels, check serving size first. 4) The heart is a muscle that pumps blood. 5) Calcium builds bones. 6) I-message: I feel ___ when ___ because ___. 7) Bullying is repeated, on purpose, with a power imbalance. 8) Fire: get out, stay out, crawl low. 9) 911: name, address, what happened. 10) Only take medicine from a trusted adult. 11) Nicotine is addictive; legal age 21. 12) Wash hands 20 seconds. Presentation rubric: 4 = clear voice, eye contact, accurate facts, all materials, answers questions; 3 = minor issues; 2 = reads everything, little interaction; 1 = incomplete. 10–12 = proficient.

HSS.overview: Grade 3 history-social science is the study of 'our community, then and now': local geography, the American Indian nations of your region, the explorers, missions, ranchos and settlers who followed, local and national government, American symbols and heroes, and basic economics. Many answers depend on where you live, so the parent researches the local facts a few days ahead (historical society, tribe's official website, city website) and the child works like a historian with maps, photographs, newspapers and interviews. Teach first peoples as living nations (present tense as well as past), and discuss the missions and the Gold Rush honestly, including the harm done to Native Californians, in age-appropriate language.

weeks.prep: A printed local street map, a world map, a California map and a globe. Find your town on each ahead of time. Prepare a 6-question map quiz from the local map (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking north always means 'up the hill' or 'forward.' North is a direction on Earth; on most maps it is at the top, shown by the compass rose.
Confusing the map key and the compass rose. The key (legend) explains symbols; the compass rose shows directions.

days.guide: Point out the four map parts on a printed local map. The child finds each and tells what it does.

questions.q: What does a map key (legend) do?
questions.a: It explains what the symbols and colors on the map stand for.

questions.q: What does the compass rose show?
questions.a: Directions: north, south, east and west (and often in-between directions like northeast).

days.guide: On a globe, find your continent, country, state and city. The child draws nested circles (biggest = planet Earth, then North America, United States, California, county, city, street).

questions.q: What continent and country do you live in?
questions.a: North America; the United States.

questions.q: Put in order from largest to smallest: city, state, country, continent.
questions.a: Continent, country, state, city.

days.guide: Show how grid letters and numbers locate places (like B4). Give 4 places to find and 2 sets of directions using north, south, east, west.

questions.q: On a grid with letters across the top (left to right, west to east) and numbers down the side, the park is in B3. Which square is one square east of it?
The sun rises in which direction?
questions.a: East.

days.guide: The child draws their neighborhood with a title, compass rose, key and at least 4 symbols.

questions.q: Why do maps use symbols instead of drawings of everything?
questions.a: Symbols save space and make maps easier to read.

days.guide: Give the map skills quiz and have the child explain their neighborhood map, including directions to one place.

questions.q: How would you tell someone to get from your house to the nearest park?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; the child should use street names and cardinal directions, e.g., 'Go north on Oak Street two blocks, then turn east.'

weeks.assessment_key: Map skills quiz key: 1) The title tells what the map shows. 2) The compass rose shows directions: north, south, east, west. 3) The map key/legend explains what the symbols mean. 4) The scale shows how distance on the map compares to real distance. 5) Grid location of a named place (answer from your map, e.g., 'the library is in C3'). 6) Direction from home to a place (e.g., 'the park is east of our house'). Neighborhood map rubric: 4 = title, compass rose, key with 4+ symbols, streets and landmarks in roughly correct positions, and the child explains how to get from home to one place using cardinal directions; 3 = missing one element; 2 = missing two; 1 = a drawing without map elements.

weeks.prep: A physical map of California (showing elevation colors), flour, salt and water for salt dough (2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, about 3/4 cup water), cardboard base. Look up which landforms and bodies of water are near your town.
misconceptions: Confusing a bay with a lake. A bay is part of an ocean or lake partly surrounded by land; a lake is a body of water surrounded entirely by land.
Reading physical-map colors as political borders. On a physical map, colors show elevation (green low, brown high).

days.guide: Define and sketch 10: mountain, hill, valley, plain, plateau, desert, island, peninsula, ocean, lake, river, bay. The child makes a picture dictionary.

questions.q: What is the difference between an island and a peninsula?
questions.a: An island is land completely surrounded by water; a peninsula is land surrounded by water on three sides.

questions.q: What is a valley?
questions.a: Low land between hills or mountains, often with a river.

days.guide: On the physical map, find the coast, Central Valley, Sierra Nevada and desert regions.

questions.q: Which California region is a large flat area used for farming between mountain ranges?
questions.a: The Central Valley.

questions.q: Which mountain range runs along California's eastern side?
questions.a: The Sierra Nevada.

days.guide: On a local physical map, the child names nearby landforms and water.

questions.q: What landforms and water are near your town?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., 'the Santa Monica Mountains and the Pacific Ocean' or 'the American River and the Sierra foothills.'

days.guide: Mix salt dough and shape a relief map of your region on cardboard: raise mountains, flatten valleys, carve rivers. Paint when dry.

questions.q: On your relief map, why are the mountains raised?
questions.a: To show they have higher elevation than the valleys and plains.

days.guide: The child labels a blank map of the region and writes 3–4 sentences describing it.

questions.q: What is the highest mountain in the lower 48 states, and where is it?
questions.a: Mount Whitney, in California's Sierra Nevada.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeled regional map key: map shows the four California regions — Coast (including the Coast Ranges and Pacific shoreline), Central Valley (Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys), Sierra Nevada (mountains in the east; Mount Whitney is the highest peak in the lower 48 states), and Desert (Mojave and Colorado deserts in the southeast; Death Valley has the lowest point in North America) — plus your town and its nearby landforms and water. Description is proficient if it names 3 correct local features. Rubric: 4 = all regions and local features correctly labeled with a description; 3 = one error; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Look up your town's average monthly temperatures and rainfall (weather.gov climate data or a weather website) and your water agency's 'where your water comes from' page. Resource picture cards.
misconceptions: Confusing weather and climate. Weather is today's conditions; climate is the usual pattern over many years.
Thinking water comes from the faucet or the store. Most California towns get water from rivers, reservoirs, aqueducts or groundwater wells.

days.guide: Look at the temperature and rainfall data. The child finds the warmest and wettest months and describes the climate (e.g., Mediterranean: dry summers, mild wet winters, common in coastal California).

questions.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
questions.a: Weather is the conditions on one day; climate is the usual weather pattern of a place over many years.

questions.q: In much of California, which season gets the most rain?
questions.a: Winter (summers are usually dry).

days.guide: Define natural resource: something from nature that people use. List local ones.

questions.q: Name three natural resources found in California.
questions.a: Any three: water, fertile soil, timber/forests, fish, gold and other minerals, oil, sunshine/wind.

days.guide: Read your water agency's page together and trace the path of your water on a map.

questions.q: Where does your town's drinking water come from?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., Sierra snowmelt carried by aqueduct, a local river or reservoir, the Colorado River, or groundwater wells.

days.guide: The child makes a resource map with a key of symbols.

questions.q: Why does a resource map need a key?
questions.a: So readers know what each symbol (like a tree for timber) means.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph about one resource's importance.

questions.q: Why is water such an important resource in California?
questions.a: California has dry summers and droughts, and water is needed for drinking, farming and industry.

weeks.assessment_key: Resource map and paragraph key: resource map uses a key with symbols for at least 4 local natural resources (e.g., water, farmland/soil, forests/timber, minerals, fish, oil) placed in the right areas. Paragraph rubric: 4 = names one resource, explains 2 ways the community uses it (jobs, food, drinking water, building) and why protecting it matters; 3 = one use explained; 2 = names the resource only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Search Calisphere (calisphere.org) for historic photos of your town or region; take or find current photos of the same places. Read a short page on the Los Angeles Aqueduct, Hetch Hetchy (O'Shaughnessy) Dam or Shasta Dam.
misconceptions: Thinking all changes to the land are bad or all are good. Most have both benefits (water, farms, electricity) and costs (lost habitat, flooded valleys, dried lakes).
Thinking the Central Valley was always farmland. Before irrigation, much of it was grassland, wetlands and seasonal lakes like Tulare Lake.

days.guide: Compare a historic and current photo of the same area. The child lists what changed.

questions.q: What is one change people made to the land in your photos?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., new roads, buildings, farms or a dam where there was open land.

days.guide: Read about one dam or aqueduct. Discuss its purpose and effects.

questions.q: What is an aqueduct?
questions.a: A channel or pipe that carries water a long distance, often from mountains to cities or farms.

questions.q: Name one benefit and one cost of building a dam.
questions.a: Benefit: stores water, prevents floods or makes electricity. Cost: floods a valley, harms fish like salmon, displaces people.

days.guide: Explain irrigation: bringing water to crops through canals. Look at a map of Central Valley canals.

questions.q: How did irrigation change the Central Valley?
questions.a: It turned dry grassland and wetland areas into one of the world's most productive farming regions.

days.guide: Make a cause-and-effect chart with 4 human changes and their effects.

questions.q: Cause: a city builds a freeway. What is one effect?
questions.a: Faster travel and more businesses, but also more traffic, pollution, and homes or habitat removed.

days.guide: The child writes about one positive and one negative change.

questions.q: Can one change be both positive and negative? Explain.
questions.a: Yes; a dam can provide water for people but also flood land and harm fish.

weeks.assessment_key: Cause/effect chart key: at least 4 rows, e.g., Dam built → reservoir stores water and makes electricity, but a valley floods and fish runs are blocked; Aqueduct built (Los Angeles Aqueduct, 1913) → city grows, but Owens Lake dried up; Irrigation → Central Valley becomes major farmland, but wetlands and Tulare Lake disappeared; Roads and buildings → easier travel and homes, but less habitat. Paragraph rubric: 4 = one positive and one negative change, each with a specific example and effect; 3 = both present but one vague; 2 = only one; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Choose a nearby park, river or hill for the field study; bring a notebook, pencils and a camera or phone. Prepare the Unit 1 test below.
misconceptions: Mixing up physical and human features. Physical features are natural (hills, rivers, trees); human features are made by people (roads, bridges, buildings).

days.guide: At the site, the child sketches landforms and plants and labels them.

questions.q: Name two physical features you saw.
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., a hill, a creek, oak trees, a pond.

days.guide: Find human features: roads, paths, buildings, bridges, fences.

questions.q: Is a bridge a physical or human feature?
questions.a: A human feature, built by people.

days.guide: The child draws a map of the site with title, key and compass rose.

questions.q: What direction is the main path from the parking lot?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; answer should use a cardinal direction checked with a compass or phone.

days.guide: The child presents findings with photos to the family.

questions.q: How did people change this place?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., built trails, planted lawns, added a bridge or parking lot.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test.

questions.q: Name California's four main regions.
questions.a: Coast, Central Valley, Sierra Nevada (mountains), desert.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key: 1) Compass rose shows directions. 2) Map key explains symbols. 3) Order: continent, country, state, city. 4) Island = land surrounded by water. 5) Peninsula = land surrounded by water on three sides. 6) California regions: coast, Central Valley, Sierra Nevada, desert. 7) Climate = usual weather over many years. 8) Natural resource example (water, soil, timber). 9) Where your water comes from (local answer). 10) One positive and one negative effect of a dam. Field map rubric: 4 = title, compass rose, key, and at least 3 physical and 2 human features placed accurately; 3 = missing one element; 2 = missing several; 1 = sketch only. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Find your region's original people on a California Indian territories map (e.g., at the California Indian Heritage Center or a native-land map) and visit that tribe's official website; note correct names and present-day facts. Check whether a language resource (word list or audio) is published by the tribe.
misconceptions: Speaking about California Indians only in the past tense. Native nations are still here today with governments, languages, schools and businesses.
Thinking all American Indians lived the same way. California alone had well over 100 distinct tribes with different languages and ways of life.

days.guide: Locate your region on a tribal territories map and name the people (e.g., Ohlone in the Bay Area, Chumash on the central coast, Tongva in the Los Angeles basin, Kumeyaay in San Diego, Miwok and Yokuts in the Central Valley and Sierra foothills).

questions.q: Whose homeland is your town in?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; the name of the local nation from the map, e.g., Tongva (Los Angeles) or Kumeyaay (San Diego).

questions.q: Were there many different tribes in California?
questions.a: Yes; California had more than 100 tribes speaking many different languages.

days.guide: Explain a land acknowledgment: a statement recognizing the Indigenous people of a place. The child writes 2–3 sentences in their own words.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a land acknowledgment?
questions.a: To recognize and respect the Native people who have lived on the land for thousands of years and still live here.

days.guide: Explore the tribe's official website together and list 3 things the community does today.

questions.q: Name one thing the local tribe does today.
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., runs a tribal government, holds cultural events or powwows, teaches its language, operates businesses or protects sacred sites.

days.guide: If the tribe publishes language resources, learn and practice 3–5 words; note who shared them.

questions.q: Why do many tribes work to teach their languages today?
questions.a: Many languages were nearly lost when children were forced to stop speaking them; teaching them keeps the culture alive.

days.guide: The child writes 5 facts: some then and some now.

questions.q: Write one 'then' fact and one 'now' fact.
questions.a: Answers vary by community; a 'then' fact about traditional life (food, homes) and a 'now' fact about the present community.

weeks.assessment_key: Facts summary rubric: 4 = names the local nation correctly, gives at least 3 accurate facts about traditional life (homeland, food, homes or crafts) and 2 about the present-day community (tribal government, cultural programs, language revival, events) with the source named; 3 = 3–4 facts total; 2 = only past facts or 1–2 facts; 1 = inaccurate or incomplete.

weeks.prep: A few acorns (oak trees or a store), Calisphere photographs of grinding stones (mortars and pestles), tule houses, redwood plank houses and baskets. Natural materials (sticks, grass, bark) for a model shelter.
misconceptions: Thinking acorns can be eaten raw. They contain bitter tannins that must be leached out with water.
Thinking all California Indians lived in tipis. Homes were built from local materials: tule reeds near marshes and lakes, bark or redwood planks in the north.

days.guide: Show the acorn process: gather, dry, crack and shell, grind into flour in a mortar with a pestle, leach with water to remove bitter tannins, then cook into mush or bread. Look at grinding stone photos.

questions.q: Why did people leach acorn flour with water?
questions.a: To wash out the bitter tannins so it was safe and good to eat.

questions.q: What tools were used to grind acorns?
questions.a: A stone mortar (or bedrock mortar hole) and a pestle.

days.guide: Compare photos of tule houses (marsh areas), redwood bark houses and plank houses (northwest). Discuss why materials differed.

questions.q: Why did people near marshes build houses from tule?
questions.a: Tule reeds grew plentifully in marshes and lakes, so they were the handy local material.

days.guide: Study Calisphere photos of tools and baskets: what material, what use.

questions.q: What were California Indian baskets used for?
questions.a: Gathering, storing and carrying food, cooking (with hot stones), cradles, ceremonies and trade.

questions.q: What were tools made from?
questions.a: Local materials such as stone (obsidian, chert), bone, wood, shell and plant fibers.

days.guide: The child builds a model shelter from natural materials.

questions.q: What material did you choose for your model and why?
questions.a: Answer matches a real regional house type and explains the material came from the local environment.

days.guide: The child explains how geography shaped food, shelter and clothing.

questions.q: How did geography shape daily life for first peoples?
questions.a: People used what their environment provided: acorns and game inland, fish and shellfish on the coast, tule near marshes, redwood in the north.

weeks.assessment_key: Shelter model and explanation rubric: 4 = model clearly resembles a regional house type (e.g., tule dome, cone of redwood bark, plank house) and the explanation names the region, the local material used and why it suited the climate; 3 = model and explanation with one gap; 2 = model without explanation of geography; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Borrow a collection of California Indian stories from the library (Coyote stories are common to many California tribes; note which tribe each comes from) and an Aesop fable. Look at a museum's California basketry page (e.g., California Indian Heritage Center or a university museum).
misconceptions: Calling Native stories 'just myths.' Oral traditions teach history, values and lessons and are respected parts of living cultures.
Thinking traditions stopped long ago. Many ceremonies, dances, basketry and storytelling are practiced today.

days.guide: Read a California Indian story aloud and discuss what lesson it teaches.

questions.q: What lesson does the story teach?
questions.a: Answer should be drawn from the story read, e.g., Coyote's greed or trickery gets him into trouble, teaching not to be greedy or boastful.

questions.q: Why are stories passed down orally?
questions.a: Many cultures shared history and lessons by speaking and remembering them, teaching each new generation.

days.guide: Read about one traditional ceremony (e.g., an acorn harvest celebration or a Big Time gathering) and its meaning.

questions.q: Why did communities hold ceremonies?
questions.a: To give thanks, mark seasons or harvests, celebrate, pray, and bring people together.

days.guide: Look at basketry photos: patterns, materials (willow, sedge root, bulrush), and uses. Discuss that weavers today still gather materials.

questions.q: Why are California Indian baskets considered so important?
questions.a: They were essential tools and are also works of art that carry family and cultural knowledge, still made today.

days.guide: Read an Aesop fable (e.g., The Tortoise and the Hare) and compare to the Native story in a Venn diagram.

questions.q: How are the two stories alike?
questions.a: Both use animal characters and teach a lesson or moral.

days.guide: The child writes about a tradition still practiced today.

questions.q: Name a California Indian tradition practiced today.
questions.a: Basket weaving, dances and ceremonies, storytelling, Big Time gatherings, or Chumash tomol canoe crossings.

weeks.assessment_key: Tradition writing rubric: 4 = names a specific tradition still practiced today (e.g., basket weaving, Big Times gatherings, Bear Dance, tomol canoe paddling by the Chumash), explains what it is, why it matters, and cites a source; 3 = tradition and meaning but vague; 2 = tradition named only; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: A map showing California Indian trade routes (search 'California Indian trade routes map'), household items to stand in for acorns, obsidian, shells and baskets. A present-day tribal enterprise page from a tribe's website.
misconceptions: Thinking trade only works with money. Barter trades goods directly; shell beads later served as money.
Thinking each tribe lived alone. Trade networks connected the coast, valleys, mountains and deserts.

days.guide: Read about trade networks and trace a route from the coast inland on a map.

questions.q: What might coastal people trade to mountain people?
questions.a: Shells, shell beads, dried fish or seaweed.

questions.q: What might mountain or eastern people trade to the coast?
questions.a: Obsidian (volcanic glass for tools), pine nuts, animal hides.

days.guide: Explain that the Chumash made beads from olivella shells, drilling and polishing them; strings of beads were used as money inland.

questions.q: Why were shell beads valuable inland?
questions.a: Shells came only from the coast, so they were rare inland and took much work to make.

questions.q: What is money?
questions.a: Something people agree has value and can be traded for goods and services.

days.guide: Play a barter game: each person starts with one 'resource' and must trade to get a set of 3 needed items. Discuss what was hard.

questions.q: What problem did you have when bartering?
questions.a: You had to find someone who wanted what you had and had what you wanted at the same time.

days.guide: Look at a present-day tribal business or enterprise on a tribe's website and compare to traditional trade.

questions.q: How is a tribal business today similar to traditional trade?
questions.a: Both exchange goods or services to meet the community's needs and bring in resources.

days.guide: The child writes the trade paragraph.

questions.q: Why did communities trade?
questions.a: To get things their own land didn't provide.

weeks.assessment_key: Trade paragraph rubric: 4 = explains that different regions had different resources (coast: shells, fish; mountains/east: obsidian, pine nuts; valleys: acorns, salt), gives a specific trade example, and explains that trade let communities get what their land lacked; 3 = general explanation with one example; 2 = no example; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: The government page of your local (or another California) tribe and a published tribal constitution excerpt (many are online). Chart paper for 3 columns.
misconceptions: Thinking tribes are just groups or clubs. Federally recognized tribes are sovereign nations with their own governments, laws and courts.
Thinking tribal members aren't U.S. citizens. Native Americans are citizens of their tribal nation, the United States and their state.

days.guide: Read how the tribal council is elected and what it decides.

questions.q: What is a tribal council?
questions.a: The elected leaders who govern a tribe and make decisions for it.

questions.q: Who elects the council?
questions.a: The tribe's adult voting members.

days.guide: Read short constitution excerpts; the child finds who can vote and what leaders do.

questions.q: What is a constitution?
questions.a: A written document that sets up a government and its rules.

days.guide: Discuss sovereignty: tribes govern themselves, make laws and work government-to-government with the U.S.

questions.q: What does it mean that tribes are sovereign?
questions.a: They have the right to govern themselves with their own laws and leaders.

days.guide: Make a 3-column chart of tribal, state and federal responsibilities.

questions.q: Name one thing the federal government does.
questions.a: Prints money, runs the military, makes treaties, delivers the mail.

days.guide: Ask the 6 questions; the child explains one fully in a paragraph.

questions.q: Are tribal members U.S. citizens?
questions.a: Yes; they are citizens of their tribe, the United States and their state.

weeks.assessment_key: Government chart and questions key: Chart — Tribal: elects council, makes tribal laws, runs tribal programs (housing, health, education, culture), decides membership; State (California): state laws, state highways, state parks, education rules; Federal: national defense, money, treaties and government-to-government relations with tribes. Questions: 1) A tribal council is the elected government of a tribe. 2) Members of the tribe vote (eligible adult members). 3) The council makes laws and decisions for the tribe. 4) Sovereignty means the right to govern yourselves. 5) A constitution is a written plan of government. 6) Tribal members are citizens of their tribe, the U.S. and their state. Paragraph proficient = explains one with an example.

weeks.prep: Short excerpts from a settler account (e.g., a diary or letter from the mission or Gold Rush era) and a Native account or oral history about the same period (many museum and tribal sites publish these). A timeline strip. Prepare the Unit 2 test. Parent preview: the arrival of newcomers brought disease, loss of land and violence; discuss honestly at a level fit for an 8-year-old.
misconceptions: Thinking newcomers arrived in empty land. California was home to many Native nations for thousands of years.
Thinking the story ended with loss. Native nations have survived and continue to revive languages and traditions.

days.guide: Read about the arrival of Spanish (1769 onward), Mexican (1821–1848) and American (1848 onward) newcomers; list changes each brought.

questions.q: Put in order: American, Spanish, Mexican.
questions.a: Spanish, Mexican, American.

questions.q: Name two changes Spanish newcomers brought.
questions.a: Missions and Christianity, cattle and horses, new crops like wheat, the Spanish language, and diseases.

days.guide: Read the two accounts and list differences in a T-chart.

questions.q: Why might two people describe the same event differently?
questions.a: They had different experiences, beliefs and points of view.

days.guide: Chart changes to land, food, language and daily life for local nations.

questions.q: How did grazing cattle change the land?
questions.a: Cattle ate the native grasses and plants that people gathered, making traditional food harder to find.

days.guide: Read about present-day efforts: language classes, basket weavers, ceremonies.

questions.q: What is resilience?
questions.a: The ability to keep going and recover after hard times.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test; the child presents one fact they'll remember.

questions.q: Name one way local nations keep their culture alive today.
questions.a: Language classes, basket weaving, ceremonies and dances, cultural centers, storytelling.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key: 1) Name of local nation (local answer). 2) Acorns were leached to remove bitter tannins. 3) Tule houses were built near marshes. 4) Baskets: storing, cooking, carrying. 5) Coastal people traded shells/shell beads; inland people traded obsidian. 6) Tribes are sovereign nations. 7) A tribal council is the elected government. 8) Newcomers (Spanish, Mexican, American) brought new animals, crops, religion, laws and diseases. 9) Different accounts can describe the same events differently because of perspective. 10) One way tribes keep culture alive today (language classes, basketry, ceremonies). 8–10 = proficient; plus one fact presented clearly.

weeks.prep: Search the Library of Congress for 'California as an island' maps (17th century). Read short biographies of Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo and Gaspar de Portolá, and an excerpt of Father Juan Crespí's diary.
misconceptions: Thinking explorers 'discovered' empty land. Native peoples already lived there and often met and helped explorers.
Thinking old mapmakers were careless. They drew from limited reports; some early maps showed California as an island.

days.guide: Read about Cabrillo's 1542 voyage and trace his route on a map from Mexico up the California coast.

questions.q: When did Cabrillo sail along the California coast and for which country?
questions.a: 1542, for Spain.

questions.q: What California bay did Cabrillo enter?
questions.a: San Diego Bay.

days.guide: Read about the 1769 Portolá expedition and an excerpt from Crespí's diary; list what the diary describes.

questions.q: Why did Spain send the Portolá expedition in 1769?
questions.a: To claim and settle Alta California and start missions and presidios before other countries could.

questions.q: What famous bay did Portolá's party see in 1769?
questions.a: San Francisco Bay.

days.guide: Examine an early map that shows California as an island; compare to a modern map.

questions.q: What did some early mapmakers get wrong about California?
questions.a: They drew it as an island.

questions.q: Why might they have made that mistake?
questions.a: They relied on incomplete reports from sailors and had not explored the whole coast and Gulf of California.

days.guide: The child makes an explorer trading card.

questions.q: How did the explorers affect local people?
questions.a: They claimed Native land for Spain and led the way for missions and settlers who changed and harmed Native ways of life.

days.guide: The child presents the card and answers questions.

questions.q: Which came first, Cabrillo or Portolá?
questions.a: Cabrillo (1542); Portolá came 227 years later (1769).

weeks.assessment_key: Explorer trading card key: Cabrillo — 1542; sailed for Spain north from Mexico; first European to explore the California coast, entered San Diego Bay; goal: find riches and a sea route; died during the voyage (1543). Portolá — 1769; led Spain's land expedition to settle Alta California with Father Junípero Serra; reached San Diego and Monterey area; his scouts were the first Europeans known to see San Francisco Bay; effects: led to missions and presidios that greatly changed Native life. Rubric: 4 = dates, route, goals and effects on Native people accurate; 3 = one missing; 2 = two missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A California missions map (21 missions from San Diego to Sonoma), Calisphere mission photographs. Research the mission nearest you: name, founding year and founder. Parent preview: Native people at missions faced forced labor, harsh punishment and deadly diseases; present this honestly and calmly.
misconceptions: Thinking missions were just churches. They were large farms and work centers designed to convert Native people and make them Spanish subjects.
Thinking Native people all came to the missions willingly and were content. Many were pressured or forced, could not leave freely, and resisted in many ways.

days.guide: Explain: missions (religious centers and farms run by priests), presidios (forts with soldiers), pueblos (farming towns). Sort facts about each.

questions.q: What was a presidio?
questions.a: A Spanish military fort that protected the missions and the colony.

questions.q: What was a pueblo?
questions.a: A Spanish farming town for settlers, such as Los Angeles or San José.

days.guide: Locate the nearest mission and research its founding.

questions.q: What is the mission nearest you and when was it founded?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., Mission San Diego de Alcalá (1769), Mission San Gabriel (1771), Mission Santa Barbara (1786), Mission Dolores (1776).

questions.q: How many California missions were there?

days.guide: Read about the Native experience at missions.

questions.q: How did mission life change Native people's daily lives?
questions.a: They had to work on mission farms and workshops, follow Spanish rules and religion, eat a different diet, and often could not leave; many died from European diseases.

questions.q: Why did diseases spread so quickly?
questions.a: Native people had never been exposed to European diseases like measles and smallpox, and crowded mission living helped them spread.

days.guide: Analyze a mission photograph with a see-think-wonder chart.

questions.q: What can a photograph tell a historian?
questions.a: What a place looked like at a time, buildings, clothing and activities, and clues for questions to research.

days.guide: The child writes the paragraph.

questions.q: What were the three main goals of the missions?
questions.a: Spread Christianity, make Native people Spanish subjects and workers, and help Spain hold the land.

weeks.assessment_key: Mission paragraph rubric: 4 = topic sentence; explains the mission's purpose (spread Christianity, make Native people Spanish subjects, claim land); gives 2 specific changes to the region (farming, cattle, buildings) and 2 effects on first peoples (forced labor, loss of language and culture, disease, population loss); concluding sentence; 3 = 3 of these details; 2 = 1–2 details; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Search Calisphere for 'diseño' (hand-drawn rancho maps). A local street map to find Spanish or rancho names. Read a short page on ranchos and the hide and tallow trade.
misconceptions: Thinking ranchos were small family farms. They were huge land grants (often thousands of acres) used mainly for cattle.
Thinking vaqueros were cowboys from the American West. Vaqueros were Mexican and Native horsemen whose skills later shaped the American cowboy.

days.guide: Read about Mexican land grants (after Mexico's independence in 1821 and the end of the missions in the 1830s) and vaquero work.

questions.q: When did California become part of Mexico?
questions.a: In 1821, when Mexico won independence from Spain.

questions.q: What did vaqueros do?
questions.a: Rode horses to herd, rope and care for cattle on ranchos.

days.guide: Look at a diseño and find landmarks used as boundaries (trees, rocks, creeks).

questions.q: What did diseños use to mark boundaries?
questions.a: Natural landmarks such as creeks, hills, trees and rocks.

days.guide: Explain the hide and tallow trade: hides (called 'California banknotes') and tallow (fat for candles and soap) were traded to ships for manufactured goods.

questions.q: What is tallow and what was it used for?
questions.a: Cattle fat, used to make candles and soap.

questions.q: What did rancheros get in return for hides?
questions.a: Manufactured goods like cloth, shoes, tools, furniture and dishes.

days.guide: Find rancho or Spanish place names on a local map and research one.

questions.q: What does a Spanish place name near you mean?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., Los Angeles = 'the angels', Sacramento = 'sacrament', Rancho Cucamonga named for a rancho.

days.guide: The child writes how the rancho economy worked and what remains.

questions.q: Name one rancho tradition that remains today.
questions.a: Rodeos, Spanish place names, ranch-style architecture, vaquero riding and roping skills.

weeks.assessment_key: Rancho explanation rubric: 4 = explains that after 1821 the Mexican government granted large ranchos; cattle were raised mainly for hides and tallow; vaqueros (many of them Native Californians) worked the cattle; hides and tallow were traded to ships (often from Boston) for goods like cloth, tools and furniture; and names a place name or tradition that remains (e.g., rodeo, a Rancho name on a street or city); 3 = most parts; 2 = some parts; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Gold Rush photographs and letters from Calisphere or the Library of Congress. Prepare the Unit 3 test below.
misconceptions: Thinking most miners got rich. Most found little gold; many who prospered sold supplies or services.
Thinking only Americans came. People arrived from China, Mexico, Chile, Europe, Hawaii and elsewhere; free and enslaved African Americans came too.

days.guide: Read about James Marshall's discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill in Coloma in January 1848 and the 1849 rush.

questions.q: Where and when was gold discovered?
questions.a: At Sutter's Mill in Coloma, January 1848.

questions.q: What were the people who came in 1849 called?
questions.a: Forty-niners.

days.guide: Read about Chinese, Mexican, Chilean and African American communities and their contributions.

questions.q: Name one contribution of Chinese immigrants in Gold Rush California.
questions.a: Mining, running businesses like restaurants and laundries, and later building the transcontinental railroad.

questions.q: Were newcomers always treated fairly?
questions.a: No. Many, such as Chinese and Mexican miners, faced unfair taxes (the Foreign Miners' Tax) and discrimination.

days.guide: Analyze a miner's letter or daguerreotype: 3 observations, 2 questions.

questions.q: What is a daguerreotype?
questions.a: An early type of photograph made on a metal plate.

days.guide: Build a timeline of newcomers to your region.

questions.q: When did California become a state?

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: Who found gold at Sutter's Mill?
questions.a: James Marshall.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) Cabrillo explored the coast in 1542 for Spain. 2) Portolá's 1769 expedition began Spanish settlement. 3) Mission, presidio, pueblo = church/farm, fort, town. 4) 21 missions. 5) Missions forced great changes on Native people: labor, religion, disease. 6) Mexico ruled California from 1821. 7) Ranchos raised cattle for hides and tallow. 8) Gold was found at Sutter's Mill (Coloma) in January 1848 by James Marshall. 9) Gold Rush newcomers came from around the world (China, Mexico, Chile, etc.). 10) California became a state in 1850. Timeline proficient: first peoples → Spanish explorers (1542) → missions (1769) → Mexican era (1821) → Gold Rush (1848) → statehood (1850) → later local arrivals. 8–10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Your local historical society website, a historic map of your town (Sanborn map at the Library of Congress or a historic USGS topo map from TopoView) and a current map. Research your town's founding year and reason.
misconceptions: Thinking towns appear randomly. Most began where there was water, a harbor, a railroad stop, good farmland or a mine.

days.guide: Research when and why your town was founded.

questions.q: Why was your town founded where it is?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., a railroad stop, near a river for water, a harbor for ships, farmland or a mine.

questions.q: Why were many towns founded along railroads?
questions.a: Railroads brought people and supplies and let farmers and businesses ship goods.

days.guide: Read about 2 founders and their contributions.

questions.q: What did one founder contribute?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; answer names a person/family and a specific contribution (built a store, mill, church, laid out streets).

days.guide: Compare a historic and current map; list 3 changes.

questions.q: Name one change between the old and new maps.
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., more streets, a freeway, a creek channeled, farms turned into neighborhoods.

days.guide: Start a community timeline with founding events.

questions.q: What goes on a timeline?
questions.a: Events placed in order with their dates.

days.guide: The child writes the founding paragraph.

questions.q: What geographic feature helped your town grow?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; e.g., a river, harbor, flat valley land or a mountain pass.

weeks.assessment_key: Founding paragraph rubric: 4 = gives the founding year, the main reason (e.g., railroad, farming, port, mining), how geography helped (river, harbor, flat land), and names a founder or founding group, citing the historical society; 3 = reason and year without geography; 2 = vague; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) search for your town or county newspaper (choose a short article ahead). 3 historic photos from Calisphere. A camera for the then-and-now photo. Ten source cards.
misconceptions: Thinking a textbook is a primary source. Primary sources were made by people at the time (diaries, letters, photos); secondary sources are written later about the past.

days.guide: Sort 10 sources into primary and secondary.

questions.q: Is a diary written in 1850 a primary or secondary source?
questions.a: Primary.

questions.q: Is an encyclopedia article about the Gold Rush primary or secondary?
questions.a: Secondary.

days.guide: Analyze 3 historic photos with see-think-wonder.

questions.q: What clues in a photo help you guess when it was taken?
questions.a: Clothing, cars or wagons, buildings, signs, technology and whether it is black-and-white.

days.guide: Read a short historic newspaper article together and summarize it.

questions.q: What can an old newspaper tell us?
questions.a: What happened and what people thought was important at that time, plus ads showing prices and goods.

days.guide: Go to the spot of a historic photo and take a matching photo.

questions.q: Why take the photo from the same spot?
questions.a: So the two photos can be compared fairly to see what changed.

days.guide: The child writes what changed and stayed the same, citing both photos.

questions.q: Name something that often stays the same over 100 years.
questions.a: Hills, rivers or mountains, and sometimes old buildings or street layouts.

weeks.assessment_key: Then-and-now comparison rubric: 4 = new photo taken from nearly the same spot; writing names at least 2 changes and 1 thing that stayed the same, pointing to specific details in each photo; 3 = 1 change and 1 sameness; 2 = general statements; 1 = incomplete. Sort key for Day 1: diary, letter, photo, newspaper from the time, map from the time = primary; textbook, encyclopedia, biography written later, documentary = secondary.

weeks.prep: A recording device (phone), an interview question sheet; arrange a time with an older relative or neighbor.
misconceptions: Asking yes/no questions. Open-ended questions ('What was school like?') get stories.
Interrupting. Listen fully, then ask a follow-up.

days.guide: The child writes 10 open-ended questions.

questions.q: Change 'Did you like your town?' into an open-ended question.
questions.a: Example: 'What did you like most about the town when you were growing up?'

days.guide: Conduct and record the interview with permission.

questions.q: Why ask permission to record?
questions.a: It's respectful and the person has the right to decide.

days.guide: Listen to the recording and note the 5 most important details.

questions.q: What makes a detail 'important'?
questions.a: It tells how the community was or how it changed, or is a meaningful personal story.

days.guide: Share 3 stories at dinner.

questions.q: Is an oral history a primary or secondary source?
questions.a: Primary; it's a firsthand account.

days.guide: The child writes the summary and adds events to the timeline.

questions.q: What is one way the community changed according to your interview?
questions.a: Answers vary by community; answer cites the interviewee.

weeks.assessment_key: Oral history summary rubric: 4 = one page naming who was interviewed, when, and their connection to the community; 5 important details in the child's own words; at least one comparison of then and now; key events added to the timeline; 3 = 3–4 details; 2 = 1–2 details; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Local business histories (historical society, chamber of commerce 'history' pages, company websites), historic photos of early stores, mills, canneries or farms.
misconceptions: Thinking a business needs no risk. Entrepreneurs risk their own money and time with no guarantee of success.

days.guide: Research 3 early businesses in town.

questions.q: What did a general store do?
questions.a: Sold many kinds of goods (food, tools, cloth) to the community in one place.

days.guide: Read about one local entrepreneur and the risks taken.

questions.q: What is an entrepreneur?
questions.a: A person who starts a business and takes a risk to make a profit.

questions.q: Name one risk an entrepreneur takes.
questions.a: Losing the money they invested if the business fails.

days.guide: Discuss private property: when people own land and businesses, they have reasons to build, improve and invest.
