Proficient: 5+/6 and a bar-model explanation with both steps labeled.

weeks.prep: Addition table (0–10) and multiplication table (0–10), colored pencils. Write the Unit 5 test and a 20-fact mixed check.
misconceptions: Believing odd × odd is even — test examples: 3 × 5 = 15 is odd.
Naming an input/output rule from only one pair — check the rule against every row.

days.guide: The child tests many examples and fills a chart for even + even, even + odd, odd + odd, then the same for products, and states the rules. Ask the child to explain why the rule works using pairs (an odd number always has one left over).

questions.q: Is odd + odd even or odd? Give an example.
Is even × odd even or odd?

days.guide: Color patterns in the addition table (equal sums along diagonals, rows increasing by 1). The child writes 3 rules.

questions.q: What happens moving down one column of the addition table?
questions.a: Each sum increases by 1.

questions.q: Along a diagonal from bottom-left to top-right, what stays the same?
questions.a: The sums are all equal (3 + 5, 4 + 4, 5 + 3 all equal 8).

days.guide: Fill in input/output tables and name each rule (× 4, + 7, ÷ 5 …). Check the rule on every pair.

questions.q: In: 2, 3, 5 → Out: 8, 12, 20. What is the rule, and what is the output for 7?
In: 10, 15, 20 → Out: 2, 3, 4. What is the rule?

days.guide: The child writes why 4 times any number is even: 4 × n = 2 × (2 × n), so it is a double, and doubles are always even. Ask them to test the rule with three numbers, including an odd one, before writing.

questions.q: Why is 4 × 7 even?
questions.a: 4 × 7 = 2 × 14 — a double — and doubles are even, so 28 is even.

questions.q: Is 4 × 9 even?
questions.a: Yes, 36.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test plus the 20-fact mixed check. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Is odd × odd even or odd?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test: 1) 4 packs of 6 juice boxes, 5 drunk → 19 2) $40 − 3 × $8 → $16 3) Equation with a letter for #2 → m = 40 − 3 × 8 4) 7 + 9 even or odd → even 5) 5 × 7 even or odd → odd 6) In 1, 2, 3 → Out 6, 12, 18: rule × 6, output for 5 = 30 7) Why is 2 × any number even? → it is a double. Proficient: 6+/7 and 18+/20 facts.

weeks.prep: Paper rectangles, circles and squares; scissors; 12-inch paper strips (6 per child) for fraction strips; markers; an envelope to store strips.
misconceptions: Calling unequal parts 'fourths' — fractions need equal parts; cut and stack the parts to compare.
Thinking a larger denominator means a bigger piece — 1/8 is smaller than 1/4 because the whole is cut into more parts.

days.guide: Fold rectangles and circles into halves, thirds (fold into a Z), fourths, sixths and eighths. Count the parts and name them.

questions.q: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. What is one slice called?
questions.a: One sixth (1/6).

questions.q: How many fourths make a whole?

days.guide: Label each part with a unit fraction 1/b. Show a circle cut into 4 unequal parts and ask if each part is 1/4.

questions.q: Is a shape cut into 3 unequal pieces showing thirds?
questions.a: No — thirds must be 3 equal parts.

questions.q: What does the 8 in 1/8 tell you?
questions.a: The whole is cut into 8 equal parts.

days.guide: Partition paper squares into fourths three ways (4 strips, 4 small squares, 4 triangles using both diagonals). Cut and overlay to prove each part has equal area.

questions.q: Can triangle-shaped fourths and strip-shaped fourths of the same square be equal?
questions.a: Yes — each is 1/4 of the same square, so each has the same area even though the shapes differ.

questions.q: A square made of 16 small squares is split into 4 equal parts. How many small squares are in each part?

days.guide: Make strips all the same length: whole, halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths; label every piece. Save them in an envelope for the unit.

questions.q: Which is longer, 1/3 or 1/6?
How many eighths fit on one half?

days.guide: Give the 10-item identification check. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Draw a rectangle and shade 1/5.
questions.a: A rectangle split into 5 equal parts with 1 part shaded.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) Circle in 2 equal parts, 1 shaded → 1/2 2) Rectangle in 4, 1 shaded → 1/4 3) Hexagon in 6 → 1/6 4) Bar in 8 → 1/8 5) Triangle in 3 equal parts → 1/3 6) Square in 4 unequal parts → 'not fourths — the parts aren't equal' 7–10) Draw 1/2, 1/3, 1/6, 1/8 with equal parts. Proficient: 9+/10.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips from last week, pattern blocks (or printed paper ones), 8 counters in two colors.
misconceptions: Reading 3/4 as '3 and 4' — say '3 fourths,' meaning 3 pieces of size 1/4.
Writing the unshaded count as the numerator — the numerator counts the parts being described (shaded).

days.guide: Join three 1/4 strips and say '1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 is 3 fourths, 3/4.' Build 5/6 and 2/3 the same way.

questions.q: How many 1/6 pieces make 5/6?
What is 2/3 made of?
questions.a: Two 1/3 pieces.

days.guide: Use the yellow hexagon as 1 whole: trapezoid = 1/2, blue rhombus = 1/3, triangle = 1/6. Build fractions like 2/3 (2 rhombuses).

questions.q: How many triangles cover the hexagon, and what fraction is one triangle?
What fraction of the hexagon do 2 rhombuses cover?

days.guide: Line up 8 counters with 3 red: 3/8 are red. Change colors to show other fractions of the set.

questions.q: 8 counters, 3 red. What fraction are red? Not red?
questions.a: 3/8 red; 5/8 not red.

questions.q: 4 of 8 counters are blue. What fraction is blue?
questions.a: 4/8 (also equal to 1/2).

days.guide: Draw pizzas and chocolate bars to solve fraction stories. Ask the child to say what the whole is and how many equal parts it has before writing each fraction.

questions.q: Ana ate 3 of 8 equal slices. What fraction did she eat? What fraction is left?
questions.a: 3/8 eaten; 5/8 left.

questions.q: A bar has 6 equal parts and Ben ate 4. What fraction did he eat?

days.guide: Give 12 shaded models to name and 4 fractions to draw. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Draw 2/5.
questions.a: A whole split into 5 equal parts with 2 shaded.

weeks.prep: Number line strips (0 to 1 and 0 to 2), a ruler marked in halves and fourths of an inch.
misconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of spaces (calling the first mark 1/5 on a line split into 4) — count the jumps (intervals), not the lines.
Starting at 1 instead of 0 — every fraction is a distance from 0.

days.guide: Fold a 0-to-1 strip into 4 equal parts, then mark and label 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4. Repeat for thirds, sixths and eighths.

questions.q: A 0–1 line is split into 3 equal spaces. Label the marks.
How many spaces are needed to show eighths from 0 to 1?

days.guide: Locate 3/4 by counting 3 jumps of 1/4 from 0. Then locate 5/8 and 2/3.

questions.q: How do you find 5/8 on a number line?
questions.a: Split 0 to 1 into 8 equal spaces and count 5 spaces from 0.

questions.q: Is 2/3 closer to 0 or to 1?
questions.a: Closer to 1.

days.guide: Extend lines to 2 and keep counting fourths past 1 (5/4, 6/4, 7/4, 8/4 = 2). Do the same with thirds: 6/3 = 2.

questions.q: Where is 5/4?
questions.a: One fourth past 1.

questions.q: What whole number equals 6/3?

days.guide: Look at a ruler: each inch is a 0-to-1 number line split into halves and fourths. Find 1/2 in, 1 1/4 in and 2 3/4 in.

questions.q: On a ruler, what is halfway between 0 and 1 inch?
questions.a: 1/2 inch.

questions.q: How many fourths of an inch are in 1 inch?

days.guide: Give 10 fractions to place; the child explains how they located two of them. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Explain how you placed 3/6.
questions.a: I split 0 to 1 into 6 equal spaces and counted 3 from 0 — it lands halfway.

weeks.assessment_key: Place: 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/3, 2/3, 5/6, 3/8, 7/8, 4/4 (at 1), 6/4 (halfway between 1 and 2). Each must be on a line divided into the correct number of equal spaces, counted from 0. Proficient: 9+/10 plus a clear explanation of two placements.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips and stacked number lines (halves, fourths, eighths, all the same length). Make matching cards: 1/2 & 2/4, 1/2 & 4/8, 1/3 & 2/6, 3/4 & 6/8, 1 & 4/4, 2 & 4/2, 3 & 3/1.
misconceptions: Thinking 2/4 is bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger — lay the strips side by side to show they cover the same length.
Thinking whole numbers can't be fractions — 4/4 = 1 and 3/1 = 3.

days.guide: Lay down the 1/2 strip and find other strips that exactly match its length (2/4, 3/6, 4/8). Do the same for 1/3 and 3/4.

questions.q: Name 3 fractions equal to 1/2.
What fraction in sixths equals 1/3?

days.guide: Stack 0–1 lines for halves, fourths and eighths so the 0s and 1s line up. Draw vertical lines through points that match.

questions.q: Which fourths and eighths line up with 1/2?
How many eighths equal 3/4?

days.guide: Show 3 wholes, each as one piece: 3 = 3/1. Show one whole cut into 4: 4/4 = 1; cut into 6: 6/6 = 1.

questions.q: Write 1 as a fraction with denominator 6.
Write 4 as a fraction.

days.guide: Play memory with the equivalent fraction cards; for each match the child proves it with strips or a number line. Make cards for 1/2, 2/4, 4/8, 1/3, 2/6, 3/4, 6/8, 1, 4/4, 2 and 4/2 before starting.

questions.q: Is 2/3 equivalent to 4/6? Explain.
questions.a: Yes — 4 sixths cover the same length as 2 thirds.

questions.q: Is 3/4 equivalent to 3/8?
questions.a: No — eighths are smaller, so 3/8 is less than 3/4.

days.guide: Give the 10-item quiz with strips available for drawing. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips, paper fraction circles, index cards with fractions for fraction war (use denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, 8).
misconceptions: Thinking 1/6 > 1/3 because 6 > 3 — with the same numerator, a bigger denominator means smaller pieces.
Comparing fractions of different-size wholes — half of a large pizza can be more than half of a small one, so compare only with the same whole.

days.guide: Compare 3/8 and 5/8 with strips: the pieces are the same size, so more pieces is more. Record with <, >, =.

questions.q: Compare 3/8 and 5/8.
questions.a: 3/8 < 5/8 — same-size pieces, and 5 pieces is more.

questions.q: Compare 4/6 and 2/6.

days.guide: Compare 2/3 and 2/6: the same number of pieces, but thirds are bigger. Show with circles.

questions.q: Compare 2/3 and 2/6.
questions.a: 2/3 > 2/6 — thirds are bigger pieces than sixths.

questions.q: Compare 1/8 and 1/4.

days.guide: Draw a big pizza and a small pizza; shade 1/2 of the small one and 1/4 of the big one. Ask which is more pizza — it can be the 1/4! Conclude that comparisons only work with same-size wholes.

questions.q: Is 1/2 always more than 1/4?
questions.a: Only when the wholes are the same size.

questions.q: Why must we compare fractions of the same whole?
questions.a: Because the size of each piece depends on the size of the whole.

days.guide: Play fraction war: each flips a card; compare only pairs with the same numerator or same denominator (flip again otherwise). The child draws to justify each win.

questions.q: Compare 3/4 and 3/6.
questions.a: 3/4 > 3/6 — fourths are bigger than sixths.

questions.q: Compare 5/6 and 6/6.
questions.a: 5/6 < 6/6 (6/6 is one whole).

days.guide: Give 12 comparisons; the child justifies 3 in writing. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Justify 2/4 < 2/3.
questions.a: Same numerator; thirds are bigger pieces than fourths, so 2 thirds is more than 2 fourths.

weeks.prep: Measuring cups (1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 cup), a simple recipe card (e.g., pancakes), a garden rectangle drawing, 3 stations set up (number line, comparing, equivalence). Write 5 worked problems with errors for Thursday and the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Thinking a 1/4 cup holds more than a 1/3 cup — fill each and pour into a 1-cup measure to compare.
In error analysis, accepting a larger denominator as a larger fraction — recheck with strips.

days.guide: Read the recipe and measure 1/2, 3/4 and 1/3 cup amounts with water or flour. Ask how many 1/4 cups make 3/4 cup.

questions.q: How many 1/4 cups make 3/4 cup?
How many 1/2 cups make 1 cup?

days.guide: Draw a garden rectangle and split it into 4 or 6 equal plots; label each as a unit fraction of the whole garden. Ask the child to prove the plots are equal by counting squares or measuring.

questions.q: A garden is split into 6 equal plots and 2 are tomatoes. What fraction is tomatoes?
questions.a: 2/6 (equal to 1/3).

questions.q: Each of 4 equal beds is what fraction of the garden?

days.guide: Rotate through the three stations, about 12 minutes each; check work together at the end. Circulate between stations and ask the child to explain one answer at each.

questions.q: Place 3/4 and 1/2 on a 0–1 line. Which is farther right?

days.guide: Show 5 worked problems with mistakes (e.g., '1/6 > 1/3', '3/4 is between 1 and 2', '2/4 is not equal to 1/2'). The child finds and fixes each.

questions.a: 1/6 < 1/3 — sixths are smaller pieces.

questions.q: Fix: 2/4 is not equal to 1/2.
questions.a: 2/4 = 1/2 — they cover the same length on a strip.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Which is greater, 2/8 or 2/4?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test: 1) 1 of 3 equal parts shaded → 1/3 2) 5 of 8 → 5/8 3) Place 2/4 on a 0–1 number line → halfway 4) 6/6 = 1 5) 4/2 = 2 6) 1/2 = 3/6 7) 2/3 = 4/6 8) 3/8 < 5/8 9) 2/3 > 2/6 10) Why can 1/4 of a big pizza be more than 1/2 of a small pizza? → the wholes are different sizes. Proficient: 8+/10.

weeks.prep: Analog clock with movable hands (or a paper-plate clock), open number line paper. Write the time quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Reading the hour hand wrong near the next hour (saying 3:55 is 4:55) — the hour hand points to the hour it has most recently passed.
Treating an hour like 100 minutes (2:50 to 3:10 = 60 minutes) — jump to the next hour on a number line: 10 + 10 = 20 minutes.

days.guide: Count by 5s around the clock then add ones (7:23 is 4 fives + 3 past 7). The child reads and sets 15 times.

questions.q: The hour hand is just past 4; the minute hand is 2 marks past the 7. What time is it?
Show 9:52. Where is the hour hand?
questions.a: Almost at the 10 (between 9 and 10).

days.guide: Use an open number line: 2:45 → 3:00 is 15 min, 3:00 → 3:20 is 20 min; total 35 min. The child solves 8 problems.

questions.q: How long from 2:45 to 3:20?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

questions.q: How long from 10:15 to 11:05?
questions.a: 50 minutes.

days.guide: For an unknown end time, jump forward; for an unknown start time, jump backward. Model one of each on the number line, then the child solves 6 problems, checking each by counting forward from the start time.

questions.q: Practice started at 4:20 and lasted 45 minutes. When did it end?
A show ended at 7:10 after 50 minutes. When did it start?

days.guide: The child records the start and end times of 5 activities in their day and finds the length of each. Have the child draw a number line for any activity that crosses the hour.

questions.q: Lunch was 12:05 to 12:40. How long?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

questions.q: Reading was 1:50 to 2:25. How long?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

days.guide: Give the time quiz. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: How many minutes are in an hour?

weeks.assessment_key: 1) Read a clock showing 3:47 2) Read 11:08 3) Draw hands for 6:34 (hour hand a bit past halfway between 6 and 7) 4) 8:15 to 8:50 → 35 min 5) 1:40 to 2:15 → 35 min 6) Start 9:25, lasts 40 min → ends 10:05 7) Ends 4:00 after 25 min → started 3:35 8) 10:50 to 11:30 → 40 min. Proficient: 7+/8.

weeks.prep: A 1-liter bottle, measuring cups, 5 household containers (mug, pot, vase …), water, a towel. Sketch beaker diagrams with scales counting by 1, 2 and 5 liters.
misconceptions: Thinking taller containers always hold more — pour between a tall thin container and a short wide one.
Misreading scales (counting each mark as 1 L when marks are 2 L apart) — find what each space is worth first.

days.guide: Fill a 1-liter bottle. Show household containers and ask 'More or less than 1 liter?', then test by pouring.

questions.q: Does a bathtub hold more or less than 1 liter?
questions.a: Much more.

questions.q: Does a teacup hold more or less than 1 liter?
questions.a: Less.

days.guide: Use the liter bottle (marked at 1/2 and 1/4 if possible) to measure 5 containers; record results in a table. Have the child estimate before each measurement and record both numbers in the table.

questions.q: A pot holds 3 full liter bottles of water. What is its capacity?
questions.a: 3 liters.

questions.q: A vase holds about half a bottle. About how much is that?
questions.a: About 1/2 liter.

days.guide: Read beaker diagrams: find the scale first, then read the level. Model one diagram aloud ('the marks go up by 2, so this line is 6'), then the child reads 6 more.

questions.q: Marks go 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 L and the water is at the second mark above 0. How much water?
Marks go by 5 L and the water is halfway between 10 and 15. About how much?
questions.a: About 12 1/2 L.

days.guide: Solve liquid-volume word problems by drawing. Have the child draw jugs or bars for each problem and write an equation with units (L).

questions.q: 4 jugs hold 3 L each. How much in all?
A 20 L tank has 7 L used. How much is left?

days.guide: Give the quiz and an estimation challenge: the child guesses each container's capacity, then measures. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: A 9 L bucket is filled 3 L per trip. How many trips?

weeks.assessment_key: 1) Spoon: more or less than 1 L → less; kitchen sink → more 2) Read a scale (marks by 2) showing 6 L → 6 L 3) 5 bottles × 2 L → 10 L 4) 18 L shared into 3 jugs → 6 L each 5) 15 L + 8 L → 23 L 6) 40 L − 26 L → 14 L. Proficient: 5+/6; estimation is proficient if the child uses the 1-liter benchmark and estimates are reasonable.

weeks.prep: Kitchen scale (grams), paper clips, a 1 kg bag of rice or flour, a coat hanger with string and two paper cups for a balance. Write the Unit 7 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: Thinking bigger objects always have more mass — compare a large balloon with a small rock.
Mixing up grams and kilograms — a paper clip is about 1 gram; a 1 kg bag of rice is 1,000 grams.

days.guide: Hold a paper clip (about 1 g) and the 1 kg bag. Estimate 8 objects and say whether each is better measured in grams or kilograms.

questions.q: Would you measure a pencil in grams or kilograms?
questions.a: Grams.

questions.q: Would you measure a dog in grams or kilograms?
questions.a: Kilograms.

days.guide: Weigh 8 objects on the kitchen scale and compare with the estimates. Have the child record estimate and actual mass side by side and circle the closest estimate.

questions.q: How many grams are in 1 kilogram?
An apple is about 200 g. Is that more or less than 1 kg?
questions.a: Less.

days.guide: Build a hanger balance with a cup on each end and compare two objects; the lower side is heavier. Ask the child to predict which side will go down before placing each pair.

questions.q: Which side of a balance goes down?
questions.a: The side with more mass.

questions.q: If the balance is level, what do you know?
questions.a: The two masses are equal.

days.guide: Solve one-step mass word problems. Have the child draw a simple picture and write an equation with units for each problem.

questions.q: 3 bags of apples have a mass of 4 kg each. What is the total mass?
questions.a: 12 kg.

questions.q: A box has a mass of 45 kg. 18 kg is removed. What is its mass now?
questions.a: 27 kg.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Is 500 grams more or less than 1 kilogram?
questions.a: Less — it is half a kilogram.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test: 1) Read 2:38 2) 3:15 to 3:55 → 40 min 3) Starts 5:40, lasts 35 min → 6:15 4) More or less than 1 L: drinking glass → less; bathtub → more 5) 6 jugs × 2 L → 12 L 6) 24 L ÷ 4 → 6 L 7) Grams or kilograms: paper clip → grams; bicycle → kilograms 8) 9 kg + 6 kg → 15 kg 9) 50 g − 18 g → 32 g 10) 4 bags × 5 kg → 20 kg. Proficient: 8+/10.

weeks.prep: Grid paper, a survey tally sheet, a sample picture graph where one symbol = 5. Draw the pets bar graph from the answer key for Friday.
misconceptions: Counting symbols instead of using the key (3 stars = 3 instead of 15) — always read the key first.
Bar graph scales that skip unevenly — number the axis by the same amount at every line.

days.guide: Show a picture graph with ★ = 5 votes. Ask how much each row is worth, skip counting by 5s for each star. The child answers 6 questions.

questions.q: ★ = 5. Apples has 4 stars. How many votes?
Bananas has 2 stars and apples has 4. How many more votes for apples?

days.guide: The child surveys 10–20 family members and friends about their favorite fruit and records tallies. Show how to make a tally chart with one row per fruit and remind them to ask each person only once.

questions.q: What number does a bundle of 5 tally marks plus 3 more show?
Why do we group tallies in 5s?
questions.a: It makes counting faster — you can count by 5s.

days.guide: Draw a bar graph with a scale of 2 (axis labeled 0, 2, 4, 6 …). Bars for odd numbers end halfway between lines. Add a title and labels.

questions.q: On a scale of 2, where does a bar for 7 end?
questions.a: Halfway between 6 and 8.

questions.q: What does a bar graph need?
questions.a: A title, category labels, a numbered scale and axis labels.

days.guide: Ask one- and two-step comparison questions from the child's graph. Have the child write an equation for each answer (12 − 7 = 5).

questions.q: Apples 12, grapes 7, bananas 5. How many more chose apples than grapes?
How many fewer chose bananas than apples and grapes together?

days.guide: The child interprets the new graph in the answer key and makes a picture graph with a key from their survey. Check that the picture graph's key is used correctly for every row.

questions.q: If ● = 4, how many does ●●● show?

weeks.assessment_key: Graph (bar graph, scale of 2): Pets — dogs 8, cats 6, fish 4, birds 2. 1) Most popular → dogs 2) Number of cats → 6 3) How many more dogs than fish → 4 4) Total → 20 5) How many more dogs and cats together than fish and birds together → 14 − 6 = 8. Picture graph: proficient if it has a title, a key, and the right number of symbols for each category.

weeks.prep: A ruler marked in 1/2 and 1/4 inches, 15 leaves or pencils, a line-plot template. Write the Unit 8 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: Starting at the end of the ruler instead of 0 — line the object up with the 0 mark.
An unevenly spaced line plot — mark 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1 … with equal spaces.

days.guide: Measure drawn lines to the nearest half and quarter inch; name the marks 1/4, 2/4 (= 1/2) and 3/4. Model lining up the end of the line at 0 and counting quarter marks after the last whole inch.

questions.q: A line ends at the third quarter mark after 2 inches. How long is it?
questions.a: 2 3/4 inches.

questions.q: What is 2/4 inch also called?
questions.a: 1/2 inch.

days.guide: The child measures 15 leaves or pencils to the nearest 1/4 inch and lists the measurements. Have the child record each measurement in a list so the data can be plotted tomorrow.

questions.q: A leaf ends between 3 1/4 and 3 1/2 inches but closer to 3 1/2. What do you record?
questions.a: 3 1/2 inches.

questions.q: Why do we line up the object at 0?
questions.a: So we measure the length from the very start.

days.guide: Draw a number line scaled in fourths that covers the range of the data; place one X for each measurement. Model the first two Xs, stacking repeated values neatly above the same mark.

questions.q: What does each X on a line plot stand for?
questions.a: One measurement.

questions.q: If four leaves are 4 1/4 inches, how many Xs go above 4 1/4?

days.guide: Answer questions about the line plot. Have the child count Xs to answer each question and point to the line plot as evidence.

questions.q: Data: 3, 3 1/4, 3 1/4, 3 1/2, 4. What is the most common length?
questions.a: 3 1/4 inches.

questions.q: What is the longest minus the shortest?
questions.a: 4 − 3 = 1 inch.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What is a line plot used for?
questions.a: To show how often each measurement occurs.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test: 1) ★ = 10; 3 stars → 30 2) 2 1/2 stars when ★ = 10 → 25 3) Bar graph: soccer 35, baseball 20 — how many more chose soccer? → 15 4) Measure a 2 1/4-inch line → 2 1/4 in 5) Line plot data 1, 1 1/4, 1 1/4, 1 1/2, 1 1/2, 1 1/2: most common → 1 1/2 in 6) How many measurements → 6 7) Longest − shortest → 1/2 inch. Proficient: 6+/7.

weeks.prep: Shape cards (draw and cut squares, rectangles, rhombuses, trapezoids, kites, triangles, pentagons, hexagons), a geoboard with rubber bands or dot paper. Write the quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Thinking a square is not a rectangle — a square has 4 right angles, so it is a special rectangle.
Thinking a tilted square is a 'diamond', not a square — rotate the card; attributes, not position, define a shape.

days.guide: Sort shape cards by number of sides, then by right angles, then by parallel sides; name each sorting rule. Ask the child to say the attribute out loud each time they place a card in a group.

questions.q: How many sides does a quadrilateral have?
Which shapes have 4 right angles?
questions.a: Squares and rectangles.

days.guide: Make a chart: quadrilaterals → rectangles (4 right angles) and rhombuses (4 equal sides); squares belong in both groups. Draw it as nested circles or a family tree, and have the child place a square card in every group it belongs to.

questions.q: Why is a square a rhombus?
questions.a: It has 4 equal sides.

questions.q: Why is a rectangle a quadrilateral?
questions.a: It has 4 sides.

days.guide: Build quadrilaterals on a geoboard that are not rectangles, rhombuses or squares (trapezoid, kite, irregular). Have the child count sides and check right angles with a paper corner to prove each shape fits.

questions.q: Name a quadrilateral that is not a rectangle, rhombus or square.
questions.a: A trapezoid (or a kite, or any irregular 4-sided shape).

questions.q: Is a trapezoid a quadrilateral?
questions.a: Yes — it has 4 sides.

days.guide: Discuss statements as always, sometimes or never true and justify each. Have the child draw an example or counterexample to support each answer.

questions.q: 'A square is a rhombus.'
questions.a: Always — it has 4 equal sides.

questions.q: 'A rectangle is a square.'
questions.a: Sometimes — only when all 4 sides are equal.

days.guide: Give the shape attributes quiz. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Does a rhombus always have right angles?
questions.a: No — only when it is a square.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) A quadrilateral has → 4 sides 2) Is a square a rectangle? → yes 3) Is a rhombus a square? → sometimes 4) Draw a quadrilateral that is not a rectangle → e.g., trapezoid 5) Is a triangle a quadrilateral? → no 6) Shape with 4 equal sides and 4 right angles → square 7) A rectangle has 4 right angles: always/sometimes/never → always 8) Is a kite a quadrilateral? → yes. Proficient: 7+/8.

weeks.prep: Ruler, string, grid paper, a book, a picture frame, a table to measure. Write the perimeter quiz.
misconceptions: Confusing perimeter with area — perimeter is the distance around (add the sides), not the squares inside.
Forgetting unlabeled sides of rectangles — opposite sides are equal, so add all 4.

days.guide: Wrap string around a book, mark it, and measure the string. Then measure each side and add to check.

questions.q: A book is 9 in by 6 in. What is its perimeter?
What does perimeter measure?
questions.a: The distance around a shape.

days.guide: Count unit lengths around polygons on grid paper and add side lengths. Remind the child to mark a starting corner so no side is skipped or counted twice.

questions.q: A triangle has sides of 5, 7 and 8 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.a: 20 cm.

questions.q: A square has 6 m sides. What is its perimeter?

days.guide: Subtract the known sides from the perimeter to find a missing side. Model one problem by writing the known sides on a sketch, then the child solves 5 more.

questions.q: A rectangle has perimeter 20 cm and one side of 6 cm. How long is the other side?
A triangle has perimeter 18 in with sides of 5 in and 7 in. Third side?
questions.a: 6 in.

days.guide: Solve fencing word problems by drawing the pen or garden and labeling every side. Ask 'Are we going around or covering?' to confirm it is a perimeter problem.

questions.q: A dog pen is 8 ft by 5 ft. How much fence is needed?
questions.a: 26 ft.

questions.q: A square garden has 4 m sides. How much fence?

days.guide: Give the perimeter quiz. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What is the perimeter of a 10 by 3 rectangle?
questions.a: 26 units.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 7 × 4 rectangle → 22 2) Square with side 9 → 36 3) Triangle with sides 4, 6, 9 → 19 4) Pentagon with all sides 3 → 15 5) Rectangle with P = 30 and one side 10 → other side 5 6) Hexagon with sides 2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4 → 18 7) Fence for a 12 ft by 6 ft garden → 36 ft. Proficient: 6+/7.

weeks.prep: Square tiles (at least 24), grid paper. Write the mixed problem set.
misconceptions: Believing shapes with the same area must have the same perimeter — compare 1 × 24 (P = 50) with 4 × 6 (P = 20).
Using area when a question needs perimeter — ask 'Are we covering it or going around it?'

days.guide: Build every rectangle with 24 tiles (1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6) and record each perimeter in a table. Ask the child what they notice: the closer to a square, the smaller the perimeter.

questions.q: What are the perimeters of all the rectangles with area 24?
Which has the smallest perimeter?
questions.a: 4 × 6 (the one closest to a square).

days.guide: Draw every rectangle with whole-number sides and perimeter 20 (1 × 9, 2 × 8, 3 × 7, 4 × 6, 5 × 5) and record areas. Have the child describe the pattern: the closer to a square, the larger the area.

questions.q: What are the areas for the perimeter-20 rectangles?
Which has the greatest area?

days.guide: With 24 ft of fence, list the pens: 1 × 11 (11 sq ft), 2 × 10 (20), 3 × 9 (27), 4 × 8 (32), 5 × 7 (35), 6 × 6 (36). Have the child sketch each pen on grid paper and circle the winner.

questions.q: Which rectangular pen made with 24 ft of fence has the most area?
questions.a: 6 ft by 6 ft, with 36 sq ft.

questions.q: What is the area of the 2 × 10 pen?
questions.a: 20 sq ft.

days.guide: Decide whether each of 10 real situations needs area or perimeter, explaining why. Sort the situations into two piles and discuss any the child is unsure about.

questions.q: Buying carpet for a floor: area or perimeter?
questions.a: Area.

questions.q: Putting ribbon around a picture frame?
questions.a: Perimeter.

days.guide: Give the mixed area/perimeter problem set. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: A 5 × 3 rectangle: what are its area and perimeter?
questions.a: Area 15 sq units; perimeter 16 units.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 6 × 4 rectangle: A = 24, P = 20 2) 8 × 2: A = 16, P = 20 3) Can rectangles have the same perimeter but different areas? → yes (8 × 2 and 5 × 5 both have P = 20; areas 16 and 25) 4) All rectangles with area 36: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6 5) Tiling a floor → area 6) Fencing a yard → perimeter 7) Square with P = 28 → side 7, A = 49. Proficient: 6+/7.

weeks.prep: Large grid paper, colored pencils, a ruler. Write the Unit 9 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: Calculating area for every section but forgetting perimeter (or the reverse) — use a table with both columns.
Partitioning the picnic area into unequal parts — check equal areas by counting squares.

days.guide: The child begins designing a park on grid paper (1 square = 1 meter) with at least 4 rectangular areas (playground, garden, picnic area, field). Encourage at least 4 sections of different sizes and labels for each.

questions.q: If the playground is 6 squares by 5 squares, what is its area?
questions.a: 30 sq m.

questions.q: What shape must each section be for this project?
questions.a: A rectangle drawn along the grid lines.

days.guide: Fill in a table: section, length, width, area, perimeter. Check two rows of the table together with a calculator.

questions.q: A garden is 4 m by 7 m. Area and perimeter?
questions.a: Area 28 sq m; perimeter 22 m.

questions.q: A field is 10 m by 8 m. Area and perimeter?
questions.a: Area 80 sq m; perimeter 36 m.

days.guide: Partition the picnic area into 4 equal parts, one for each family, and label each part 1/4. Have the child count squares in each part to prove they are equal.

questions.q: An 8 × 4 picnic area (32 sq m) is split equally for 4 families. What does each get?
questions.a: 1/4 of the area, which is 8 sq m.

questions.q: If it were split into 8 equal parts instead, what fraction is each?

days.guide: The child presents the park design and explains each calculation to the family. Ask one follow-up question about area and one about perimeter.

questions.q: How do you know which section has the largest area?
questions.a: Compare the products of length × width; the largest product is the largest area.

questions.q: Explain how you found a perimeter.
questions.a: Add all four side lengths (or 2 × length + 2 × width).

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Is a rhombus a quadrilateral?
questions.a: Yes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test: 1) Is a square a rectangle? → yes 2) Draw a quadrilateral that is not a rectangle, rhombus or square → trapezoid or kite 3) Perimeter of 9 × 4 → 26 4) Area of 9 × 4 → 36 5) Rectangle with P = 24 and one side 8 → other side 4 6) L shape of 6 × 3 and 2 × 2 → 22 sq units 7) 2 × 8 and 4 × 4 have the same area (16); perimeters → 20 and 16 8) Shape split into 6 equal parts → each 1/6. Proficient: 7+/8. Park project: 4 = all sections' areas and perimeters correct, equal partition, clear presentation; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Fact cards, a review packet with problems from Units 1–5, a board game and dice for the target-number game. Write the cumulative test.
misconceptions: Rushing fluency and making careless errors — encourage known-fact strategies instead of guessing.
Skipping estimation on 3-digit problems — always check reasonableness.

days.guide: Give a full multiplication and division fact assessment (all facts through 10 × 10). Record facts that still need practice.
Solve mixed 3-digit addition and subtraction problems, estimating first. Have the child circle any answer that is far from the estimate and redo it.

questions.q: Estimate, then solve 467 + 285.
questions.a: Estimate 470 + 290 = 760; exact 752 — reasonable.

days.guide: Solve 5 multi-step word problems and explain the thinking aloud. Ask the child to draw a bar model for any problem they find tricky.

questions.q: A class has 4 tables of 6 kids, and 5 kids go home. How many are left?
You have $100 and buy 3 items at $25 each. How much is left?

days.guide: Play a fact board game, then a target-number game: roll dice and use any operations to hit a target. Keep it playful and have the child say each equation aloud as they play.

questions.q: Use 3, 4 and 2 to make 24.
Use 5, 6 and 1 to make 31.

days.guide: Give the cumulative operations test. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What is 8 × 70?

weeks.prep: Fraction strips, number lines, a clock, measuring cups and scale, a scavenger-hunt list of shapes, a portfolio folder. Write the end-of-year assessment.
misconceptions: Forgetting that equivalent fractions name the same point on the number line — revisit stacked number lines.
Mixing up area and perimeter in review — ask 'Inside or around?'

days.guide: Review equivalence and comparison with strips and number lines. Have the child explain one comparison to you using a strip or number line drawing.

questions.q: Compare 3/4 and 3/8.

days.guide: Review time, liquid volume, mass and area problems. Mix 2 problems of each type and have the child name the unit for every answer.

questions.q: How long is it from 9:40 to 10:15?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

questions.q: What is the area of a 7 × 6 rectangle?
questions.a: 42 square units.

days.guide: Go on a scavenger hunt for rectangles, squares and other quadrilaterals around the house and measure perimeters. Have the child record the shape, its attributes and its perimeter for each find.

questions.q: What is the perimeter of a 12 in × 8 in tray?
questions.a: 40 inches.

questions.q: Is every square a rhombus?
questions.a: Yes.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year assessment without help. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Which is greater, 1/3 or 1/6?

days.guide: The child chooses best work from each unit for a portfolio and writes a reflection on their growth. Help the child choose one piece per unit and write a sentence about why it shows growth.

questions.q: What should a good reflection include?
questions.a: What they learned, what was hard, how they improved (with an example), and a goal for next year.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 538 + 276 → 814 2) 700 − 285 → 415 3) Round 763 to the nearest 100 → 800 4) 8 × 7 → 56 5) 72 ÷ 9 → 8 6) Place 3/4 on a number line → 3 of 4 equal spaces from 0 7) 2/3 = ?/6 → 4 8) Compare 5/8 and 3/8 → 5/8 > 3/8 9) 2:25 to 3:10 → 45 min 10) 3 bottles × 2 L → 6 L 11) Area of 5 × 8 → 40 sq units 12) Perimeter of 5 × 8 → 26 units 13) Is a square a rhombus? → yes 14) 3 packs of 6 juice boxes, 4 drunk → 14. Proficient: 11+/14. Reflection: 3 = specific examples and a goal; 2 = general statements; 1 = minimal.

PE.overview: Third-grade PE is taught in 30-minute daily sessions that always start with the dynamic warm-up and end with a cool-down. Demonstrate each skill with 2–4 short cues, let the child practice many repetitions while you give one specific correction at a time, then check with the week's skill check. Keep a fitness and skill log all year so the child compares to their own baseline, not to others; stress safety rules, soft landings, and fair play in every game.

weeks.prep: Clear an open, flat play area free of furniture, rocks and holes; set 4 cones as boundaries. Make sure the child has sneakers and a water bottle. Write 4–5 PE safety rules on a card (stay in boundaries, keep personal space, stop on the signal, use equipment only as taught, tell an adult if hurt) and pick a stop signal (whistle or 'Freeze!').
misconceptions: Thinking a warm-up means static stretching cold muscles. A warm-up should be moving (dynamic) to raise heart rate and body temperature; hold-still stretches belong in the cool-down.
Thinking the cool-down is optional or means sitting down right away. Slowing down gradually and then stretching helps the heart rate come down and muscles relax.

days.guide: Read the safety rules card aloud and have the child repeat each rule. Show 'personal space' by having them spin slowly with arms out (their bubble). Play 5 minutes of bubble-space tag: everyone moves with arms out and must not pop anyone's bubble; freeze on your signal and check that they stop right away.

questions.q: What is personal space?
questions.a: The space around your body you can reach with arms out (your 'bubble'); in PE you keep your bubble from touching anyone else's.

questions.q: What do you do when you hear the stop signal?
questions.a: Stop moving right away, freeze, and look and listen to the adult.

days.guide: Demonstrate each of the 6 moves (jog, high knees, arm circles, skips, lunges, butt kicks) once, then do them together for about 30 seconds each. Watch that lunges keep the front knee over the ankle and that the child moves under control. Ask how their body feels at the end (warmer, breathing faster).

questions.q: Name 3 moves in our dynamic warm-up.
questions.a: Any 3 of: jog, high knees, arm circles, skips, lunges, butt kicks.

questions.q: Why do we warm up before exercise?
questions.a: To raise heart rate and body temperature and loosen muscles and joints so they work better and are less likely to be injured.

days.guide: After a short jog, lead 4–5 static stretches (quad stretch, hamstring reach, calf stretch against a wall, arm-across-chest, triceps), holding each 15–20 seconds with no bouncing. Have the child breathe slowly and say 'stretch, not pain.' Ask them to explain why we cool down.

questions.q: How long do you hold a cool-down stretch, and should you bounce?
questions.a: About 15–30 seconds, holding still and breathing slowly — no bouncing.

questions.q: Why do muscles need a cool-down?
questions.a: It lets the heart rate and breathing slow down gradually and helps warm muscles relax and stay flexible, which reduces stiffness.

days.guide: Have the child lead the warm-up, then play 15 minutes of freeze tag inside the cones (tagged players freeze until a free player tags them). Remind them of tagging gently on the shoulders or back. Finish with the cool-down stretches.

questions.q: Where is a safe place to tag someone?
questions.a: A gentle touch on the shoulder, arm or back — never a push, grab or tag on the head or face.

questions.q: What comes first and last in our PE session?
questions.a: Warm-up first; cool-down last.

days.guide: The child leads the family through all 6 warm-up moves, calling out each one and showing correct form. Then they name 3 safety rules without the card. Use the assessment rubric below.

questions.q: Name 3 PE safety rules.
questions.a: Any 3, e.g., stay inside the boundaries, keep personal space, stop on the signal, use equipment the right way, tell an adult if you are hurt, wear sneakers.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for leading the warm-up: 4 = leads all 6 moves (jog, high knees, arm circles, skips, lunges, butt kicks) in order with correct form, clear voice and about 30 seconds each, and names 3 safety rules; 3 = leads 5–6 moves with minor form slips and names 3 rules; 2 = needs prompts for several moves or names only 1–2 rules; 1 = cannot lead the warm-up without the adult doing it.

weeks.prep: Gather a timer or phone stopwatch and make a fitness/heart-rate log (columns: date, activity, heart rate before, heart rate after). Plan 6 circuit stations with simple equipment (jump rope or jumping jacks, wall push-ups, curl-ups, sit-and-reach, plank hold, jog laps).
misconceptions: Mixing up muscular strength and muscular endurance. Strength is how much force a muscle can make once (a hard push); endurance is how many times or how long it can keep working (many curl-ups).
Counting the pulse with the thumb. The thumb has its own pulse; use the index and middle fingers on the side of the neck or the thumb side of the wrist.

days.guide: Teach the 5 components of health-related fitness: cardiorespiratory (heart-lung) endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. For each, act out an exercise together (jog in place, wall push-up, 10 curl-ups, toe-touch reach, and for body composition talk about eating well plus being active). Have the child match each card to its exercise.

questions.q: Name the 5 components of health-related fitness.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.

questions.q: Which component does a sit-and-reach stretch work on?
questions.a: Flexibility.

days.guide: Show the child how to find the pulse with two fingers on the side of the neck (carotid) or inside the wrist below the thumb (radial). Sit quietly 2 minutes, count beats for 15 seconds while you time, then multiply by 4. Record resting heart rate in the log.

questions.q: You counted 22 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate per minute?
questions.a: 22 × 4 = 88 beats per minute.

questions.q: Which fingers do you use to find your pulse, and why not the thumb?
questions.a: The index and middle fingers; the thumb has its own pulse and can confuse the count.

days.guide: Take a 15-second resting count, then do 2 minutes of jumping jacks and immediately count again. Record both numbers and the difference in the log. Ask the child to describe what else changed (breathing faster, feeling warm, sweating).

questions.q: Your heart rate was 84 before and 140 after jumping jacks. How much did it go up?
questions.a: 140 − 84 = 56 beats per minute higher.

questions.q: What else changes in your body when you exercise hard?
questions.a: You breathe faster and deeper, feel warmer, and may sweat.

days.guide: Set up 6 stations (e.g., jog laps = cardio, wall push-ups = strength, curl-ups = endurance, sit-and-reach = flexibility, plank = endurance, jumping jacks = cardio) and work 45–60 seconds at each with a short rest. At each station the child says which fitness component it builds.

questions.q: Which component does jogging laps build?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance (heart and lungs).

questions.q: Which component do push-ups build?
questions.a: Muscular strength (and muscular endurance when you do many).

days.guide: Review the log together. Ask the child to explain in their own words why the heart rate rose during exercise, then check the log for completeness.

questions.q: Why does your heart rate rise when you exercise?
questions.a: Working muscles need more oxygen and energy, so the heart pumps faster to send more oxygen-rich blood to them (and you breathe faster to get more oxygen).

questions.q: What happens to your heart rate after you stop and rest?
questions.a: It slowly goes back down toward your resting heart rate.

weeks.assessment_key: Heart rate log check: proficient log shows a resting heart rate correctly calculated (15-second count × 4, typically about 70–110 bpm for this age), a post-exercise rate that is higher, the difference subtracted correctly, and a sentence explaining that the heart beats faster to deliver more oxygen to working muscles. 4 = all parts correct; 3 = one math slip; 2 = numbers recorded but no explanation; 1 = log incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather a tape measure or yardstick, a box about 12 inches high for sit-and-reach (or tape a yardstick to the floor), a mat, a stopwatch, and mark a half-mile route (or a 20-meter lane with cones for the PACER; free PACER audio is online). Print a fitness log with baseline columns. Warm up before every test.
misconceptions: Thinking the tests are a competition with others. These scores are a starting point to compare against yourself later in the year.
Doing push-ups or curl-ups as fast as possible. FitnessGram-style tests use a steady cadence (about one every 3 seconds) with correct form; reps with bad form do not count.
Writing a goal like 'get better.' A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

days.guide: Warm up, then teach curl-up form: knees bent, feet flat, arms straight with fingertips sliding along the mat about 3 inches, at a slow cadence (one every 3 seconds) until form breaks. Then 90-degree push-ups: straight body, lower until elbows bend to 90 degrees, at the same cadence. Record both counts.

questions.q: What does a 90-degree push-up mean?
questions.a: You lower your body until your elbows are bent at a right angle (upper arm parallel to the floor), keeping your body straight.

questions.q: Which fitness component do curl-ups test?
questions.a: Abdominal muscular strength and endurance.

days.guide: After warming up, do the back-saver sit-and-reach: one leg straight with the foot flat against the box, the other knee bent; reach forward slowly 4 times and hold the 4th for 1 second; measure inches, then switch legs. For the shoulder stretch, reach one hand over the shoulder and the other up the back — record yes if fingertips touch, for each side.

questions.q: Why do we warm up before the flexibility test?
questions.a: Warm muscles stretch farther and are less likely to be strained.

questions.q: Should you bounce to reach farther?
questions.a: No — reach slowly and smoothly; bouncing can pull a muscle and does not count.

days.guide: Warm up, then time the half-mile walk/run (or run the PACER, counting laps until the child misses two beeps). Remind them to pace themselves rather than sprinting at the start. Record the time or laps and cool down with walking and stretches.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you sprint at the start of the half-mile?
questions.a: You will tire out quickly; a steady pace lets you finish with your best time.

questions.q: Which fitness component does the half-mile or PACER test?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory (aerobic) endurance.

days.guide: Explain SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Look at the baseline scores and help the child choose one area and write a goal, e.g., 'I will do 15 curl-ups by the March retest by doing curl-ups 3 times a week.'

questions.q: What does SMART stand for?
questions.a: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

questions.q: Is 'I want to be stronger' a SMART goal? Fix it.
questions.a: No — it is not measurable or time-bound. Example fix: 'I will do 10 push-ups by March by practicing push-ups 3 days a week.'

days.guide: Set up the weekly fitness log (date, activity, minutes, how it felt). Have the child fill in this week's entries and copy their goal at the top. Check that all baseline scores are recorded.

questions.q: How will the log help you reach your goal?
questions.a: It shows how often you practice and lets you see progress toward your goal over time.

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline check: the log should show (1) curl-up count, (2) push-up count, (3) sit-and-reach in inches for right and left, (4) shoulder stretch yes/no for each side, (5) half-mile time or PACER laps, and (6) a written SMART goal. Proficient goal example: 'I will improve my PACER from 12 to 18 laps by the spring retest by jogging 15 minutes three times a week.' Score: 4 = all scores recorded and goal has all 5 SMART parts; 3 = goal missing 1 part; 2 = scores missing or goal vague; 1 = no goal.

weeks.prep: Set up a 'yard' lane about 20–30 yards long and 6–8 cones for pathways; have upbeat music ready. Preview the definitions: hop = one foot to the same foot; leap = one foot to the other with a long flight; skip = step-hop alternating; gallop = same foot leads forward; slide = sideways gallop.
misconceptions: Confusing a hop and a jump. A hop takes off and lands on the same one foot; a jump takes off and lands on two feet (or two to one / one to two).
Galloping and sliding look the same. In a gallop you face forward with one foot always leading; in a slide you move sideways, chest facing forward, without crossing the feet.

days.guide: Demonstrate each locomotor skill and have the child do each one across the yard: walk, run, hop (each foot), skip, gallop (each lead foot), slide (both directions) and leap. Give one cue per skill (e.g., skip: 'step-hop, swing arms').

questions.q: What is the difference between a hop and a leap?
questions.a: A hop takes off and lands on the same foot; a leap takes off on one foot and lands on the other with a long stretch in the air.

questions.q: In a slide, which way do you face?
questions.a: You face forward (chest to the front) while moving sideways, feet not crossing.

days.guide: Lay cones in a straight line, a curve and a zigzag. Have the child travel each pathway with a different skill (walk the straight, skip the curved, slide the zigzag). Then call out a pathway and a skill and let them choose the cones.

questions.q: Name the 3 pathways we practiced.
questions.a: Straight, curved and zigzag.

questions.q: Draw or describe a zigzag pathway.
questions.a: A path of straight lines with sharp turns back and forth, like the letter Z repeated.

days.guide: Model run-to-leap: 3–4 running steps, then take off on one foot and land on the other, then keep running. Then skip-to-slide: skip 4 times, turn sideways and slide 4 times without stopping. Practice each 5 times, cueing 'no stopping between skills.'

questions.q: What does a smooth transition mean?
questions.a: Changing from one movement to the next without stopping or stumbling.

questions.q: When you run into a leap, which foot do you land on?
questions.a: The opposite foot from the one you took off on.

days.guide: Build an obstacle course with 4–5 parts (e.g., zigzag run through cones, leap over a pool noodle, hop to a cone, slide to the finish). The child completes it 3 times, trying to make each change smooth.

questions.q: Which skill did you use to get over the noodle, and why?
questions.a: A leap (or jump), because it carries you up and over the object.

days.guide: The child designs and performs a 4-skill sequence (e.g., skip → gallop → slide → leap), saying it aloud first, then performing it twice. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Tell me your 4 skills in order.
questions.a: Any 4 correct locomotor skills named in the order performed, e.g., 'skip, gallop, slide, leap.'

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for 4-skill locomotor sequence: 4 = performs 4 different locomotor skills with correct form and smooth transitions (no stops), repeats it the same way; 3 = 4 correct skills with one pause or stumble; 2 = 2–3 skills correct or several stops; 1 = cannot show a sequence of skills.

weeks.prep: Gather tape or chalk for a start line, a measuring tape, chalk for the vertical jump (or sticky notes), and draw a hopscotch grid (1–10). Jump on grass or a soft surface.
misconceptions: Landing with straight, locked legs. Land on the balls of the feet and bend hips, knees and ankles to absorb force ('land like a spring').
Keeping arms still. Swinging the arms back then forward and up adds force and distance.

days.guide: Teach 'quiet landings': jump in place and land softly on both feet with knees, hips and ankles bent, as if landing on eggshells. Practice 10 small jumps and 5 jumps off a low step, checking that you can barely hear the landing.

questions.q: How do you land safely after a jump?
questions.a: On both feet (balls of the feet first), with knees, hips and ankles bent to absorb the force, arms forward for balance.

questions.q: Why does a quiet landing mean a good landing?
questions.a: It means your legs bent and absorbed the force instead of slamming down.

days.guide: Teach the standing long jump: feet shoulder-width behind the line, crouch and swing arms back, swing arms forward and jump out, land on both feet. Measure from the line to the back of the heel closest to the line. Do 3 jumps and record each.

questions.q: Where do you measure a long jump to?
questions.a: From the start line to the back of the heel (the landing mark closest to the line).

questions.q: Jumps of 42, 47 and 45 inches — which is your best?
questions.a: 47 inches.

days.guide: Have the child stand sideways to a wall, reach up with chalky fingers and mark standing reach. Then crouch, swing arms and jump, marking the highest point. Measure between the two marks. Do 3 tries.

questions.q: Your reach mark is 54 inches and your jump mark is 63 inches. What is your vertical jump?
questions.a: 63 − 54 = 9 inches.

questions.q: Should you take a running start for this test?
questions.a: No — jump from standing with two feet, using a crouch and arm swing.

days.guide: Play hopscotch: toss a marker, hop on one foot on single squares and land on two feet on side-by-side squares, skipping the marker square, then turn and come back. Add variations: hop only on the left foot, or jump with feet crossed.

questions.q: In hopscotch, when do you land on two feet?
questions.a: On the squares that are side by side (and at the turn-around).

questions.q: Is a single-square move a hop or a jump?
questions.a: A hop — one foot to the same foot.

days.guide: Review the jump log. Have the child do 2 long jumps — one without arms, one with a full arm swing — measure both and explain the difference.

questions.q: How do your arms help you jump farther?
questions.a: Swinging the arms back and then forcefully forward and up adds momentum and force that carries the body farther.

questions.q: What should you do with your legs when you land?
questions.a: Bend the knees, hips and ankles to absorb the force.

weeks.assessment_key: Jump measurements check: proficient record shows 3 standing long jumps measured to the nearest inch from line to heel with the best circled, a vertical jump calculated as jump mark minus reach mark, and soft two-foot landings with bent knees on every trial. 4 = all measurements correct and safe landings; 3 = one measurement error; 2 = missing a test or landings stiff; 1 = record incomplete.

weeks.prep: Make a 10-foot tape line on the floor (or use a curb or low 2x4 beam no higher than a few inches). Lay cushions or a mat nearby for falls. Have a stopwatch to time 5-second holds.
misconceptions: Holding the breath and looking down. Keep breathing, look at a fixed point ahead, and tighten the belly to stay steady.
Thinking fewer body parts touching makes a balance easier. Fewer points of contact (a smaller base of support) make it harder; a wide base is more stable.

days.guide: Call out balances on different body parts: 4 points (hands and knees), 3 points (lift one arm), 2 points (one hand, one foot, or two feet), 1 point (one foot, arms out). Hold each 5 seconds while the child counts. Teach 'eyes on a spot, tight tummy.'

questions.q: Which is harder to hold: a balance on 4 body parts or on 1? Why?
questions.a: On 1, because the base of support is smaller, so it is easier to tip over.

questions.q: What helps you hold a balance?
questions.a: Looking at one spot, tightening your stomach muscles, arms out to the sides, and breathing steadily.

days.guide: Walk forward heel-to-toe along the line, then backward (toe reaching back), then sideways with slide steps. Add arms out to the side. Finish each pass with a controlled dismount: step off and land with bent knees.

questions.q: Where should your eyes be when walking the line?
questions.a: Looking ahead at the end of the line or a spot in front, not down at your feet.

questions.q: How do you dismount safely?
questions.a: Step or jump off with control and land on both feet with bent knees.

days.guide: Show counterbalance (partners face each other, hold wrists, lean back together) and counter-tension; also try back-to-back sitting down and standing up together. Stress slow movement and talking to each other.

questions.q: In a counterbalance, why do you both need to lean equally?
questions.a: Each partner's weight holds the other up; if one leans more or lets go, both lose balance.

questions.q: What should partners do before letting go?
questions.a: Agree and come back to standing slowly together, then release.

days.guide: The child chooses 3 balances (e.g., stork stand, V-sit, 3-point bridge) and links them with smooth transitions. Have them write or draw the sequence, then practice it 3 times.

questions.q: Name your 3 balances and how many body parts touch in each.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., stork stand (1 foot), V-sit (seat), bridge (2 hands, 2 feet = 4).

days.guide: The child performs the 3-balance sequence, holding each balance still for 5 seconds with smooth transitions. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: What is a base of support?
questions.a: The body parts touching the ground that hold you up.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for balance sequence: 4 = 3 different balances, each held still for 5 seconds, smooth transitions, controlled start and end; 3 = all 3 balances but one wobble or brief pause; 2 = holds only 1–2 balances for 5 seconds; 1 = cannot hold balances.

weeks.prep: Use a tumbling mat, old mattress or soft grass; make a gentle incline by putting a cushion or folded blanket under one end of the mat. Clear the area. Parent spots every forward roll. Skip forward rolls if the child has any neck or back problems.
misconceptions: Rolling on the top of the head. Tuck chin to chest so the back of the head and shoulders touch the mat, never the top of the head.
Opening the body mid-roll. Stay in a tight ball (hold shins) so the rounded back rolls smoothly.

days.guide: Lie the child on the mat with arms stretched overhead and body straight like a pencil. They roll sideways the length of the mat 5 times each direction, keeping legs together and arms up.

questions.q: What shape is your body in a log roll?
questions.a: Long and straight like a pencil, arms overhead, legs together.

days.guide: Teach the egg roll: kneel in a tight tuck with forearms and head tucked, roll sideways onto the back and back to knees. Then rocking chair: sit in a tuck holding shins, chin to chest, rock back and forth on a rounded back 10 times.

questions.q: Why do we practice rocking chairs before a forward roll?
questions.a: To learn to keep a rounded back and tucked chin so we roll smoothly and safely.

questions.q: Where should your chin be during a roll?
questions.a: Tucked to your chest.

days.guide: On the incline mat: squat at the high end, hands on the mat shoulder-width, chin to chest, push with the legs and roll over the back of the head and shoulders, finishing in a squat. Spot with one hand on the back of the neck/head and one under the hips/thighs. Repeat 5–8 times.

questions.q: What part of your body touches the mat first in a forward roll?
questions.a: The hands, then the back of the head and shoulders (never the top of the head).

questions.q: Why use a gentle incline?
questions.a: Gravity helps you roll over easily, making it safer while you learn.

days.guide: The child plans a 3-part routine: a balance (held 3–5 seconds), a roll (log, egg or forward), and a jump with a soft landing. Practice the transitions and finish with a still end position.

questions.q: How should you land the jump at the end of your routine?
questions.a: On both feet with bent knees, arms up or forward, holding still.

days.guide: The child performs the routine. Then ask them to explain 'chin to chest' and show it. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why do we say 'chin to chest'?
questions.a: It rounds the back and keeps the top of the head and neck off the mat so the neck is protected during the roll.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for tumbling routine: 4 = balance held still, roll performed with chin tucked and rounded back, jump landed softly on two feet, smooth transitions, explains 'chin to chest' protects the neck; 3 = all parts safe with one wobble or pause; 2 = roll unsafe (head not tucked) or a part missing; 1 = cannot complete safely.

weeks.prep: Get a jump rope (beaded or PVC rope works well). Size it: stand on the middle with one foot; handles should reach the armpits. Jump on a flat, non-slip surface (driveway, gym floor). Prepare a jump log and pick a slow and a faster song.
misconceptions: Turning the rope with big arm circles. Elbows stay close to the sides and the rope turns from the wrists.
Jumping too high or double-bouncing. Jump only an inch or two off the ground, on the balls of the feet, one jump per turn.

days.guide: Size the rope (stand on the middle; handles to the armpits). Hold both handles in one hand and swing the rope at your side to feel the rhythm from the wrist. Then hold one in each hand and turn the rope over the head and let it stop in front of the toes, step over, repeat 10 times.

questions.q: How do you know your rope is the right size?
questions.a: Standing on the middle with one foot, the handles reach about to your armpits.

questions.q: What part of your arm turns the rope?
questions.a: The wrists (with elbows close to your sides).

days.guide: Practice the basic bounce: feet together, small jump on the balls of the feet as the rope passes under. Do 5 sets of 20-second tries with 30-second rests. Cue 'small jumps, quiet feet, wrists turn.'

questions.q: How high should you jump in the basic bounce?
questions.a: Just an inch or two — enough for the rope to pass under.

questions.q: Why do we rest between sets?
questions.a: Jump rope is hard work for the heart and legs; rest lets you recover so you can keep good form.

days.guide: Do 3 trials of counting consecutive jumps without a miss. Record each number and circle the best in the jump log.

questions.q: Trials were 14, 22 and 19 jumps. What is your best? What is the difference between best and worst?
What counts as 'consecutive' jumps?
questions.a: Jumps in a row without the rope stopping or a miss.

days.guide: Jump to a slow-tempo song, trying to land one jump per beat. Then switch to a faster song. Talk about which was easier and why.

questions.q: What do you need to change when the music gets faster?
questions.a: Turn the rope faster with the wrists and make smaller, quicker jumps to stay on the beat.

days.guide: Warm up, then do 3 trials to try for a new personal best and record it. Ask the child to compare this week's first count to the best.

questions.q: How did practice change your count?
questions.a: Answer should compare numbers, e.g., 'I went from 14 to 30 because I kept my jumps small and turned with my wrists.'

weeks.assessment_key: Jump log check: proficient log lists 3 counted trials on Day 3 with the best circled, a Day 5 personal best, and a sentence comparing them using numbers and a reason (e.g., better timing, wrist turning, smaller jumps). Form check: rope sized to armpits, elbows in, wrists turning, small two-foot jumps. 4 = all present; 3 = log complete but reason vague; 2 = missing trials; 1 = no log.

weeks.prep: Have the jump rope, a timer, a trick checklist (skier, bell, side swing, alternate foot) and the heart-rate log from week 2 with the resting heart rate.
misconceptions: Swinging the whole body for skier or bell. Keep feet together and move only a few inches side to side or front to back, with small jumps.
Thinking the side swing needs a jump. In the side swing, both handles go to one side and the rope swings past without jumping over it.

days.guide: Draw a line on the ground. Teach the skier: feet together, jump side to side over the line without the rope, then with the rope, one jump per turn. Complete 3 sets of 10.

questions.q: In the skier, which direction do your feet move?
questions.a: Side to side (left and right), feet together.

days.guide: Teach the bell: feet together, jump forward and back over the line like a bell swinging. Then the side swing: bring both hands together and swing the rope on one side of the body, then open the hands and jump the next turn.

questions.q: How is the bell different from the skier?
questions.a: In the bell you jump forward and backward; in the skier you jump side to side.

questions.q: Do you jump during a side swing?
questions.a: No — the rope swings beside your body; you jump on the next turn after you open your arms.

days.guide: Teach the alternate-foot step: jog in place, one foot lands per turn of the rope (right, left, right, left). Practice without the rope first, then try for 20 in a row.

questions.q: In the alternate-foot step, how many feet land on each turn of the rope?
questions.a: One foot each turn, switching feet like jogging.

days.guide: Take resting heart rate (15 s × 4). Jump for 1 minute (any tricks), then immediately take the pulse again and record. Compare the numbers.

questions.q: Resting was 80 bpm; after jumping you counted 36 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate after jumping, and how much higher?
Which fitness component does jumping rope build most?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance (also muscular endurance in the legs).

days.guide: The child performs 3 tricks in a row (e.g., skier, bell, alternate foot) while a family member checks each off on the checklist.

questions.q: Name the 3 tricks you performed.
questions.a: Any 3 of: basic bounce, skier, bell, side swing, alternate foot.

weeks.assessment_key: Trick checklist: check each trick performed correctly for 5 or more consecutive jumps: basic bounce (feet together, small jumps), skier (side to side), bell (front to back), side swing (rope swings at side, no jump), alternate foot (one foot per turn). 4 = 3 tricks in a row smoothly; 3 = 3 tricks with a stop between them; 2 = 2 tricks; 1 = basic bounce only.

weeks.prep: Get a long rope (about 14–16 feet) and two turners, or tie one end to a fence or post. Pick a song about 30–60 seconds long with a steady beat for the routine. Look up the traditional jump-rope chants 'Teddy Bear, Teddy Bear' and 'Cinderella' (short, public-domain playground rhymes).
misconceptions: Running in at the wrong moment. Use the 'front door' (the rope comes over the top toward you): wait until the rope hits the ground in front of you, then follow it in.
Standing near the end of the rope. Jump in the middle of the rope where the arc is highest.

days.guide: Turners swing the rope in big, steady circles. Teach 'front door' entry: stand beside a turner, watch the rope hit the ground, and run in to the middle just after it passes. Jump 5 times, then exit by running out diagonally toward the opposite turner's side right after a jump.

questions.q: Where in the long rope should you jump?
questions.a: In the middle, where the rope is highest.

questions.q: When do you run in?
questions.a: Right after the rope hits the ground and moves away from you, so you have time to get to the middle before it comes around.

days.guide: Teach the rhymes and their actions (e.g., 'Teddy Bear' — turn around, touch the ground). Jump while chanting and doing each action on the beat. Turners keep a steady rhythm.

questions.q: Why do we chant rhymes while jumping?
questions.a: The rhyme keeps a steady beat so the jumper and turners stay in time, and it adds actions to practice.

days.guide: Help the child pick 4 tricks (e.g., basic bounce, skier, bell, side swing) and decide how many jumps of each (e.g., 8 each) to fill about 30 seconds of music. Write the plan in order.

questions.q: If you do 8 jumps of each of 4 tricks, how many jumps is your routine?
questions.a: 8 × 4 = 32 jumps.

questions.q: Write your routine order.
questions.a: Any 4 tricks in order with counts, e.g., 8 basic, 8 skier, 8 bell, 8 alternate foot.

days.guide: Rehearse the routine 5 times with the music. After each run, choose one transition to smooth (e.g., keep turning the rope while changing tricks).

questions.q: How do you change tricks without stopping the rope?
questions.a: Keep the wrists turning at the same speed and change your feet on the next jump.

days.guide: The child performs the routine for family and then names one trick to keep improving and how.

questions.q: What trick will you keep improving, and what will you practice?
questions.a: Any trick plus a specific fix, e.g., 'bell — keep feet together and jump smaller.'

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for jump rope routine: 4 = 4 different tricks performed in planned order for about 30 seconds, mostly on the beat, with 2 or fewer misses and smooth restarts; 3 = 4 tricks with 3–4 misses or one long stop; 2 = 2–3 tricks or many misses; 1 = basic bounce only. Long rope: entered, jumped 5 and exited (yes/no).

weeks.prep: Gather 10–20 tennis balls (or rolled socks indoors). Tape a target about 2 feet square on a garage or fence wall with the center about 3 feet high; mark a throw line 15 feet away. Find an open field for distance throws. Make a 4-cue checklist.
misconceptions: Stepping with the same foot as the throwing arm. Step with the opposite foot (right-handers step with the left).
Facing the target squarely and pushing the ball. Start with the non-throwing side toward the target so the hips and shoulders can rotate.

days.guide: Teach the 4 cues: 1) side to the target, 2) arm way back, 3) step with the opposite foot, 4) follow through across the body. Have the child say the cues and shadow-throw (no ball) 20 times while you watch each cue.

questions.q: If you throw with your right hand, which foot steps forward?
questions.a: The left foot (the opposite foot).

questions.q: Name the 4 overhand throwing cues.
questions.a: Side to target, arm back, step with opposite foot, follow through.

days.guide: From the 15-foot line, the child throws 20 tennis balls at the wall target using all cues. Tally hits on paper.

questions.q: You hit the target 7 times out of 20. How many misses?
questions.a: 20 − 7 = 13 misses.

days.guide: In an open field, throw for distance: run-up optional, big step with the opposite foot, full follow-through. Mark the best throw with a cone and pace or measure it.

questions.q: What should you change to throw farther?
questions.a: Take a bigger step, rotate hips and shoulders, and throw with more force with a full follow-through (aim a little upward).

days.guide: Partners take turns: one throws 5 times while the other checks each cue on the checklist. Then switch and discuss.

questions.q: Your partner stepped with the same foot. What cue do you give?
questions.a: 'Step with the opposite foot' — the foot on the other side from the throwing arm.

days.guide: The child explains all 4 cues, then throws 10 at the target and compares the hit rate with Day 2.

questions.q: Monday: 7 of 20 hits. Today: 5 of 10 hits. Which day was more accurate?
questions.a: Today — 5 of 10 is half; 7 of 20 is less than half (10 would be half).

weeks.assessment_key: Throw cue checklist (score each throw yes/no): side to target, arm back, opposite-foot step, follow through. Proficient = all 4 cues on at least 4 of 5 observed throws, plus a target tally recorded for Day 2 and Day 5 with a correct comparison. 4 = all 4 cues consistently; 3 = 3 cues consistently; 2 = 2 cues; 1 = 0–1 cues.

weeks.prep: Gather a beanbag, a soft playground ball and a tennis ball. Make 'reach and give' and 'thumbs/pinkies' cue cards. Open space for partner catch and jogging.
misconceptions: Trapping the ball against the chest. Catch with the hands, reaching out and 'giving' (pulling the ball in) to soften it.
Using the same hand position for every catch. Above the waist: thumbs together; below the waist: pinkies together.

days.guide: Self-toss a beanbag a little above head height and catch with hands, saying 'reach and give' (reach out to the object, pull it in softly). Do 20, then repeat with a ball.

questions.q: What does 'reach and give' mean?
questions.a: Reach your hands out toward the ball, then bend your elbows and pull it in to soften the catch.

questions.q: Where should your eyes be when catching?
questions.a: On the ball all the way into your hands.

days.guide: Toss to the child at different levels. High balls: hands up, thumbs together. Low balls: hands down, pinkies together. Mix levels and call out the hand position after each catch.

questions.q: A ball is coming at your knees. How do you hold your hands?
questions.a: Pinkies together, palms up/forward.

questions.q: A ball is coming above your head. How do you hold your hands?
questions.a: Thumbs together, fingers up.

days.guide: Play partner catch starting 5 steps apart; after each 3 successful catches in a row, the child takes one step back. Count the farthest distance reached.

questions.q: Why do you step back only after 3 good catches?
questions.a: It makes sure you are successful at one distance before making it harder.

days.guide: The child jogs across the yard while you toss the ball slightly ahead of them. They catch without stopping. Switch roles.

questions.q: When catching on the move, where should the ball be thrown?
questions.a: Slightly ahead of the runner so they can catch it without stopping.

days.guide: Play partner catch and count the best streak of consecutive catches in 3 tries. Record the best.

questions.q: Streaks of 12, 18 and 15. What is your best streak?

weeks.assessment_key: Catching streak record: proficient = best streak of 10 or more consecutive partner catches at about 10 feet using hands (not trapping), with correct thumbs/pinkies hand position at high and low levels. 4 = 15+ catches and correct hand positions; 3 = 10–14; 2 = 5–9 or frequent trapping; 1 = fewer than 5.

weeks.prep: Gather a playground ball, a flying disc, a small/junior football and 4–6 cones. Set a straight cone path for the receiver.
misconceptions: Throwing to where the runner is now. A lead pass goes to where the runner will be.
Flicking the disc with a straight arm and wobble. Curl the arm across the body, step toward the target, and snap the wrist keeping the disc flat.

days.guide: Set a straight cone path. The child jogs it while you throw a lead pass to the space ahead; switch so the child throws to you. Talk about aiming at the space ahead.

questions.q: What is a lead pass?
questions.a: A throw to the space ahead of a moving teammate so they can catch it without slowing down.

days.guide: Teach the backhand: grip with the thumb on top and fingers underneath on the rim, stand sideways, curl the disc across the body, step toward the target and snap the wrist, releasing it flat. Play catch 15 minutes; catch with a 'pancake' (one hand on top, one under).

questions.q: How should the disc be when you release it?
questions.a: Flat (level with the ground), with a wrist snap to spin it.

questions.q: What is a pancake catch?
questions.a: Catching the disc between one hand on top and one hand underneath, clapping it.

days.guide: Teach the football grip: fingers on the laces, ball held near the back, throw over the shoulder with the overhand cues and let the ball roll off the fingers for a spiral. Throw to a stationary partner, then to a moving one.

questions.q: Where do your fingers go on the football?
