questions.a: On the laces, toward the back half of the ball.

days.guide: Watch a partner make 5 throws. The child gives two specific compliments ('Great step with the opposite foot') and one cue ('Follow through toward me').

questions.q: What makes feedback specific?
questions.a: It names exactly what was done well or what to fix, like 'Your arm went way back,' not just 'Good job.'

days.guide: Run a 10-pass moving drill: receiver jogs the cone path, thrower makes a lead pass; count completions out of 10.

questions.q: You completed 7 of 10 passes. How many were incomplete?

weeks.assessment_key: Moving passing drill scoring: count completions out of 10 lead passes. 4 = 8–10 completions with passes thrown ahead of the receiver; 3 = 6–7; 2 = 4–5 or passes thrown behind; 1 = 0–3. Also note whether the child gave 2 specific compliments and 1 cue on Day 4.

weeks.prep: Collect 10 plastic bottles (add a little sand or water so they stand), 2–3 balls, tape for a throw line, and the week 11 target tally. Graph paper for the accuracy graph. For hit-the-pin, set a bottle or cone 'pin' in front of each player.
misconceptions: Faking means throwing for real. A fake is a pretend throw motion to make a defender move, then you pass to the open side.
Thinking fair play only matters when winning. Fair play means following rules, taking turns and being honest whether winning or losing.

days.guide: Set 10 bottles in a triangle or line. The child throws overhand from the line, using all 4 cues, and counts how many throws it takes to knock all 10 down.

questions.q: Which cues help you hit the bottles?
questions.a: Side to target, arm back, step with the opposite foot, follow through toward the target.

days.guide: Play monkey in the middle: two throwers pass while the middle player tries to intercept. Teach the fake (start a throw one way, pass another way) and quick passes. Rotate after an interception.

questions.q: Why use a fake?
questions.a: It makes the defender move the wrong way, opening space for a pass.

questions.q: What kind of pass is hard for the monkey to catch?
questions.a: A quick, accurate pass away from the defender — over or around them, not right at them.

days.guide: Re-test 20 throws at the week 11 target from 15 feet. Make a bar graph comparing week 11 hits to today's hits.

questions.q: Week 11: 7 hits. Today: 12 hits. How much did you improve?
questions.a: 12 − 7 = 5 more hits.

days.guide: Play hit-the-pin: each player protects a pin; take turns throwing to knock down others' pins. Set fair-play rules first (take turns, no throwing at people, honest calls).

questions.q: What should you do if your pin is knocked down?
questions.a: Admit it honestly, say 'Nice shot,' and follow the game rule (reset or rotate).

days.guide: Skill check: observe 5 throws and 5 catches; score each throw on the 4 cues and each catch on reach and give / correct hand position.

questions.q: Show me how you'd catch a ball thrown at your belly button and one at your ankles.
questions.a: Belly button: thumbs together (or hands ready to pull in); ankles: pinkies together.

weeks.assessment_key: Throw/catch skill check: Throws (5) — 1 point per cue observed on each throw (side, arm back, opposite step, follow through), max 20. Catches (5) — 1 point each for a clean hands catch with correct hand position. Proficient = 16+ throw points and 4 of 5 catches. 4 = 18–20 and 5/5; 3 = 14–17 and 4/5; 2 = 10–13 or 3/5; 1 = below.

weeks.prep: Use a playground ball or junior basketball (size 5) inflated to bounce to about waist height. Flat surface such as a driveway; set 6 cones about 5 feet apart for Friday.
misconceptions: Slapping the ball with the palm. Push the ball down with the finger pads, wrist and fingers relaxed.
Looking at the ball. Keep eyes up so you can see where you are going and where others are.

days.guide: Demonstrate dribbling: knees bent, push the ball down with the finger pads at waist height, ball beside (not in front of) the body. Dribble 30 times with the right hand, then 30 with the left.

questions.q: What part of your hand pushes the ball?
questions.a: The finger pads (fingertips), not the palm.

questions.q: How high should the ball bounce?
questions.a: About waist high or lower.

days.guide: Dribble walking to a cone 20 feet away, turn, switch hands and walk back. Repeat 4 times. Cue 'ball slightly ahead and to the side.'

questions.q: Why switch hands at the turn?
questions.a: To keep the ball on the side away from where you are turning and to practice both hands.

days.guide: Dribble while jogging the length of the driveway. The ball is pushed out in front a little more and bounces a bit higher than walking. Jog back and repeat 5 times.

questions.q: How is a running dribble different from a stationary one?
questions.a: You push the ball a little farther in front of you so you can move forward without kicking it.

days.guide: While the child dribbles in place, hold up fingers; they call out the number without stopping. Then do the same while walking.

questions.q: Why practice dribbling with your eyes up?
questions.a: So you can see teammates, defenders and where you're going while still controlling the ball.

days.guide: Set the 6-cone course. The child dribbles around each cone and back without losing control. Time it if desired.

questions.q: What counts as losing control?
questions.a: The ball bouncing away, being caught/held with two hands, or stopping the dribble.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble course rubric: 4 = completes 6-cone course with finger-pad dribble, ball at waist height or lower, eyes mostly up, no loss of control; 3 = one loss of control or eyes mostly down; 2 = two or more losses; 1 = cannot dribble continuously.

weeks.prep: Ball and 6–8 cones set in a zigzag (cones alternating about 4 feet left and right). Agree on 'red light/green light' signals.
misconceptions: Crossing over high. A crossover bounce should be low (below the knee) and quick so a defender can't steal it.
Stopping the dribble to tag in dribble tag. Players must keep dribbling the whole time; if you pick up the ball you must restart.

days.guide: Teach the crossover: dribble low with the right hand, push the ball in a V-shape across the body to the left hand, bounce below the knee. Practice 3 sets of 20.

questions.q: Where should the ball bounce in a crossover?
questions.a: Low, in front of your body (a V shape), below the knees.

questions.q: Why keep the crossover low?
questions.a: A low, quick bounce is harder for a defender to steal.

days.guide: Dribble through the zigzag cones, switching to the outside hand (the hand farther from the cone) at each one.

questions.q: If a cone is on your left, which hand should you dribble with?
questions.a: Your right hand — the hand away from the cone or defender, protecting the ball.

days.guide: Play red light/green light: green = speed dribble, yellow = slow, red = stop and control the ball dribbling in place (or hold it). Practice quick changes.

questions.q: How do you dribble fast?
questions.a: Push the ball farther ahead and a bit higher, and run.

days.guide: Play dribble tag in a small area: everyone dribbles; the tagger tries to tag others while dribbling. Lost balls must be recovered before playing on.

questions.q: In dribble tag, how do you protect your ball from a tagger?
questions.a: Keep your body between the tagger and the ball and dribble with the hand away from them.

days.guide: Skills check: 10 crossovers in place, one zigzag pass through the cones switching hands, and a speed change on call.

questions.q: Which hand do you use after a crossover from right to left?
questions.a: The left hand.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble skills check (1 point each, 6 total): crossover low and controlled (1) for 10 in a row (1); zigzag with hand switches (1) and no loss of control (1); speed change on 'red/green' (1) with control maintained (1). 4 = 6; 3 = 5; 2 = 3–4; 1 = 0–2.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball (size 3 or 4) and 6–8 cones; open grass. A stopwatch for Friday's timed course.
misconceptions: Kicking the ball far ahead when dribbling. Use small touches so the ball stays within a step of your feet.
Using only the toes. Use the inside and outside of the foot for control; toe kicks are hard to control.

days.guide: Teach toe taps (lightly tap the top of the ball with alternating soles, 50 times) and inside-foot touches (pass the ball between the insides of both feet, 50 times). Keep on the balls of the feet.

questions.q: Which parts of the foot do you use to dribble a soccer ball?
questions.a: The inside and outside of the foot (and the sole to stop); small touches, not toe pokes.

days.guide: Dribble through a line of cones using small touches with both feet, keeping the ball close. Go 4 times through.

questions.q: How far should the ball be from your feet while dribbling?
questions.a: Close — within about one step so you can control it.

days.guide: Dribble in an open space; when you shout 'Stop!' the child puts the sole of the foot on top of the ball to stop it. Practice 10 times.

questions.q: How do you stop the ball quickly?
questions.a: Step on top of it lightly with the sole of your foot.

days.guide: Play soccer dribble tag: the child dribbles in a marked square while a defender tries to touch or kick the ball out. Teach shielding: body between the defender and the ball.

questions.q: What is shielding?
questions.a: Keeping your body between the defender and the ball to protect it.

days.guide: Set the cone course. Time the child dribbling through and back; do 2–3 trials and record the best time.

questions.q: Trial times were 28, 25 and 26 seconds. What is your best time?
questions.a: 25 seconds (lowest time is best).

weeks.assessment_key: Timed foot-dribble course: record best of 3 times. Form rubric: 4 = small touches with both feet, ball stays close, weaves every cone without missing; 3 = mostly controlled, one missed cone or ball runs away once; 2 = big kicks or several missed cones; 1 = cannot complete course with the ball.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, a small goal or two cones 6 feet apart for the target, 15-foot mark, open field.
misconceptions: Kicking with the toe for passes. Pass with the inside of the foot for accuracy; shoot with the laces (top of the foot).
Planting the support foot far behind the ball. Plant the non-kicking foot beside the ball, toe pointing to the target.

days.guide: Teach the inside-foot pass: plant foot beside the ball pointing at the target, turn the kicking foot out, strike the middle of the ball with the inside, follow through. Make 30 passes with a partner about 15 feet apart.

questions.q: Where does your plant foot go for a pass?
questions.a: Beside the ball, toes pointing toward your target.

questions.q: Which part of the foot passes the ball?
questions.a: The inside of the foot.

days.guide: From 15 feet, kick 20 passes through two cones 6 feet apart and tally successes. Narrow the gap if it's easy.

questions.q: You got 14 of 20 through. How many missed?

days.guide: Teach the laces shot: approach at an angle, plant beside the ball, toe pointed down, strike with the laces and follow through toward the goal. Take 15 shots.

questions.q: Which part of the foot do you shoot with?
questions.a: The laces (top of the foot) with the toe pointed down.

days.guide: Partner jogs across the field; the child passes ahead of them (lead pass) with the inside of the foot.

questions.q: Where should you pass to a moving teammate?
questions.a: Into the space in front of them, so they can run onto it.

days.guide: Kicking check: 5 inside-foot passes through the cones and 5 laces shots on goal; score each on the cues.

questions.q: Why is the inside of the foot more accurate than the toe?
questions.a: It's a bigger, flatter surface, so the ball goes where you aim.

weeks.assessment_key: Kicking check (score each of 10 kicks on cues: plant foot beside ball, correct foot surface, follow through toward target): 4 = 4–5 accurate passes and 3+ shots on goal with all cues; 3 = 3 accurate passes, 2 shots on goal; 2 = 1–2 passes accurate or toe-kicking; 1 = no accurate kicks.

weeks.prep: Ball (soccer ball or playground ball), 4 cones for a small field and 2 more for goals. Invite a sibling, parent or friend for 2v1 and the mini game. Paper for Friday's reflection.
misconceptions: Everyone chasing the ball ('beehive soccer'). Teammates spread out into open space so they can receive a pass.
Facing the ball and standing still on defense. Use a ready stance (knees bent, on balls of feet) and stay between the attacker and the goal.

days.guide: Play 2-person keep-away in a square with one defender (parent). The child practices moving to open space — a spot where the passer has a clear lane — and calling for the ball. Freeze play occasionally and ask 'Where is the open space?'

questions.q: What is open space?
questions.a: An area away from defenders where a teammate can pass you the ball without it being intercepted.

questions.q: Why move after you pass?
questions.a: To get open again for a return pass.

days.guide: Teach the defensive stance: feet apart, knees bent, weight on balls of feet, arms out. The child shuffles to stay between the attacker and the goal as you dribble slowly.

questions.q: Where should a defender stand?
questions.a: Between the attacker and the goal they are protecting.

questions.q: Describe a good defensive stance.
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width apart, knees bent, on the balls of the feet, arms out, eyes on the attacker's body/ball.

days.guide: Play 2v1: two attackers try to score past one defender. Teach 'draw and pass': dribble at the defender, and when they come to you, pass to your open teammate.

questions.q: In 2v1, when should you pass?
questions.a: When the defender commits to you, pass to your teammate who is now open.

days.guide: Play a mini soccer or basketball game (2v2 or 3v3) for 15–20 minutes with simple rules. Pause to praise spacing, passing and fair play.

questions.q: What does fair play look like in a game?
questions.a: Following the rules, being honest about calls, no rough play, encouraging teammates and congratulating opponents.

days.guide: The child writes 3–5 sentences: one strategy they used (e.g., moving to open space, draw and pass, staying goal-side) and one fair-play moment.

questions.q: Give an example of a strategy and how it helped.
questions.a: E.g., 'I moved to open space so my brother could pass to me, and I scored.'

weeks.assessment_key: Game play observation and reflection rubric: 4 = during play the child moves to open space, uses a defensive stance goal-side, and passes when a teammate is open; reflection names a specific strategy, how it helped, and a specific fair-play moment; 3 = shows 2 of the 3 skills and reflection names a strategy and fair-play moment with less detail; 2 = mostly follows the ball, reflection vague; 1 = no reflection or unsafe play.

weeks.prep: Gather a paddle or short-handled racket (ping-pong paddle, paddleball or badminton racket), balloons and a tennis or foam ball. A flat wall such as a garage door for Thursday.
misconceptions: Swinging the whole arm wildly. Keep the paddle face flat and use small, controlled movements with a firm wrist.
Gripping too tight or holding the paddle at the end of the handle. Use a 'shake hands' grip close to the face for control.

days.guide: Teach the shake-hands grip. The child keeps a balloon up by tapping it gently with a flat paddle face, counting hits. Goal: 20 in a row.

questions.q: How do you hold the paddle?
questions.a: With a 'shake hands' grip, firm but relaxed.

days.guide: Bounce a ball upward on the paddle (paddle face flat, waist high), letting it rise only a few inches. Count consecutive hits in 3 trials.

questions.q: Why keep the paddle face flat?
questions.a: A flat face sends the ball straight up; a tilted face sends it sideways.

days.guide: Turn the paddle face down and 'dribble' the ball toward the ground while standing, then while walking slowly.

questions.q: How is a paddle down-dribble like a hand dribble?
questions.a: You push the ball down at a steady height and keep control while moving.

days.guide: Stand 6–8 feet from a wall. Drop the ball, let it bounce, hit it to the wall, let it bounce once, hit again. Count hits.

questions.q: How many bounces are allowed between wall hits?
questions.a: One.

days.guide: The child does 3 trials of up bounces and 3 of wall hits and records the best of each.

questions.q: Up bounce trials: 9, 15, 12. Best?

weeks.assessment_key: Paddle control counts: record best counts. Benchmarks for proficient: balloon 20 in a row, up bounces 10+, wall hits 5+ with one bounce between hits, with a flat paddle face and shake-hands grip. 4 = meets all benchmarks; 3 = meets 2; 2 = meets 1; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Paddle and ball, a wall, a rope or line on the ground as a 'net', and 2 hula hoops (or chalk circles) placed near and far.
misconceptions: Swinging down at the ball (chopping). Swing low to high to lift the ball over the net.
Facing the net. Turn the non-paddle side toward the target before swinging, just like the overhand throw.

days.guide: Teach forehand cues: 1) side to target (non-paddle shoulder toward the target), 2) swing low to high, 3) follow through toward the target and up. Shadow 20 swings, saying the cues.

questions.q: Name the 3 forehand cues.
questions.a: Side to target, swing low to high, follow through.

days.guide: Drop the ball beside the front foot, let it bounce, and hit a forehand to the wall 20 times. Count good hits that reach the wall above a chalk line.

questions.q: Where do you drop the ball for a drop hit?
questions.a: Out to the side and slightly in front of your body, on your paddle side.

days.guide: Rally over a rope or line with a partner, using forehands and counting hits in a row.

questions.q: Why swing low to high when hitting over a net?
questions.a: It lifts the ball up so it clears the net.

days.guide: Place hoops near and far. Hit forehands into each target, adjusting force: softer swing for near, firmer for far.

questions.q: How do you hit the far target?
questions.a: Use a bigger, firmer swing with more follow-through (more force).

days.guide: Forehand check: observe 5 forehands and score each on the 3 cues.

questions.q: Which foot is forward when a right-hander hits a forehand?
questions.a: The left foot (non-paddle side toward the target).

weeks.assessment_key: Forehand check: 5 hits × 3 cues = 15 points (side to target, low-to-high swing, follow through). 4 = 13–15 points; 3 = 10–12; 2 = 6–9; 1 = 0–5.

weeks.prep: Plastic bat, batting tee (or a tall cone), whiffle balls, and cones for left, center and right field. Mark a safety zone (a circle about 10 feet around the batter) where no one else may stand.
misconceptions: Hands apart or wrong hand on top. Right-handed batters put the left hand on the bottom, right hand on top, hands touching (stacked).
Throwing the bat after hitting. Drop or place the bat on the ground before running.

days.guide: Teach the grip (hands stacked, knuckles lined up, right-handers left hand on bottom) and side stance (feet shoulder-width, front shoulder toward the pitcher/tee, bat up). Take 20 dry swings with a level swing, stepping toward the target.

questions.q: For a right-handed batter, which hand goes on the bottom?
questions.a: The left hand.

questions.q: Which way does a batter face?
questions.a: Sideways, with the front shoulder pointing toward the pitcher/tee.

days.guide: Hit 20 balls off the tee at belly height, focusing on a level swing and following through. Count solid contacts.

questions.q: What is a level swing?
questions.a: A swing that moves flat across, through the ball, not chopping down or uppercutting.

days.guide: Show that hitting the ball earlier (out front) pulls it, and later sends it to the opposite field; open or close the stance to aim. Try to hit to left, center and right cones.

questions.q: If you turn your front foot slightly toward left field, where does the ball tend to go?
questions.a: Toward left field (for a right-handed batter).

days.guide: Mark the bat safety zone. Practice: check the zone is clear before swinging, then after hitting place the bat down and run. Practice 10 hit-and-place runs.

questions.q: What do you do with the bat after you hit?
questions.a: Drop or place it on the ground (never throw it) and run.

questions.q: Who can stand in the safety zone?
questions.a: Only the batter.

days.guide: Batting check: 10 swings off the tee, scored for contact and form (grip, stance, level swing, safe bat placement).

questions.q: Why do we place the bat instead of throwing it?
questions.a: A thrown bat can fly and hurt someone.

weeks.assessment_key: Batting check (10 hits): 1 point per solid contact (max 10) plus form points: correct stacked grip (1), side stance (1), level swing (1), bat placed safely each time (1). 4 = 7+ contacts and all 4 form points; 3 = 5–6 contacts and 3 form points; 2 = 3–4 contacts or 2 form points; 1 = fewer.

weeks.prep: Bat, tee, whiffle balls, paddles and a soft ball, bases (paper plates), cones for fielders; a score sheet.
misconceptions: Hitting straight to the fielder. Look for open space between or behind fielders and aim there.
Arguing calls. Agree on rules before playing and settle disagreements calmly (do-over or rock-paper-scissors).

days.guide: Play family whiffle ball with tee or soft underhand pitch: hit, run to first, simple outs (catch in air or ball to base before runner). Review bat safety.

questions.q: How can a fielder get a runner out?
questions.a: Catch the ball in the air, or get the ball to the base before the runner arrives (or tag the runner).

days.guide: Play paddle ball over a line: serve underhand, rally, and score a point when the ball lands in open space on the opponent's side.

questions.q: Where should you aim to score in paddle ball?
questions.a: Into open space away from your opponent.

days.guide: Place 2 fielders (cones or people). Discuss where the gaps are; the child tries to hit balls into the gaps and counts successes.

questions.q: Why place your hit away from fielders?
questions.a: So they can't catch it or field it quickly, giving you more time to run.

days.guide: The child chooses a striking game and keeps score fairly for the family, calling the score after each point.

questions.q: What does keeping score fairly mean?
questions.a: Counting points honestly for both sides and announcing the score accurately.

days.guide: Unit check: 5 paddle forehands to a target and 5 tee hits aimed at gaps.

questions.q: Name one cue that is the same for batting and the paddle forehand.
questions.a: Side to target (or step toward the target / follow through).

weeks.assessment_key: Striking unit check: paddle (5 forehands, 1 point each for landing in target zone with correct cues) + batting (5 tee hits, 1 point each for solid contact toward a gap) = 10. 4 = 9–10 plus fair, accurate scorekeeping; 3 = 7–8; 2 = 4–6; 1 = 0–3.

weeks.prep: Choose 4 songs with clearly different tempos (slow, medium, fast) that you have previewed for content. Clear space. For Thursday, choose a GoNoodle dance video (gonoodle.com, free account) and preview it.
misconceptions: Moving faster than the beat. Listen first and clap the steady beat before moving.
Thinking dance has to be fancy. Simple movements done on the beat with changes in level and direction make a strong dance.

days.guide: Play each song; first clap the steady beat, then march, then step side to side to it. Discuss which songs are fast (high tempo) and slow.

questions.q: What is tempo?
questions.a: How fast or slow the beat of the music is.

questions.q: How do you find the beat?
questions.a: Listen for the steady pulse and clap or tap along to it.

days.guide: Call 'high' (on tiptoes, arms up), 'middle' (standing normal), 'low' (crouched, near the floor) while dancing; switch every 8 counts.

questions.q: Name the 3 levels in dance.
questions.a: High, middle and low.

days.guide: Face each other; the leader moves in slow motion and the follower mirrors exactly, like a reflection. Switch every minute.

questions.q: If the leader raises their right arm, which arm does the mirror raise?
questions.a: Their left arm (like a reflection in a mirror).

days.guide: Watch the GoNoodle dance once, then follow along twice, then try to do parts without watching.

questions.q: How do you learn a dance from a video?
questions.a: Watch first, follow along, then practice small parts until you can do them without looking.

days.guide: Count '1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8' to the music. The child creates 8 counts of movement (e.g., 4 steps right, 2 claps, a turn) and performs it 3 times in a row on the beat.

questions.q: How many counts in a dance phrase like ours?
questions.a: 8 counts.

weeks.assessment_key: 8-count phrase rubric: 4 = original 8-count phrase performed on the beat, repeated 3 times the same way, uses at least 2 levels; 3 = on the beat with small changes between repeats; 2 = off the beat often or fewer than 8 counts; 1 = cannot create a phrase.

weeks.prep: Find instrumental music for each dance (a lively fiddle reel for the Virginia Reel and the traditional Jarabe Tapatío music, both widely available) and a short video of each to preview. Need at least 2 people for the reel (more is better).
misconceptions: Thinking the Mexican Hat Dance is just about a hat. The Jarabe Tapatío is Mexico's national folk dance from Jalisco; the hat comes from the part where the man's sombrero is placed on the ground and the woman dances around its brim.
Thinking folk dances were made up recently or by one person. Folk dances grow out of the traditions of a community and are passed down over generations.

days.guide: Teach Virginia Reel figures in two facing lines: forward and back (4 steps in, 4 out), right-hand turn, left-hand turn, two-hand turn, do-si-do (pass right shoulders, back to back, return). Then the head couple sashays down the middle and back.

questions.q: What is a do-si-do?
questions.a: Partners walk forward, pass right shoulders, step side by side back to back, and walk backward to their places without turning around.

days.guide: Teach the basic heel-toe pattern: hop slightly and touch the right heel forward, then the left heel, then a quick three-step stamp (zapateado) pattern. Practice slowly counting aloud.

questions.q: Which country does the Jarabe Tapatío come from?
questions.a: Mexico (the state of Jalisco).

days.guide: Practice each dance to music, counting steps aloud. Slow the music or count slowly at first.

questions.q: Why count aloud when learning a dance?
questions.a: It keeps the steps matched to the beat and helps you remember the order.

days.guide: Share background: the Virginia Reel is an American country dance with roots in English and Scottish reels, popular in colonial and pioneer times at social gatherings. The Jarabe Tapatío is Mexico's national dance from Jalisco ('tapatío' means from Guadalajara), a courtship dance performed at celebrations and fiestas. Find both places on a map.

questions.q: Where do the roots of the Virginia Reel come from?
questions.a: English and Scottish country dances (reels), brought to America.

questions.q: Why are folk dances danced?
questions.a: To celebrate and share a community's culture at gatherings, festivals and holidays.

days.guide: Perform both dances for family. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Tell your audience one fact about each dance.
questions.a: Virginia Reel: American country dance from English/Scottish reels; Jarabe Tapatío: Mexico's national dance from Jalisco.

weeks.assessment_key: Folk dance performance rubric: 4 = performs the main figures of the Virginia Reel (forward and back, turns, do-si-do) and the Jarabe heel-toe steps in order and on the beat, and states where each dance comes from; 3 = most figures correct with a few prompts; 2 = needs frequent prompts or off beat; 1 = cannot perform figures.

weeks.prep: Preview recordings of the 'Cha-Cha Slide' and an Electric Slide song (radio edits are fine; check content). Clear space with room to step 4 steps in each direction. Timer and heart-rate log.
misconceptions: Crossing in front in the grapevine. The trailing foot crosses behind the leading foot.
Turning the wrong way in a line dance. In the Electric Slide, the quarter turn goes to the left so the group faces a new wall each time.

days.guide: Teach the grapevine to the right: step right to the side (1), left foot crosses behind (2), step right to the side (3), touch left beside right (4); then reverse to the left (5–8). Practice slowly, then to music.

questions.q: In a grapevine to the right, where does the left foot cross?
questions.a: Behind the right foot.

questions.q: How many counts is a grapevine right and left?
questions.a: 8 counts (4 right, 4 left).

days.guide: Play the Cha-Cha Slide; the song calls out each move, so the child listens and responds (slides, hops, stomps, cha-cha). Practice the moves without music first, then with it.

questions.q: Why is the Cha-Cha Slide easy to learn?
questions.a: The song tells you which move to do next, so you just listen and follow the calls.

days.guide: Teach the Electric Slide pattern: grapevine right, grapevine left, walk back 3 and touch, rock forward and back, then a quarter turn to the left and repeat facing the new wall.

questions.q: After one full pattern, which way do you face?
questions.a: A new wall, a quarter turn to the left.

days.guide: Take resting heart rate. Dance 3 songs in a row, then immediately take a 15-second pulse × 4 and compare.

questions.q: Resting 84 bpm; after dancing you count 33 in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate and how much did it rise?
Is line dancing exercise? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes — your heart rate and breathing go up, which works your heart and lungs.

days.guide: The child performs the Electric Slide (or Cha-Cha Slide) start to finish without you calling the steps.

questions.q: What is a line dance?
questions.a: A dance where people stand in lines and do the same steps at the same time, often turning to face new walls.

weeks.assessment_key: Line dance performance rubric: 4 = performs a full line dance with correct steps in order, on the beat, with correct turns and no cues; 3 = one or two small errors, recovers quickly; 2 = needs some cues; 1 = needs cues throughout.

weeks.prep: Help the child choose a song (instrumental works well) about 1 minute long. Paper for the dance plan. Review vocabulary: levels (high/middle/low), pathways (straight/curved/zigzag), tempo, force (strong/light).
misconceptions: Making each part different with no repetition. Repeating a phrase gives the dance structure, like a chorus in a song.
Forgetting the beginning and ending shapes. A dance starts and ends with a still shape to frame it.

days.guide: Choose a song and theme (ocean, storm, animals). Brainstorm 4 movement ideas that match the theme and name the level and pathway for each (e.g., waves = low, curved pathway).

questions.q: How could you show a storm with force?
questions.a: Strong, sharp, fast movements (stamping, quick arm slashes) — and a calm part with light, slow movements.

questions.q: Give a movement idea that uses a low level.
questions.a: E.g., crawling like a crab or rolling like a wave close to the floor.

days.guide: Build a 32-count dance: beginning shape, three 8-count phrases, and an ending shape (the shapes and phrases add up to 32 counts — e.g., 4 counts start shape, 3 × 8 phrases, 4 counts end shape). Write it in a chart.

questions.q: How many 8-count phrases fit in 32 counts?
If your start and end shapes take 4 counts each, how many counts are left for phrases?
questions.a: 32 − 8 = 24, which is 3 phrases of 8.

days.guide: Rehearse 5 times. Add one tempo change (e.g., slow-motion phrase) and one level change.

questions.q: What is a tempo change in dance?
questions.a: Moving faster or slower than before (e.g., switching to slow motion).

days.guide: Perform for family, then teach them one phrase by demonstrating and counting.

questions.q: How do you teach a phrase to someone?
questions.a: Show it, break it into small parts with counts, do it together, then let them try alone.

days.guide: The child describes how they used force, levels and pathways and what they would change next time.

questions.q: Describe one place in your dance you used a curved pathway.
questions.a: Answer should name a specific part, e.g., 'I skipped in a circle during phrase 2 to show swirling water.'

weeks.assessment_key: Original dance rubric: 4 = 32 counts with beginning and ending shapes, 3 phrases matching the theme, uses all 3 levels, at least 2 pathways, a tempo change and clear force changes; child explains choices; 3 = most elements present, one missing; 2 = dance is short or unclear and few elements; 1 = no planned dance.

weeks.prep: Gather a hula hoop, an old blanket or tarp, 3 balloons, a blindfold or scarf, and soft 'mines' (shoes, pillows, cones). Gather 3+ family members. Timer for each challenge.
misconceptions: Thinking the fastest person should do all the work. Teamwork means every member has a role and the group plans together.
Thinking cooperative games have no winner so effort doesn't matter. The team competes against the clock or a goal, so everyone's effort counts.

days.guide: Stand in a circle holding hands. Pass the hula hoop all the way around by stepping through it without letting go of hands. Time 3 rounds and talk about strategies that made it faster.

questions.q: What strategy helped your team get faster?
questions.a: E.g., talking/helping each other, dipping a shoulder, the next person getting ready early.

days.guide: Everyone stands on the blanket. Without anyone stepping off, the group flips the blanket over. Plan first, then try.

questions.q: Why is planning before trying important?
questions.a: It gives everyone a role and an idea so the team works together instead of guessing.

days.guide: Keep 3 balloons in the air for 60 seconds using only assigned body parts (e.g., elbows, heads, knees). Restart the timer if one touches the ground.

questions.q: What did you do when a balloon was about to fall near someone else?
questions.a: Called out to warn them or moved to help, while keeping my own balloon up.

days.guide: Set up 'minefield': one partner is blindfolded, the other guides them through the mines using only words. Switch. Discuss trust and clear directions.

questions.q: What makes a good guide?
questions.a: Clear, calm, specific directions ('two small steps forward, stop, step left'), and keeping your partner safe.

questions.q: Why is trust important in this game?
questions.a: The blindfolded partner can't see and must believe the guide will keep them safe.

days.guide: Repeat the fastest challenge, time it, and have the child name encouraging words that helped.

questions.q: Name two encouraging things teammates said.
questions.a: E.g., 'You've got this,' 'Nice job,' 'Almost there,' 'Let's try again.'

weeks.assessment_key: Team challenge rubric: 4 = participates fully, shares an idea in planning, uses encouraging words, follows safety rules, and names specific encouraging words; 3 = participates and encourages others with prompting; 2 = participates but discourages others or ignores the plan; 1 = refuses to participate.

weeks.prep: Belt flags or scarves tucked into waistbands, cones for boundaries and lanes, two 'flags' (bandanas) for capture the flag; invite friends or siblings if possible.
misconceptions: Running straight at a tagger. Use fakes, quick changes of direction and open space.
Thinking an honest call loses the game. Honesty keeps the game fair and fun, and others will trust you.

days.guide: Tuck a flag in each side of the waistband. Players try to pull others' flags while protecting their own, using open space. A pulled flag means do 5 jumping jacks and rejoin.

questions.q: How do you avoid taggers in flag tag?
questions.a: Move into open space away from them, keep your eyes up and change direction quickly.

questions.q: Is it fair to hold your flag with your hand?
questions.a: No — you protect it by moving, not by holding or blocking it.

days.guide: Set a cone lane. A defender stands in the middle; the child gets past using a fake (lean one way, go the other), a pivot, or a change of speed.

questions.q: Name 3 dodging moves.
questions.a: Fake, pivot (turn on one foot), change of speed (and change of direction).

days.guide: Play capture the flag: two territories, a flag at the back of each. Plan roles: defenders guard, attackers try to grab the opposing flag. Tagged players go to 'jail' until freed.

questions.q: Why have both offense and defense players?
questions.a: So you can try to capture the other flag while still protecting your own.

days.guide: Role-play situations: you feel a tag but no one saw; the score is close and you step out of bounds. Practice saying 'I was tagged' or 'I was out.'

questions.q: Why does honesty keep games fun?
questions.a: Everyone trusts the game is fair, there are fewer arguments, and people want to keep playing together.

days.guide: Write a 3–5 sentence reflection: which strategy helped your team most and why, with an example.

questions.q: Give an example of a team strategy in capture the flag.
questions.a: E.g., two players run at once so defenders can't guard both; one gets the flag.

weeks.assessment_key: Strategy reflection rubric: 4 = names a specific strategy (e.g., fake, use open space, split offense/defense), explains why it worked with an example from play, and mentions fair play; 3 = names a strategy with a basic reason; 2 = vague ("we ran fast"); 1 = no reflection.

weeks.prep: Balloon or beach ball, a rope tied between two chairs at about the child's head height as a net, a playground ball, chalk to draw a four-square court (4 squares, each about 5–6 feet), and a wall.
misconceptions: Hitting the balloon with a fist. Use two-hand volleys with fingers spread and slightly bent, pushing up.
Catching or holding the ball in four square. Hit it with an open palm; no catching or carrying.

days.guide: Teach the two-hand volley: hands above forehead in a triangle shape, fingers spread, push up. Rally a balloon over the rope net, counting team hits.

questions.q: Where should your hands be for a volley?
questions.a: Above your forehead, fingers spread like holding a big ball, pushing up and out.

days.guide: Teach four square rules: the ball bounces once in your square, then you hit it with an open palm (underhand) to another square; you are out if it bounces twice, you miss, or you hit it out of bounds. The server is in the highest square (4 or 'king').

questions.q: When are you out in four square?
questions.a: If the ball bounces twice in your square, you hit it out of bounds or on a line (by your rules), or you don't hit it after it bounces in your square.

questions.q: How do you hit the ball in four square?
questions.a: With an open palm (or both hands), underhand, after one bounce — no catching.

days.guide: Partners take turns hitting a playground ball against a wall after one bounce, alternating hits. Count the longest rally.

questions.q: Why is moving your feet important in a rally?
questions.a: It gets you in position behind the ball so you can make a controlled hit.

days.guide: Play 2v2 over the net with a balloon or beach ball, aiming for open spaces on the other side; up to 3 team hits per side.

questions.q: Where should you aim to win the point?
questions.a: Into open space where the other team isn't standing.

days.guide: Skill check: 10 two-hand volleys to a partner, counting controlled ones (reach the partner and are catchable).

questions.q: Out of 10 volleys, 8 reached your partner. What percent is that?

weeks.assessment_key: Volley skill check: count controlled two-hand volleys (correct hand shape, ball goes up and reaches partner) out of 10. 4 = 9–10; 3 = 7–8; 2 = 4–6; 1 = 0–3.

weeks.prep: Rubber playground ball (kickball), 4 bases (paper plates or cones) about 30–45 feet apart, a stopwatch, and players (family/co-op). Review rules on a card.
misconceptions: Running straight to first base and stopping. Run through first base; when going for second, round first by curving out a little before the base.
Thinking a fly ball means the runner keeps running. On a caught fly ball, runners must tag up (return to touch their base) before advancing.

days.guide: Teach rules: pitcher rolls the ball; the kicker kicks it; fair if it lands inside the first and third base lines; foul outside. Outs: caught fly, ball to base before runner, or tagging/hitting the runner below the shoulders (if your family allows). 3 outs switch sides. Practice smooth rolling pitches.

questions.q: When is a kick foul?
questions.a: When it goes outside the first-base or third-base line (out of fair territory).

questions.q: How many outs before the teams switch?
questions.a: 3 outs.

days.guide: Roll pitches. The child kicks to left, center or right, aiming between fielders (cones).

questions.q: Where should you aim your kick?
questions.a: Into open space between or past fielders.

days.guide: Time runs to first (run through the base) and around all bases (rounding each by curving out before the base). Practice tagging up: start on the base and leave only after the catch.

questions.q: What does tagging up mean?
questions.a: After a fly ball is caught, the runner must touch their base before running to the next one.

questions.q: Why do you round a base?
questions.a: Curving out a little before the base lets you turn and keep running at full speed to the next base.

days.guide: Play 3 innings. Everyone cheers for both teams with specific encouragement ('Great kick to open space!').

questions.q: Give an example of specific encouragement.
questions.a: E.g., 'Nice catch with your hands out!' or 'Great job rounding first!'

days.guide: Game play check: observe kicking (contact, aiming), fielding (moving to the ball, throwing to base), and sportsmanship.

questions.q: If you are fielding a ground ball and a runner is going to first, where do you throw?
questions.a: To first base (to get the runner out).

weeks.assessment_key: Game play check rubric: Kicking — makes contact and aims to open space; Fielding — moves to the ball, fields it and throws to the correct base; Sportsmanship — follows rules, encourages both teams. 4 = proficient in all 3; 3 = proficient in 2; 2 = proficient in 1; 1 = needs help in all.

weeks.prep: Fitness log with baseline scores from week 3, tape measure, sit-and-reach box, mat, stopwatch, the same half-mile route or PACER lane and audio. Use the same procedure and cadence as week 3 so results compare fairly.
misconceptions: Thinking a lower score means failure. Growth in any test or effort matters; compare to your own baseline, not to others.
Skipping the warm-up to save energy. Warming up gives more accurate, safer results.

days.guide: Warm up. Retest curl-ups and 90-degree push-ups using the week 3 cadence and form. Record and compare to baseline.

questions.q: Baseline curl-ups: 12. Today: 19. How many more?

days.guide: Warm up with dynamic moves, then retest back-saver sit-and-reach (each leg) and the shoulder stretch. Record.

questions.q: Why must the warm-up be the same as in week 3?
questions.a: So the test conditions are the same and the comparison is fair.

days.guide: Retest the half-mile walk/run or PACER, pacing steadily. Record time or laps and cool down.

questions.q: Baseline half-mile 6:10; today 5:40. Did you improve, and by how much?
questions.a: Yes — 30 seconds faster (6:10 − 5:40 = 0:30).

days.guide: Make a double bar graph: for each test, a bar for baseline and a bar for current. Label axes and title.

questions.q: For a timed run, is a taller bar better?
questions.a: No — for time, a shorter (lower) bar means faster, which is better. For counts like curl-ups, taller is better.

days.guide: The child writes whether they met their SMART goal, using numbers, and what helped most (practice, warm-up, effort).

questions.q: Did you meet your goal? Show with numbers.
questions.a: Answer should compare goal and result, e.g., 'My goal was 15 curl-ups and I did 19, so I met it.'

weeks.assessment_key: Fitness progress comparison: proficient work includes all retest scores recorded beside baseline, differences computed correctly (e.g., 12 → 19 curl-ups = +7; run time decreases are improvement), a labeled double bar graph, and a written statement of whether the SMART goal was met with numbers and a reason. 4 = all parts; 3 = one error; 2 = missing graph or statement; 1 = scores only.

weeks.prep: Water bottle and a cup-tally sheet, snack cards (e.g., banana, apple, whole-grain crackers, yogurt, candy bar, chips, soda, cookies, orange slices, water), 6 stations for the circuit, timer and heart-rate log.
misconceptions: Waiting until you are thirsty to drink. Drink water before, during and after activity; thirst means you are already starting to dry out.
Thinking sports drinks or soda are needed for normal play. For kids' everyday activity, water is the best choice.

days.guide: Before a 20-minute active play session, drink a cup of water; drink small sips during and a cup after. Tally cups. Talk about signs of dehydration (thirst, dry mouth, headache, dizziness, dark yellow urine).

questions.q: When should you drink water during exercise?
questions.a: Before, during (small sips at breaks) and after.

questions.q: Name two signs your body needs more water.
questions.a: Any two: thirst, dry mouth, headache, feeling tired or dizzy, dark yellow urine.

days.guide: Sort snack cards: good pre-activity fuel (fruit, whole-grain crackers, yogurt, a small sandwich) vs. sometimes foods (candy, chips, soda, cookies). Explain that carbohydrates give energy. Then do a 15-minute jog-and-skip workout.

questions.q: Why is a banana a good snack before playing?
questions.a: It gives carbohydrates for energy (and potassium) without making you feel heavy or sick.

questions.q: Why are candy and soda 'sometimes' foods?
questions.a: They have lots of sugar and few nutrients, so the energy doesn't last and they don't help your body grow.

days.guide: Complete a 6-station circuit, 1 minute each. After each round, take a 15-second pulse × 4 and record.

questions.q: Round 1 count: 30 beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate per minute?

days.guide: Look at the circuit data and explain how heart rate and breathing changed and why.

questions.q: Why did your heart rate and breathing rise during the circuit?
questions.a: Muscles needed more oxygen; the heart beat faster to pump blood and the lungs breathed faster to bring in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What happened when you rested?
questions.a: Heart rate and breathing slowed back down.

days.guide: Give the quiz below orally or on paper.

questions.q: Is water or soda the better drink for exercise?
questions.a: Water.

weeks.assessment_key: Fuel quiz (5 questions): 1) Best drink for everyday exercise? — Water. 2) Name a good pre-activity snack. — Any healthy carbohydrate food, e.g., banana, apple, whole-grain crackers, yogurt. 3) When should you drink water? — Before, during and after activity. 4) What happens to heart rate during exercise and why? — It goes up to pump more oxygen-rich blood to working muscles. 5) Name a sign of dehydration. — Thirst, dry mouth, headache, dizziness or dark urine. Proficient = 4 of 5 correct.

weeks.prep: Cones, a baton (paper-towel tube), pillowcases for sack hops, a scarf or soft tie for the three-legged race, a softball, measuring tape. Mark a start/finish line and a 50-yard course if possible.
misconceptions: Looking back and slowing down during a baton pass. The receiver starts moving and reaches back; the passer says 'Stick!' and places the baton in the hand.
Rushing the three-legged start. Partners agree which legs are tied and say 'tied leg, outside leg' together to stay in step.

days.guide: Practice a baton pass: receiver reaches back with an open hand while jogging; the runner places the baton in it. Then shuttle relays: run to a cone, tag the next runner.

questions.q: In a shuttle relay, when can the next runner go?
questions.a: Only after being tagged (or receiving the baton) by the incoming runner.

days.guide: Practice pillowcase hops (hold the top, small two-foot jumps). Then practice three-legged starts with a partner: tie inside legs, step 'tied leg first' together.

questions.q: What's the trick to a fast three-legged race?
questions.a: Move together in rhythm, calling out which leg to step with.

days.guide: Use the overhand cues to throw a softball for distance. Do 3 throws, measure the best.

questions.q: Which cue helps distance most?
questions.a: A big step with the opposite foot plus full rotation and follow through.

days.guide: Do 3 standing long jumps and record the best; compare to week 5.

questions.q: Week 5 best: 47 inches. Today: 52 inches. How much farther?
questions.a: 5 inches.

days.guide: Run a mini field day with 4 events (e.g., relay, sack hop, softball throw, long jump). Record personal results on a sheet.

questions.q: Why is it good to compare to your own past results?
questions.a: It shows your personal improvement no matter how others did.

weeks.assessment_key: Mini field day check: results sheet lists 4 events with a recorded time/distance for each, measured correctly, and the child shows good effort and sportsmanship. 4 = all 4 results recorded accurately plus a comparison to an earlier result; 3 = all 4 recorded; 2 = 2–3 recorded; 1 = fewer.

weeks.prep: Arrange field day with family or co-op friends. Equipment: cones, measuring tape, stopwatch, softball, pillowcases, ties, water balloons, relay obstacle items (ball, hoops, cones). Have water and shade. Make simple sportsmanship award certificates.
misconceptions: Thinking only winners did well. Effort, improvement and kindness are also wins.
Throwing water balloons too hard. Use a soft underhand toss and 'reach and give' to catch.

days.guide: Run the 50-yard dash, standing long jump and softball throw. Record each result.

questions.q: How do you start a sprint?
questions.a: Ready position: one foot forward, knees bent, leaning forward, eyes ahead; push off on 'Go.'

days.guide: Run the sack race, three-legged race and water-balloon toss (step back after each successful catch).

questions.q: How do you catch a water balloon without breaking it?
questions.a: Reach out, catch with soft hands and 'give' by pulling it in gently.

days.guide: Run the team obstacle relay: dribble through cones, jump into hoops, throw at a target, then tag the next runner.

questions.q: Which skills from this year did you use in the relay?
questions.a: Dribbling, jumping/landing, and overhand throwing.

days.guide: The child writes and presents a sportsmanship award to each teammate, naming a specific kind action.

questions.q: Give an example of a specific sportsmanship award.
questions.a: E.g., 'Cheerful Teammate Award to Sam for clapping for everyone on the sack race.'

days.guide: Write a reflection comparing field day results to fall fitness scores and earlier unit results.

questions.q: Example comparison sentence?
questions.a: E.g., 'In fall my long jump was 47 inches and on field day it was 53 inches, 6 inches farther.'

weeks.assessment_key: Field day participation rubric: 4 = takes part in all events with full effort, records results, gives specific sportsmanship awards, and writes a reflection that compares at least 2 results with numbers; 3 = all events and a reflection with 1 comparison; 2 = partial participation or reflection without comparisons; 1 = minimal participation.

weeks.prep: Print a summer calendar (June–August) and a weekly activity log. Plan a family hike or bike ride (bring water, sunscreen, helmet). Preview a new activity option for safety (e.g., swimming only with adult supervision, skateboarding with helmet and pads).
misconceptions: Thinking 60 minutes must happen all at once. Daily activity can add up in chunks (e.g., 20 + 20 + 20 minutes).
Doing only one activity all summer. Mixing activity types works different fitness components and keeps it fun.

days.guide: Explain that kids need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day. The child fills a summer calendar with at least 4 activity types (e.g., swimming, biking, jump rope, soccer, dance, hiking).

questions.q: How many minutes of activity should kids get each day?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes.

questions.q: You biked 25 minutes and swam 20 minutes. How many more minutes to reach 60?
questions.a: 60 − 45 = 15 more minutes.

days.guide: Try a new activity for 30 minutes with proper safety gear and supervision, then rate it 1–5 and explain the rating.

questions.q: What safety gear would you need for skateboarding or biking?
questions.a: A helmet (and for skateboarding, knee pads, elbow pads and wrist guards).

days.guide: Go on a family hike or bike ride and measure the distance with a phone app, map or odometer. Bring water and sunscreen.

questions.q: Which fitness component does a long hike build most?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance (and leg muscular endurance).

days.guide: Fill in a week of the summer log and write a summer skill goal that is SMART (e.g., 'I will jump rope 50 times in a row by August 1 by practicing 10 minutes 4 days a week').

questions.q: Make your skill goal SMART.
questions.a: It must be specific, measurable (a number), achievable, relevant and have a date.

days.guide: The child shares the summer plan with the family and leads their favorite warm-up.

questions.q: Why warm up even in the summer?
questions.a: Warming up prepares muscles and the heart for activity and helps prevent injury every time.

weeks.assessment_key: Summer plan rubric: 4 = calendar shows 60 minutes of activity daily across 4+ activity types, a week of the log is filled in, and a SMART skill goal with number and date; child leads a correct warm-up; 3 = plan complete but goal missing one SMART part; 2 = plan incomplete or fewer than 4 activity types; 1 = no plan.

SCI.overview: Science is taught through hands-on investigations: ask a question, predict, test fairly, record data in the science notebook, and explain results with evidence. Let the child do the hands-on work while you ask 'What do you notice? Why do you think that happened?' Use claim–evidence–reasoning for every written explanation, and keep all safety notes (adult handles pins and plaster; return live animals unharmed).

weeks.prep: Science notebook, a rope or towel, a toy car, several books. Preview a Mystery Science (free lessons) or similar video on balanced and unbalanced forces.
misconceptions: Thinking a still object has no forces on it — a book on a table is pushed down by gravity and up by the table; the forces are balanced.
Thinking a bigger object always wins a push — what matters is which force is stronger (unbalanced).

days.guide: Explain that a force is a push or a pull. Walk through the house together naming pushes and pulls (opening a drawer = pull, closing a door = push). The child records 20 in a T-chart and you check that each is sorted correctly.

questions.q: Is opening a refrigerator door a push or a pull?
questions.a: A pull.

questions.q: What is a force?
questions.a: A push or a pull on an object.

days.guide: Play a gentle towel tug-of-war: first pull equally so nothing moves, then let one person pull harder. The child draws arrows for each pull — equal-length arrows for balanced, a longer arrow for the stronger pull.

questions.q: When both people pull equally and the towel doesn't move, what kind of forces are these?
questions.a: Balanced forces — equal in strength and opposite in direction.

questions.q: What happens when one side pulls harder?
questions.a: The forces are unbalanced, so the towel moves toward the stronger pull.

days.guide: Push a book from both sides with equal force (it stays still), then push harder on one side (it slides). The child records what happens each time and labels the forces balanced or unbalanced.

questions.q: Predict: if you push a book from the left harder than from the right, which way will it move?
questions.a: To the right — the stronger push from the left moves it away from the left side.

days.guide: Watch a short video on forces. The child draws arrow diagrams for a book sitting on a table (gravity down, table pushing up — equal arrows) and a cart being pushed (a longer arrow in the direction it moves).

questions.q: What forces act on a book sitting still on a table?
questions.a: Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up; the forces are balanced.

days.guide: The child writes an explanation with diagrams of why an object starts moving only when forces are unbalanced, using an example from the week. Check that the arrows match the explanation.

questions.q: Why does a soccer ball on the ground start rolling when kicked?
questions.a: The kick is a force that makes the forces unbalanced, so the ball changes its motion.

weeks.assessment_key: Explanation rubric: 4 = defines balanced and unbalanced forces, gives a home example, draws correct arrows (equal/opposite for balanced; one stronger for unbalanced) and states that motion changes only when forces are unbalanced; 3 (proficient) = correct idea with one diagram; 2 = partly correct; 1 = incorrect (e.g., says still objects have no forces).

weeks.prep: Toy car, a board and books for a ramp, a tape measure, and three floor surfaces (carpet, tile, towel). Draw a data table with columns for 3 trials.
misconceptions: Changing more than one thing at a time — in a fair test only one variable changes.
Thinking one trial is enough — repeat trials to make results reliable.

days.guide: Ask: Does ramp height change how far a car travels? The child writes the question, a prediction, the one thing they will change (height) and the things that stay the same (car, release point, floor, no pushing).

questions.q: What must stay the same in this test?
questions.a: The car, the surface, the starting spot on the ramp, and releasing without pushing — only the ramp height changes.

questions.q: Why is it called a 'fair test'?
questions.a: Only one variable changes, so we know that variable caused the result.

days.guide: Run 3 trials at each of 3 ramp heights (1, 2 and 3 books), measuring from the bottom of the ramp to where the car stops. The child records each distance in the table.

questions.q: Predict: will the car go farther from a higher ramp?
questions.a: Yes — a higher ramp gives the car more speed, so it usually travels farther.

days.guide: Keep the ramp the same height and change the surface at the bottom: carpet, tile, towel. Measure and record distances, 3 trials each.

questions.q: On which surface will the car go farthest, and why?
questions.a: Tile — it is smoothest, so there is the least friction slowing the car.

questions.q: What is friction?
questions.a: A force between surfaces rubbing together that slows motion.

days.guide: Help the child find the middle (or typical) result for each test and make a bar graph. The child writes a claim supported by data, e.g., 'Higher ramps make the car go farther, and rough surfaces stop it sooner.'

questions.q: What does a rough surface do to a moving car?
questions.a: It creates more friction, which slows the car and makes it stop sooner.

days.guide: The child writes how they kept the test fair and one thing to improve. Discuss sources of error (pushing the car, measuring to different points).

questions.q: Name one way to improve the investigation.
questions.a: Do more trials, release the car the same way every time, or measure more carefully to the back wheels.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report: 4 = question, prediction, controlled variables named, complete data table with 3 trials, graph, claim supported by numbers, and an improvement; 3 (proficient) = most parts with a data-based claim (higher ramp → farther; more friction → shorter distance); 2 = data but no claim; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: String, metal washers, tape, a timer, a ball and a meter stick or tape measure. Find a doorframe or table edge to hang the pendulum from.
misconceptions: Thinking heavier washers change a pendulum's swing rate — mainly the length changes it; test to see.
Thinking a ball should bounce back to the same height — some energy changes to sound and heat each bounce.

days.guide: Tape a string with a washer to the edge of a table so it can swing freely. Pull it back a little and release (don't push); count complete back-and-forth swings in 15 seconds. Repeat 3 times and record.

questions.q: What is a pendulum?
questions.a: A weight hanging from a fixed point that swings back and forth.

questions.q: Why count swings 3 times?
questions.a: To make sure the result is reliable.

days.guide: Shorten and then lengthen the string, counting swings in 15 seconds for each. The child looks for the pattern and predicts the result for the next length before testing.

questions.q: What happens to the number of swings when the string gets longer?
questions.a: There are fewer swings in 15 seconds — a longer pendulum swings more slowly.

questions.q: Predict for a very short string.
questions.a: Many quick swings.

days.guide: Drop a ball from 1 meter next to a wall marked with tape and record the height of each bounce. The child describes the pattern.

questions.q: What pattern do the bounces show?
questions.a: Each bounce is lower than the one before until the ball stops.

questions.q: Why does each bounce get lower?
questions.a: Some energy changes into sound and heat every time the ball hits the ground.

days.guide: Watch a swing or seesaw (or a video) and describe the repeating motion. The child draws arrows to show the back-and-forth or up-and-down pattern.

questions.q: How is a playground swing like a pendulum?
questions.a: It hangs from a fixed point and swings back and forth in a repeating pattern.

days.guide: Using their data, the child predicts the number of swings for a new string length, then tests it. They explain whether the prediction matched and why.

questions.q: If a 20 cm pendulum swings 16 times in 15 seconds and a 40 cm one swings 11 times, predict a 30 cm pendulum.
questions.a: Between 11 and 16 swings (about 13) — it is between the two lengths.

weeks.assessment_key: Prediction test: proficient (3) = prediction falls between or beyond the data in the correct direction (longer = fewer swings), test performed fairly (same release height), and explanation compares result to prediction; 2 = prediction made but not explained; 1 = prediction ignores the pattern.

weeks.prep: Cardboard, paper towel tubes, straws, tape, marbles, a cup, a meter stick. Write the Unit 1 quiz.
misconceptions: Blaming 'bad luck' when a design fails — identify the force (gravity, friction, a collision) causing it.
Changing several things at once while improving — change one thing, then retest.

days.guide: Present the challenge: a marble must travel at least 1 meter along the run and stop in a cup. The child sketches a plan with labels and lists materials.

questions.q: What force pulls the marble down the run?
questions.a: Gravity.

days.guide: The child builds the run from the sketch, taping tubes and folded cardboard to a wall, box or chair. Help with cutting but let them make the design choices.

questions.q: Why must the run slope downward?
questions.a: So gravity keeps pulling the marble forward along the run.

days.guide: Test the run 3 times and record where the marble fails (falls off, stops, misses the cup). For each failure, the child names the force involved.

questions.q: The marble flies off at a sharp turn. What is happening?
questions.a: It is moving too fast to change direction; there isn't enough sideways push from the wall to turn it, so it needs a taller wall or a gentler curve.

questions.q: The marble stops halfway. Why?
questions.a: Friction slowed it and the slope wasn't steep enough for gravity to keep it moving.

days.guide: The child changes one part of the design to fix the biggest problem, retests and records the result.

questions.q: Why change only one thing at a time?
questions.a: So you know which change made the difference.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 quiz and review the testing log. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What happens to a moving object when forces are balanced?
questions.a: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction (or stays still if it was still).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 quiz: 1) A force is → a push or pull 2) Balanced forces → equal and opposite, no change in motion 3) Unbalanced forces → cause a change in motion (start, stop, speed up, turn) 4) Friction → slows moving objects 5) Longer pendulum → swings more slowly (fewer swings) 6) Bouncing ball → each bounce lower 7) Draw arrows for a tug-of-war that is balanced. Proficient 6+/7. Testing log: proficient if failures, the force involved, the change made and the retest result are recorded.

weeks.prep: Refrigerator and bar magnets, paper clips, 15 household objects (spoon, foil, coins, nail, eraser, key, plastic toy …), paper, cardboard, a cup of water.
misconceptions: Thinking magnets attract all metals — magnets attract iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, but not aluminum, copper or most coins.
Thinking magnetic force needs contact — it acts at a distance and passes through many materials.

days.guide: The child predicts whether each object will be attracted, then tests it with a magnet. Sort into attracted / not attracted and look for a pattern.

questions.q: Will a magnet pick up aluminum foil?
questions.a: No — aluminum is not magnetic.

questions.q: What do the attracted objects have in common?
questions.a: They contain iron or steel (or nickel).

days.guide: Bring the ends of two bar magnets together in all combinations and record which attract and which repel.

questions.q: What happens when two north poles face each other?
questions.a: They repel (push apart).

questions.q: What happens when north faces south?
questions.a: They attract (pull together).

days.guide: Test whether a magnet can move a paper clip through paper, cardboard, plastic and water (put the clip in a cup of water and move the magnet outside the cup).

questions.q: Can magnetic force pass through paper and water?
questions.a: Yes — the magnet still pulls the paper clip through them.

days.guide: Stack sheets of paper between a magnet and a paper clip, adding sheets until the clip no longer jumps. Record the number of sheets for two different magnets.

questions.q: What happens to magnetic force as distance increases?
questions.a: It gets weaker.

questions.q: How could you compare two magnets' strength?
questions.a: See which one can pull the clip through more sheets of paper.

days.guide: The child writes 4 cause-and-effect sentences ('Because the poles are the same, the magnets repel').

questions.q: Complete: When a magnet is moved closer to a paper clip, …
questions.a: the pull gets stronger and the clip may jump to the magnet.

weeks.assessment_key: Cause/effect explanation: proficient (3) = 4 accurate sentences covering attraction of iron/steel, like poles repel/unlike attract, force through materials, and force weakens with distance; 2 = 2–3 accurate; 1 = misconceptions (e.g., all metals attracted).

weeks.prep: Balloons, tissue paper torn into small bits, a plastic comb, an empty aluminum can, and the free PhET 'Balloons and Static Electricity' simulation (phet.colorado.edu). Note: static works best on dry days.
misconceptions: Thinking static electricity is the same as magnetism — static comes from electric charges; it can attract paper and aluminum, which magnets cannot.
Thinking rubbing 'creates' electricity — rubbing moves tiny negative charges (electrons) from one object to another.

days.guide: Rub a balloon on dry hair for 10 seconds and hold it near tissue bits. The child records what happens, then tests whether it still works after touching the balloon to a metal doorknob.

questions.q: What happens when a rubbed balloon is held near tissue bits?
questions.a: The tissue jumps up and sticks to the balloon — it is attracted.

questions.q: Why did rubbing change the balloon?
questions.a: Rubbing moved negative charges from the hair onto the balloon, giving it a static charge.

days.guide: Lay an empty can on its side on a smooth floor. Hold a charged balloon close (without touching) and slowly move it away; the can rolls after it. Try racing the can.

questions.q: Why does the can roll toward the balloon?
questions.a: The charged balloon attracts the can with electric force, even without touching.

days.guide: Charge two balloons hung from strings and bring them near each other. The child records and explains what happens.

questions.q: What happens when two balloons with the same charge come close?
questions.a: They push apart (repel) because like charges repel.

days.guide: Explore the PhET simulation: rub the balloon on the sweater and watch the negative charges move. The child draws the charges on the sweater and balloon before and after.

questions.q: In the simulation, what moves from the sweater to the balloon?
questions.a: Negative charges (electrons).

days.guide: The child writes 3 testable cause-and-effect questions (e.g., 'Does rubbing longer make the balloon pick up more tissue?') and tests one, recording results.

questions.q: Give an example of a testable question about static electricity.
questions.a: Does the number of rubs change how many tissue bits a balloon picks up?

weeks.assessment_key: Observation log: proficient if it records attraction (tissue, can) and repulsion (two balloons) with drawings. Questions: 3 = three testable cause/effect questions and one tested with recorded results and a conclusion; 2 = questions not testable or untested; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Magnets, paper clips, cardboard, string, tape. Write the Unit 2 quiz.
misconceptions: Skipping criteria and constraints — criteria say what success looks like; constraints are limits (materials, time).
Building the first idea without comparing options.

days.guide: Discuss problems magnets could solve. The child chooses one (a cabinet door that won't stay shut, finding dropped pins) and writes the problem, criteria (what it must do) and constraints (limits).

questions.q: What is the difference between criteria and constraints?
questions.a: Criteria describe what the design must do to succeed; constraints are limits like materials, cost or time.

days.guide: The child sketches 3 different magnet solutions and rates each against the criteria in a table, then picks the best.

questions.q: Why brainstorm more than one solution?
questions.a: Comparing several ideas helps you find the best one.

days.guide: The child builds a prototype of the chosen solution using magnets, cardboard and tape.

questions.q: What is a prototype?
questions.a: A first model of a design used for testing.

days.guide: Test the prototype several times and record results. The child notes what worked and what to improve.

questions.q: If a magnetic latch won't hold the door, what could you change?
questions.a: Use a stronger magnet, add more magnets, or move the magnet closer to the steel part.

days.guide: The child presents the design to the family and takes the Unit 2 quiz.

questions.q: Why won't a magnet latch work on a wooden door alone?
questions.a: Wood is not magnetic; you need a piece of steel or iron on the door for the magnet to attract.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 quiz: 1) Which are attracted: nail, penny, paper clip, foil → nail and paper clip 2) N and N → repel 3) N and S → attract 4) Magnetic force through paper? → yes 5) Force as distance increases → weaker 6) Why balloon sticks to wall → static charge attracts 7) Two charged balloons → repel. Proficient 6+/7. Design presentation: 3 = problem, criteria/constraints, test results and an improvement explained.

weeks.prep: Dry bean seeds (lima beans are easiest to open), paper towels, zip bags, a ruler, a flower (lily or alstroemeria from a store shows parts clearly), a hand lens. Soak a few beans overnight before Tuesday.
misconceptions: Thinking seeds need soil to sprout — germination needs water, air and the right temperature; the seed has its own food.
Thinking flowers are just for decoration — flowers make seeds.

days.guide: Wet a paper towel, place 3 beans in a zip bag against it, and tape the bag to a window. The child predicts what will happen and draws day 1.

questions.q: What do seeds need to germinate?
questions.a: Water, air and warmth; they use stored food inside the seed.

days.guide: Open a soaked bean along its seam with a fingernail. The child finds and labels the seed coat, the two halves of stored food (cotyledons) and the tiny embryo (baby plant).

questions.q: What is the job of the seed coat?
questions.a: To protect the seed.

questions.q: What is the embryo?
questions.a: The tiny baby plant inside the seed.

days.guide: Gently take apart a flower and lay the parts on paper. The child labels petals, sepals, stamens (make pollen) and the pistil (where seeds form).

questions.q: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
questions.a: The stamen (the anther at its tip).

questions.q: Where do seeds form?
questions.a: In the ovary at the base of the pistil.

days.guide: Measure the root and sprout in the germination bag with a ruler and draw it. Record date and length in a table.

questions.q: What grows first from a germinating bean?
questions.a: The root.

days.guide: The child draws a circular life-cycle diagram: seed → germination/seedling → adult plant → flower → pollination → fruit with seeds → back to seed.

questions.q: Why is a plant life cycle drawn as a circle?
questions.a: Because the adult plant makes seeds that start the cycle again.

weeks.assessment_key: Life cycle model: 4 = all stages in a correct circle (seed, seedling, adult, flower, pollination, fruit/seed) with arrows and descriptions; 3 (proficient) = stages in order with arrows; 2 = missing stages or wrong order; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A butterfly life cycle video (e.g., a time-lapse), grasshopper pictures, clay in 4 colors, and the germinating beans.
misconceptions: Thinking caterpillars and butterflies are different animals — they are the same insect at different stages.
Thinking all insects have a pupa — grasshoppers grow through nymph stages instead (incomplete metamorphosis).

days.guide: Watch a butterfly metamorphosis video. The child puts egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis) and adult cards in order and describes each stage.

questions.q: What are the four stages of complete metamorphosis?
questions.a: Egg, larva, pupa, adult.

questions.q: What does the caterpillar mostly do?
questions.a: Eat and grow.

days.guide: Show the grasshopper life cycle: egg, nymph (looks like a small adult without full wings), adult. The child makes a Venn diagram comparing it to the butterfly.

questions.q: How is a grasshopper's life cycle different from a butterfly's?
questions.a: It has no pupa stage; young nymphs look like small adults and molt as they grow (incomplete metamorphosis).

questions.q: What do both life cycles share?
questions.a: Both start as eggs, grow, and become adults that reproduce.

days.guide: The child models the ladybug life cycle in clay: egg (tiny yellow), larva (spiky, dark), pupa, adult. They label and arrange them in a circle.

questions.q: Does a ladybug go through complete or incomplete metamorphosis?
questions.a: Complete — egg, larva, pupa, adult.

days.guide: Measure the bean sprouts, add the data to the table and make a simple bar or line graph of growth over time.

questions.q: What does the graph show if the line goes up each day?
questions.a: The plant is growing taller over time.

days.guide: The child writes what all insect life cycles have in common.

questions.q: What do all insect life cycles have in common?
questions.a: They begin as eggs, the young grow and change, and adults reproduce to make new eggs.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn diagram: proficient if butterfly side has larva and pupa, grasshopper side has nymph and molting, middle has egg, growth, adult reproduces. Written explanation: 3 = birth/egg, growth, reproduction, and death/cycle repeats; 2 = partial; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Life cycle picture cards (frog, chicken, human, dog), a raw egg and a small bowl, a hand lens.
misconceptions: Thinking a tadpole is a fish — it is a young frog that breathes with gills and later grows lungs and legs.
Thinking all animals change form — mammals and birds look like small adults when young.

days.guide: Sequence frog cards: egg, tadpole, tadpole with legs, froglet, adult frog. The child describes what changes at each stage.

questions.q: Name two changes from tadpole to adult frog.
questions.a: It grows legs and loses its tail; gills are replaced by lungs so it can breathe air.

questions.q: Where do frogs lay eggs?
questions.a: In water.

days.guide: Crack an egg into a bowl. Find the shell, membrane, yolk and white, discussing each part's job. The child diagrams the chicken life cycle: egg → chick → young chicken → adult.

questions.q: What is the yolk's job?
questions.a: It provides food for the developing chick.

questions.q: How long does a chicken egg take to hatch?
questions.a: About 21 days.

days.guide: Make two timelines: human (baby, child, teen, adult) and dog (puppy, adult). The child compares how long each stage lasts.

questions.q: How are human and dog life cycles alike?
questions.a: Both are born alive, drink milk from their mothers, grow into adults and can reproduce.

questions.q: Which grows up faster?
questions.a: The dog — it is an adult in about 1–2 years.

days.guide: The child fills a chart comparing stages and approximate life spans of 5 organisms (e.g., butterfly, frog, chicken, dog, human).

questions.q: About how long does a pet dog live?
questions.a: Usually about 10–13 years.

days.guide: Ask questions about which stages all life cycles share.

questions.q: What stages do all animal life cycles share?
questions.a: Birth (or hatching), growth, reproduction and death.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart: proficient if 5 organisms have correct stages and reasonable life spans (e.g., monarch adult a few weeks to months, frog several years, chicken 5–10 years, dog 10–13 years, human 70–80 years). Shared stages: birth, growth, reproduction, death.

weeks.prep: Paper plates (2 per model), markers, brads (paper fasteners), library books or kid-safe websites about sea turtles, salmon or oak trees, potting soil and a pot. Write the Unit 3 quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking life cycles end at adulthood — the adult reproduces, which restarts the cycle.
Mixing up plant and animal stages (calling a seedling a larva).

days.guide: The child chooses an organism and researches its stages, writing each on a note card.

questions.q: What are the stages of a salmon's life?
questions.a: Egg (in a freshwater stream) → alevin → fry → smolt (moves to the ocean) → adult that returns to its home stream to spawn.

questions.q: What are the stages of an oak tree?
questions.a: Acorn (seed) → seedling → sapling → mature tree that makes acorns.

days.guide: Divide one plate into sections and draw a stage in each. Cut a window in the top plate and join them with a brad so turning shows one stage at a time.

questions.q: How many sections should a sea turtle model have?
