days.guide: Demonstrate wash (watery paint brushed smoothly over an area), dry-brush (little paint, dry brush for scratchy texture) and stipple (dabbing dots with the brush tip). Practice each, then clean brushes: rinse, wipe with soap if needed, reshape, lay flat.

questions.q: How do you care for a brush after painting?
questions.a: Rinse it in water until clean (soap for tempera if needed), blot, reshape the bristles and lay it flat or store bristles up.

days.guide: The child labels all 12 colors and explains how to mix any one of them.

questions.q: Explain how to make red-violet.
questions.a: Mix red and violet (violet is red + blue), so it's mostly red with some blue.

weeks.assessment_key: 12-color wheel key: in order around the wheel — red, red-orange, orange, yellow-orange, yellow, yellow-green, green, blue-green, blue, blue-violet, violet, red-violet. Rubric: 4 = all 12 in correct order, neatly painted and labeled, and the child explains a mixing recipe correctly; 3 = 1–2 colors misplaced or muddy; 2 = only 6 colors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Paints (red, orange, yellow, blue, green, violet, white), paper, magazine scraps or paint chips from a hardware store. Pull up Pablo Picasso's 'The Old Guitarist' (1903–04, Art Institute of Chicago website).
misconceptions: Thinking warm and cool means the actual temperature of the paint. It describes how colors feel: reds/oranges/yellows remind us of fire and sun; blues/greens/violets of water, ice and shade.
Thinking a color can only be one mood. Context matters, but warm colors often feel energetic or happy and cool colors calm, quiet or sad.

days.guide: Sort chips or scraps into two piles: warm (reds, oranges, yellows) and cool (blues, greens, violets). Point out where they sit on the color wheel (two halves).

questions.q: Name the warm colors and the cool colors.
questions.a: Warm: red, orange, yellow. Cool: blue, green, violet.

questions.q: Why are they called warm and cool?
questions.a: Warm colors remind us of sun and fire; cool colors remind us of water, ice and sky.

days.guide: Show 'The Old Guitarist.' Tell the child it is from Picasso's 'Blue Period,' when he painted mostly in blues during a sad time. Ask: What do you notice about the man? How do the blues make you feel?

questions.q: What mood do the blue colors create in 'The Old Guitarist'?
questions.a: A sad, lonely, cold or quiet mood.

questions.q: What is Picasso's 'Blue Period'?
questions.a: A time early in his career when he painted mostly in shades of blue, often of poor or lonely people.

days.guide: Sketch a simple landscape (horizon, hills, a tree, sun or moon). Paint it using only warm colors.

questions.q: Which color could you use for the sky in a warm painting?
questions.a: A warm color such as yellow, orange or red (e.g., a sunset sky).

days.guide: Sketch the same landscape again and paint it using only cool colors.

questions.q: What could you use instead of yellow for the sun?
questions.a: A cool color such as pale blue, green or violet (or white mixed with a cool color).

days.guide: Display both paintings. The child writes 3 sentences comparing moods.

questions.q: How is the mood different between your two paintings?
questions.a: Example: 'The warm painting feels hot and exciting like a desert afternoon; the cool painting feels calm and chilly like night.'

weeks.assessment_key: Warm/cool landscape pair rubric: 4 = same landscape painted twice, one with only warm and one with only cool colors, plus 3 sentences comparing moods with specific color words; 3 = one stray color or 2 sentences; 2 = colors mixed between groups, comparison vague; 1 = one painting missing.

weeks.prep: Paint in one color plus white and black, brushes, palette, thick paper. Pull up images of Georgia O'Keeffe's flower paintings (e.g., 'Red Canna' or 'Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1'). Draw a 7-box strip for the value scale.
misconceptions: Adding a lot of black at once. Black is strong; add a tiny bit at a time for shades (and add color to white, not white to color, for tints).
Thinking value means price. In art, value means how light or dark a color is.

days.guide: Paint the pure color in the middle box. Add a little white for each box going one way (tints) and a little black for each box going the other way (shades), making 7 steps from light to dark.

questions.q: What is a tint? A shade?
questions.a: A tint is a color plus white (lighter); a shade is a color plus black (darker).

questions.q: What is value?
questions.a: How light or dark a color is.

days.guide: Paint a small tree using only one color plus its tints and shades (monochromatic).

questions.q: What does monochromatic mean?
questions.a: Using only one color (hue) with its tints and shades.

days.guide: Look at O'Keeffe's flowers. Explain she painted flowers enormous and up close so busy people would stop and really look at them. Ask how the size changes how we see a flower.

questions.q: Why did O'Keeffe paint flowers so large?
questions.a: So people would notice the small details and take time to really look at the flower, as if seen up close.

questions.q: Where did O'Keeffe often paint (later in life)?
questions.a: New Mexico (the American Southwest).

days.guide: Paint a large close-up flower that fills the whole page and runs off the edges, using at least 4 tints and shades to show curved petals.

questions.q: How can value make a petal look curved?
questions.a: Use lighter tints where light hits it and darker shades where it curves away or is in shadow.

days.guide: The child points to where they used light and dark values and explains how that makes the flower look 3D (form).

questions.q: Where should the darkest values go?
questions.a: In shadowed areas — deep in the center of the flower and where petals overlap or curve away from the light.

weeks.assessment_key: Value scale and flower rubric: 4 = 7-step scale that moves evenly from lightest tint to darkest shade; flower fills the page with at least 4 values placed to show form; the child explains light and dark placement; 3 = scale has 1–2 uneven jumps or flower uses 3 values; 2 = scale incomplete or flower flat; 1 = little work.

weeks.prep: Paints, large paper, a recording of Bedřich Smetana's 'The Moldau' (Vltava) from 'Má vlast'; one calm piece (e.g., Debussy's 'Clair de Lune') and one energetic piece (e.g., Rimsky-Korsakov's 'Flight of the Bumblebee'). A simple song to sing loud and soft.
misconceptions: Thinking forte means fast. Forte means loud; tempo (fast/slow) is separate from dynamics (loud/soft).
Thinking any color matches any music. Choose colors, strokes and values that match the music's dynamics and tempo.

days.guide: Explain 'The Moldau' follows a river in what is now the Czech Republic from two small springs to a big river. Play it while the child paints freely, letting the colors and strokes follow the music (small trickles at first, wider sweeping strokes as it grows).

questions.q: What does 'The Moldau' describe?
questions.a: The Vltava (Moldau) river flowing from two small springs, growing bigger, and passing through the countryside to the city of Prague.

questions.q: Who composed it?
questions.a: Bedřich Smetana, a Czech composer.

days.guide: Teach forte (f, loud) and piano (p, soft). Sing a familiar song, switching between forte and piano when you hold up a card.

questions.q: What does the symbol 'p' mean in music?
questions.a: Piano — play or sing softly.

questions.q: What does 'f' mean?
questions.a: Forte — loud.

days.guide: Paint two small pieces: one to the calm piece and one to the energetic piece.

questions.q: What colors and brushstrokes might match the energetic piece?
questions.a: Bright warm colors and quick, short, zigzag or jabbing strokes.

days.guide: The child explains how the colors in each painting match the music's dynamics and tempo.

questions.q: How did your painting show soft, slow music?
questions.a: E.g., 'I used light cool colors and long smooth strokes.'

days.guide: The child chooses their best painting and scores it on a color rubric: colors match the mood; uses warm/cool on purpose; uses tints and shades; brushwork matches the tempo.

questions.q: Which rubric point is strongest in your painting? Explain.
questions.a: Answers vary but should point to specific evidence in the painting.

weeks.assessment_key: Color-use rubric (self- and parent score): Colors match the music's mood (1–4), warm/cool colors chosen on purpose (1–4), tints and shades used (1–4), brushstrokes match tempo/dynamics (1–4). Proficient = average of 3 or more, with a written or spoken explanation for each score.

weeks.prep: A xylophone, keyboard, or free piano app. Prepare 10 sounds to compare (e.g., bird whistle, tuba recording, small bell, big drum, high and low piano keys). Melody maps: paper and crayons.
misconceptions: Confusing high/low with loud/soft. Pitch is how high or low a sound is; dynamics is how loud or soft.
Thinking bigger instruments are higher. Bigger, longer or thicker sound makers usually make lower pitches.

days.guide: Play 10 sounds; the child stands tall for high and crouches for low, then sorts them on paper.

questions.q: Is a tuba high or low in pitch?
questions.a: Low.

questions.q: What is pitch?
questions.a: How high or low a sound is.

days.guide: Sing 'Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star' (traditional) slowly. The child draws a line that goes up when the melody goes up and down when it goes down.

questions.q: Does the melody of 'Twinkle, Twinkle' go up or down at the start?
questions.a: It starts on one note, then leaps up and rises a little more, then steps back down.

questions.q: How does the song end — higher or lower than the middle?
questions.a: Lower — it steps down back to the starting note.

days.guide: Sing 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat' while showing pitch with the hand (high hand = high note). Notice the 'merrily' part jumps high and then comes down.

questions.q: Where is the highest part of 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat'?
questions.a: The 'merrily, merrily' part.

days.guide: Draw melody maps (lines or dots going up and down) for 2 short songs, then find and play them on the keyboard app.

questions.q: On a piano, which direction goes higher?
questions.a: To the right.

days.guide: Listening quiz: play 6 short melodies; the child marks each 'up,' 'down' or 'same.'

questions.q: If notes go C-D-E-F-G, is the melody going up or down?
questions.a: Up.

weeks.assessment_key: Pitch direction listening quiz (6 items): play these on a keyboard and the key is — 1) C-D-E-F-G = up, 2) G-F-E-D-C = down, 3) E-E-E-E = same, 4) C-E-G-C' = up, 5) high C-A-F-C = down, 6) G-G-G-G = same. Proficient = 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Print or display a solfege hand-sign chart (Curwen hand signs: do = fist, re = flat hand slanting up, mi = flat hand level, sol = palm facing body, la = hand drooping down). Songs: 'Rain, Rain, Go Away,' 'Ring Around the Rosie,' 'Hot Cross Buns,' 'Bow Wow Wow' (all traditional).
misconceptions: Thinking solfege names are fixed letter names. Solfege shows a note's place in the scale (do is home), not a fixed pitch.
Making hand signs at the same height. Place higher notes higher in front of the body to show pitch.

days.guide: Teach sol (higher) and mi (lower) hand signs. Sing 'Rain, Rain, Go Away' with sol-mi signs — it uses only these two notes.

questions.q: Which is higher, sol or mi?
questions.a: Sol.

questions.q: Which two notes does 'Rain, Rain, Go Away' use?
questions.a: Sol and mi.

days.guide: Add la (one step above sol). Sing 'Ring Around the Rosie' with signs (sol-sol-mi-la-sol-mi).

questions.q: Where is la compared to sol?
questions.a: One step higher than sol.

days.guide: Add do, re and mi and sing the pentatonic scale do-re-mi-sol-la up and down with signs.

questions.q: Which notes are in the pentatonic scale we sang?
questions.a: Do, re, mi, sol, la (five notes).

questions.q: Which two notes are skipped from the full scale?
questions.a: Fa and ti.

days.guide: Sing 'Hot Cross Buns' in solfege: mi-re-do. Then sing it with words and signs.

questions.q: What solfege notes begin 'Hot Cross Buns'?
questions.a: Mi, re, do.

days.guide: Sing 8 short solfege patterns; the child echoes with correct signs (e.g., sol-mi-la-sol, do-re-mi, mi-re-do).

questions.q: Show the hand sign for do.
questions.a: A closed fist at about waist height.

weeks.assessment_key: Solfege echo check (8 patterns): suggested patterns — 1) sol-mi 2) sol-sol-mi 3) sol-la-sol-mi 4) mi-re-do 5) do-re-mi 6) do-mi-sol 7) la-sol-mi 8) do-re-mi-sol-la. 1 point for correct pitch and 1 for correct hand signs each (16 total). Proficient = 13+.

weeks.prep: Staff paper, pencil, keyboard app. Make flash cards for treble staff notes (E4 to F5). Mnemonics: lines E-G-B-D-F 'Every Good Boy Does Fine'; spaces F-A-C-E spell 'FACE.'
misconceptions: Counting lines and spaces from the top. Count from the bottom: the bottom line is line 1 (E).
Mixing up line notes and space notes. A line note has the line through its middle; a space note sits between lines.

days.guide: Show the 5 lines and 4 spaces of the staff, numbered from the bottom. Teach drawing the treble clef starting on the second line (it curls around G). Draw 5 treble clefs.

questions.q: How many lines and spaces are on a staff?
questions.a: 5 lines and 4 spaces.

questions.q: Why is the treble clef also called the G clef?
questions.a: Its curl wraps around the second line, which is the note G.

days.guide: Teach line notes E-G-B-D-F and space notes F-A-C-E with the mnemonics. Quiz with flash cards.

questions.q: Name the line notes from bottom to top.
questions.a: E, G, B, D, F.

questions.q: Name the space notes from bottom to top.
questions.a: F, A, C, E.

days.guide: The child writes 10 notes on the staff from letter names (e.g., G, E, C, A, F (top line), D, B, F (first space), E (top space), C).

questions.q: Where does C go on the staff (in the spaces)?
questions.a: In the third space from the bottom.

days.guide: Show 'Hot Cross Buns' written as E-D-C (E on the bottom line, D below the staff, C on a ledger line). Find E, D, C on the keyboard and play it from notation.

questions.q: What 3 notes are in 'Hot Cross Buns'?
questions.a: E, D, C.

days.guide: 15-note naming quiz with flash cards or a worksheet.

questions.q: A note sits on the middle (third) line. What is it?
questions.a: B.

weeks.assessment_key: 15-note naming quiz key (write these on the staff, child names them): 1) bottom line E 2) 2nd line G 3) 3rd line B 4) 4th line D 5) top line F 6) 1st space F 7) 2nd space A 8) 3rd space C 9) top space E 10) 2nd line G 11) 3rd space C 12) 3rd line B 13) 2nd space A 14) 4th line D 15) bottom line E. Proficient = 13 of 15.

weeks.prep: Song sheet for 'This Land Is Your Land' (Woody Guthrie; use a lyric sheet you own or a children's songbook — don't need to print the whole text) and a lullaby and a march. Two different recorded versions of the same song (e.g., a choir version and a solo folk version).
misconceptions: Thinking crescendo means 'loud.' Crescendo means gradually getting louder; decrescendo (diminuendo) means gradually getting softer.
Singing every song the same way. Expression (dynamics, tempo, phrasing) should match the words and purpose of the song.

days.guide: Teach forte, piano, crescendo (<, getting louder) and decrescendo (>, getting softer). Sing the song with you signaling each with your hands.

questions.q: What does a crescendo sign look like and mean?
questions.a: An opening wedge (<); gradually get louder.

questions.q: What is the opposite of crescendo?
questions.a: Decrescendo (or diminuendo) — gradually getting softer.

days.guide: Sing a lullaby slowly and softly and a march quickly and strongly. Discuss why each tempo fits its purpose.

questions.q: Why is a lullaby slow and soft?
questions.a: It is meant to calm a baby to sleep.

questions.q: Why is a march fast and steady?
questions.a: It is for walking or marching together in step.

days.guide: Listen to two recordings of the same song. Make a T-chart comparing tempo, dynamics, instruments and voices.

questions.q: Name one difference you heard between the two versions.
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., 'The choir version was louder and had piano; the folk version was slower with just a guitar.'

days.guide: Mark dynamics (p, f, <, >) on the song sheet to match the meaning of the words; e.g., softer for quiet images, louder for big ideas.

questions.q: Where would you put a crescendo, and why?
questions.a: Answers vary but should connect to the words, e.g., building up toward a big, important line.

days.guide: Perform the song for family using the marked expression.

questions.q: What makes a performance expressive?
questions.a: Using dynamics, tempo and phrasing that match the meaning and feeling of the song.

weeks.assessment_key: Expressive performance rubric: 4 = sings with accurate words and pitch and clearly follows at least 3 marked expressions (p, f, crescendo, decrescendo) that fit the words; 3 = follows 2 markings; 2 = mostly one dynamic level; 1 = does not complete performance.

weeks.prep: A phone or tablet to record, the chosen song sheet, and Chrome Music Lab 'Song Maker' set to a pentatonic scale (Settings: Scale = Pentatonic, Start on C).
misconceptions: Thinking criticism means 'bad.' Feedback names specific things to keep and to fix.
Thinking audiences can talk or move during a performance. Audiences listen quietly and clap at the end.

days.guide: The child rehearses a chosen song from this unit twice, then records one full performance.

questions.q: Why record yourself?
questions.a: So you can hear what you sound like and find things to improve.

days.guide: Listen to the recording together. Pick 2 specific things to fix (pitch in a certain line, forgotten words, more dynamics). Practice just those parts.

questions.q: Name one thing you will fix and how.
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., 'I went flat on the high part, so I will practice it slowly with the piano.'

days.guide: In Song Maker (pentatonic: do-re-mi-sol-la), compose an 8-beat melody that ends on do. Play it back and adjust.

questions.q: Which note should your melody end on to sound finished?
questions.a: Do (the home note).

days.guide: Discuss etiquette: performers walk on, wait for quiet, perform, then bow; audiences listen quietly, don't talk or use phones, and applaud at the end.

questions.q: What does the performer do at the end?
questions.a: Bows to thank the audience.

questions.q: Name two things a good audience does.
questions.a: Listens quietly, stays seated, and claps at the end.

days.guide: Concert: the child introduces and performs the song and the melody for family using concert etiquette.

questions.q: Why do audiences wait until the end to clap?
questions.a: So they don't interrupt the music and everyone can hear the whole piece.

weeks.assessment_key: Song and melody performance rubric: 4 = song performed with accurate pitch and words, 2 planned fixes improved, 8-beat pentatonic melody that ends on do, and proper concert etiquette (introduction, bow); 3 = minor errors in one area; 2 = several errors or no original melody; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Crayons with paper peeled off, thin copy paper, textured objects (leaves, coins, window screen, bark, sandpaper, basket, sole of a shoe). Pull up Albrecht Dürer's 'Young Hare' (1502, Albertina Museum, Vienna). Scissors, glue, background paper.
misconceptions: Thinking texture is only something you touch. Actual texture can be felt; visual (implied) texture is drawn or painted to look like it would feel a certain way.
Pressing too hard or using the crayon tip for rubbings. Use the side of a peeled crayon and rub evenly.

days.guide: Place copy paper over each textured surface and rub with the side of a peeled crayon. Collect 10 rubbings and label each.

questions.q: What is texture?
questions.a: How something feels or looks like it would feel (rough, smooth, bumpy, fuzzy).

days.guide: Make a 6-box grid in the sketchbook and draw visual texture for fur (short flicking lines), bark (long wavy lines and cracks), scales (overlapping U-shapes), feathers, brick and water.

questions.q: What is the difference between actual and visual texture?
questions.a: Actual texture can be felt with your hands; visual texture is drawn to look rough, smooth, etc., but feels flat.

days.guide: Look closely at 'Young Hare.' Explain Dürer painted it in watercolor and gouache over 500 years ago. Ask how he made each hair (tiny fine brushstrokes in different directions, light and dark).

questions.q: How did Dürer make the hare look furry?
questions.a: He painted thousands of tiny, fine brushstrokes in the direction the fur grows, using light and dark colors.

questions.q: Is the hare's fur actual or visual texture?
questions.a: Visual texture.

days.guide: Draw a simple animal outline on background paper. Cut the rubbings into shapes and glue them to build the animal (e.g., bark texture for legs, screen for body).

questions.q: Why choose different rubbings for different parts?
questions.a: Different textures show different parts, like fur on the body and scales or rough skin on feet.

days.guide: The child presents the collage and names the texture used for each part.

questions.q: Which rubbing did you use for the body, and what real texture does it show?
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., 'The basket rubbing looks like the turtle's patterned shell.'

weeks.assessment_key: Texture animal collage rubric: 4 = at least 5 different rubbings cut and arranged to form a recognizable animal, textures chosen to match parts, neat gluing, and the child names each texture; 3 = 3–4 textures; 2 = 2 textures or animal unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Clean foam meat trays (cut off the rims), dull pencils, tempera paint (slightly thick), a brayer/roller or sponge, a flat tray for rolling paint, paper. A potato and a butter knife or sponges for stamps (an adult cuts potatoes). Phone or sketchbook for pattern hunting.
misconceptions: Thinking a print comes out the same direction as the plate. A print is a mirror image, so letters must be drawn backward.
Pressing too lightly on the foam. Lines must be pressed deep, or paint fills them in and they disappear.

days.guide: Find and sketch or photograph 5 patterns in fabrics, tiles and nature (pinecone, honeycomb, plaid shirt). Name the repeating unit in each.

questions.q: What is a pattern?
questions.a: A design where lines, shapes or colors repeat in a planned way.

questions.q: What is an alternating pattern?
questions.a: A pattern where two (or more) elements take turns, like circle-square-circle-square.

days.guide: An adult cuts a potato in half; the child draws a simple shape and the adult carves away the background (or cut sponge shapes). Print an alternating pattern border around a page (e.g., star, circle, star, circle).

questions.q: What part of a stamp prints?
questions.a: The raised part (the part left standing); carved-away areas stay blank.

days.guide: Draw a design on paper first, then trace it firmly into the foam with a dull pencil, pressing deep lines. Remind: words must be written backward.

questions.q: Will the lines you press into foam print in color or stay white?
questions.a: They stay the color of the paper (white) because the paint sits on the raised surface, not in the grooves.

questions.q: Why write letters backward on the plate?
questions.a: The print is a mirror image, so backward letters print the right way.

days.guide: Roll a thin, even layer of paint onto the plate, place paper on top, rub with the palm, peel off. Make 3 prints. Sign in pencil under each print and number them 1/3, 2/3, 3/3.

questions.q: What does '2/3' written under a print mean?
questions.a: It is the 2nd print in an edition of 3 prints.

questions.q: What is a print edition?
questions.a: A set of matching prints made from the same plate.

days.guide: Choose the best print and explain using criteria: clear lines, even ink, clean edges, centered on paper.

questions.q: Why might a print look blotchy?
questions.a: Too much or uneven paint, or the paper moved while rubbing.

weeks.assessment_key: Print edition rubric: 4 = 3 prints from the same plate with clear deep lines, even ink and clean edges, each signed and numbered (1/3, 2/3, 3/3); best print chosen with 2+ criteria; 3 = 3 prints with one blotchy or minor numbering slip; 2 = fewer than 3 prints or lines unclear; 1 = no edition. Pattern border: alternating pattern repeated correctly around the page.

weeks.prep: Images of Ghanaian adinkra cloth and symbols (the Metropolitan Museum and Smithsonian National Museum of African Art websites have them). Fabric scrap or paper, foam or cardboard to make stamps, paint or ink, ruler for a grid. Image of Hokusai's 'Under the Wave off Kanagawa' ('The Great Wave').
misconceptions: Thinking adinkra symbols are just decoration. Each symbol has a name and meaning (often a proverb or value) for the Akan people of Ghana.
Thinking a print is only one copy. Printmaking makes many copies, which is why woodblock prints could spread pictures widely.

days.guide: Explain adinkra cloth comes from the Akan (Asante) people of Ghana; symbols were traditionally stamped with carved calabash (gourd) stamps. Learn 6 symbols: Gye Nyame (supremacy of God), Sankofa (learn from the past), Dwennimmen (ram's horns: humility and strength), Akoma (heart: patience and love), Adinkrahene (chief of symbols: leadership/greatness), Funtunfunefu (joined crocodiles: unity, sharing).

questions.q: What country does adinkra cloth come from?
questions.a: Ghana (West Africa), from the Akan/Asante people.

questions.q: What does the Sankofa symbol mean?
questions.a: Go back and get it — learn from the past to move forward.

days.guide: The child picks 3 family values (kindness, courage, togetherness) and designs a simple, bold symbol for each that could be cut as a stamp.

questions.q: Why should a stamp symbol be simple and bold?
questions.a: Fine details don't print clearly; bold shapes make strong, readable prints.

days.guide: Make stamps (foam shapes glued to cardboard). Rule a grid on fabric or paper and print the symbols in a repeating pattern in the squares.

questions.q: How are your symbols arranged?
questions.a: In a grid, repeating in a pattern, like traditional adinkra cloth.

days.guide: Show 'The Great Wave' by Katsushika Hokusai (about 1831), a woodblock print from Japan in the series 'Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.' Explain woodblock prints were made in many copies and sold cheaply, so many people could own and share pictures and stories.

questions.q: What is small and far away in 'The Great Wave'?
questions.a: Mount Fuji, in the background beneath the wave.

questions.q: How did printmaking help art spread?
questions.a: Many copies could be printed from one carved block, so art was affordable and could be shared widely.

days.guide: The child presents the symbol cloth and explains each symbol's meaning and how adinkra inspired it.

questions.q: What value does each of your symbols stand for?
questions.a: The child names each symbol and the value it represents.

weeks.assessment_key: Symbol cloth presentation rubric: 4 = 3 original bold symbols printed clearly in an organized grid pattern; the child explains each meaning and correctly states adinkra is from Ghana with symbols that carry meanings; 3 = all printed, one meaning unclear; 2 = disorganized or only 1–2 symbols; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Listen ahead to Benjamin Britten's 'The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra' (about 17 minutes); Classics for Kids (classicsforkids.com) has instrument pages and audio. Make 4 cards: Strings, Woodwinds, Brass, Percussion. Shoebox (lid off), rubber bands of different thicknesses, 2 pencils as bridges.
misconceptions: Thinking all woodwinds are made of wood. Flutes are usually metal and saxophones are brass but are woodwinds because of how sound is made (air across an edge or through a reed).
Thinking only drums are percussion. Percussion includes anything struck, shaken or scraped, like xylophones, triangles, cymbals and timpani.

days.guide: Teach the 4 orchestra families and how each makes sound: strings (vibrating strings, bowed or plucked: violin, viola, cello, double bass, harp), woodwinds (air blown across an edge or through a reed: flute, clarinet, oboe, bassoon), brass (buzzing lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece: trumpet, French horn, trombone, tuba), percussion (struck, shaken or scraped: drums, timpani, xylophone, cymbals).

questions.q: How do brass instruments make sound?
questions.a: The player buzzes their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece.

questions.q: Name the 4 instrument families of the orchestra.
questions.a: Strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion.

days.guide: Play the Britten piece. The child raises the matching family card as each family plays the theme and as each instrument gets its variation.

questions.q: Whose tune did Britten use as the theme?
questions.a: A tune by the English composer Henry Purcell.

questions.q: Which family plays the very lowest notes in the piece?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., the tuba (brass), double bass (strings) or bassoon (woodwinds) — all low instruments.

days.guide: Play 10 instrument sound clips; the child names the instrument and family by timbre (tone color).

questions.q: What is timbre?
questions.a: The special quality or 'color' of a sound that lets you tell instruments or voices apart.

days.guide: Stretch rubber bands of different thicknesses over an open shoebox, lift them with pencils as bridges, and pluck. Compare pitches.

questions.q: Which rubber band makes the lowest pitch?
questions.a: The thickest (or loosest) one.

questions.q: What happens to pitch when you stretch a band tighter?
questions.a: The pitch goes higher.

days.guide: Instrument family quiz (oral or written).

questions.q: Is a clarinet a woodwind or brass instrument?
questions.a: Woodwind (it uses a reed).

weeks.assessment_key: Instrument family quiz key (10): 1) violin — strings 2) trumpet — brass 3) flute — woodwind 4) timpani — percussion 5) cello — strings 6) oboe — woodwind 7) trombone — brass 8) xylophone — percussion 9) harp — strings 10) French horn — brass. Bonus: brass makes sound by buzzing lips. Proficient = 8 of 10.

weeks.prep: Recordings: a mariachi performance (e.g., Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán), a California Indian song from a tribe or museum website (e.g., a Chumash, Pomo or Miwok recording shared by the tribe or the Autry Museum/California Indian Heritage Center), and 'Oh My Darling, Clementine' (traditional Gold Rush-era song, public domain). Chart paper.
misconceptions: Thinking California Indian music is only from the past. California Indian tribes continue to sing traditional songs today for ceremonies, gatherings and teaching.
Thinking 'Clementine' is a sad song only. It is a humorous ballad that exaggerates (tall-tale style) while showing miners' hard lives.

days.guide: Play mariachi music. Help the child identify violins, trumpets, the vihuela (small, round-backed guitar with a high strum) and the guitarrón (big, deep bass guitar). Explain mariachi began in western Mexico (Jalisco) and is played at celebrations in California today.

questions.q: Which instrument plays the low bass in mariachi?
questions.a: The guitarrón.

questions.q: Name 2 other mariachi instruments.
questions.a: Any 2 of: violin, trumpet, vihuela, guitar (also harp).

days.guide: Listen respectfully to a California Indian song from a tribal or museum source. Read the source's description of its purpose (e.g., ceremony, storytelling, celebrating, teaching). Discuss voice, rattles (clapper sticks, gourd or deer-hoof rattles) and steady beat.

questions.q: What purposes can California Indian songs have?
questions.a: Ceremonies, celebrations, storytelling, healing, teaching history and traditions (as described by the tribe or museum source).

days.guide: Learn to sing 'Oh My Darling, Clementine.' Discuss what it shows about miners' lives during the 1849 Gold Rush (living in a canyon cabin, hard work, danger).

questions.q: What historical event is 'Clementine' connected to?
questions.a: The California Gold Rush (1849).

days.guide: Make a chart with columns: style, instruments, tempo, purpose, and fill it in for mariachi, the California Indian song and the Gold Rush song.

questions.q: Which style used trumpets and violins?
questions.a: Mariachi.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph about the style they connected with most, with 2 reasons from the music.

questions.q: What makes a strong paragraph about music?
questions.a: A clear choice, at least 2 specific details from the music (instruments, tempo, purpose), and a personal reason.

weeks.assessment_key: Music comparison chart and paragraph: chart key — Mariachi: violins, trumpets, vihuela, guitarrón, guitar; lively/medium-fast; celebrations, serenades, festivals. California Indian song: voice with rattles/clapper sticks or drum (per recording); steady beat; ceremony, teaching, community gatherings. Clementine: voice (often guitar/banjo); moderate, waltz-like 3/4; storytelling/entertainment about Gold Rush life. Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear choice + 2 specific musical details + personal connection; 3 = choice + 1 detail; 2 = opinion only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Videos to preview: a Japanese taiko performance, an Indonesian gamelan (Javanese or Balinese) performance, and a West African djembe lesson for kids. A bucket or drum, a world map, colored pencils.
misconceptions: Thinking world music is 'just noise' because it sounds unfamiliar. Each tradition has its own rules, scales and purposes.
Hitting a drum the same way every time. On the djembe, different strokes (bass, tone, slap) make different sounds.

days.guide: Watch taiko and notice the big, powerful arm motions and shouts (kiai). Copy a simple taiko rhythm on a bucket (e.g., DON DON doko DON) with big arm swings.

questions.q: Which country does taiko drumming come from?
questions.a: Japan.

questions.q: Why do taiko players use big arm motions?
questions.a: Movement is part of the performance and creates strong, powerful sound.

days.guide: Listen to gamelan. Point out the bronze gongs and metallophones (metal keyboards) and how different layers repeat patterns at different speeds.

questions.q: Where does gamelan come from?
questions.a: Indonesia (especially the islands of Java and Bali).

questions.q: How would you describe gamelan music?
questions.a: Layers of repeating, interlocking patterns played on gongs and metal keyboard instruments, with drums leading.

days.guide: Teach djembe strokes on a bucket: bass (flat palm in the center, low), tone (fingers together on the edge, clear), slap (relaxed fingers snap on the edge, high and sharp). Play call-and-response: you play a call, the child answers.

questions.q: What are the 3 djembe strokes?
questions.a: Bass, tone and slap.

questions.q: What is call and response?
questions.a: One person or group plays/sings a phrase (call) and another answers with a phrase (response).

days.guide: Mark Japan, Indonesia and West Africa (e.g., Mali or Guinea) on a world map with a drawing of the main instrument for each.

questions.q: Where would you draw a djembe on the map?
questions.a: West Africa (e.g., Mali, Guinea, Senegal).

days.guide: Discuss how each style connects to its culture: taiko at festivals and ceremonies; gamelan for ceremonies, dance and shadow-puppet theater; djembe at community celebrations and gatherings.

questions.q: What purpose does gamelan have in Indonesia?
questions.a: It accompanies ceremonies, dances and shadow-puppet (wayang) plays.

weeks.assessment_key: World music map key: Taiko — Japan (big barrel drums); Gamelan — Indonesia, Java/Bali (gongs, metallophones); Djembe — West Africa (goblet-shaped drum). Rubric: 4 = all 3 placed correctly with instrument drawings and a sentence on each culture's purpose; 3 = all placed, purposes partial; 2 = 1–2 placed correctly; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Choose a folk song recording with a translation (e.g., 'De Colores' — a traditional Spanish-language song popular in Mexico and the Southwest; 'Sakura' — a traditional Japanese song about cherry blossoms; 'Funga Alafia' — a West African welcome song). Shakers, drum, sticks.
misconceptions: Singing words without knowing what they mean. Learn the translation so the expression matches the meaning.
Using an accompaniment that clashes with the style. Choose instruments and rhythm that fit (e.g., gentle sounds for 'Sakura,' a steady drum for 'Funga Alafia').

days.guide: Listen to 2–3 folk songs. The child chooses one and explains why (sound, culture, meaning).

questions.q: What is a folk song?
questions.a: A traditional song passed down through generations in a community, often by ear, whose original composer is usually unknown.

days.guide: Learn the words phrase by phrase by echo. Read the meaning in English and talk about what the song is about.

questions.q: What is 'Sakura' about?
questions.a: Cherry blossoms (sakura) in spring in Japan.

questions.q: What is 'De Colores' about?
questions.a: The colors of nature in spring — fields, birds and rainbows — and joy/love.

days.guide: Add a simple percussion part that fits the song's style and keep a steady beat while singing.

questions.q: Why choose a gentle accompaniment for a slow song?
questions.a: So it supports the mood and doesn't cover the voice.

days.guide: Perform for family, first introducing the song's country/culture and meaning.

questions.q: Where does your song come from, and what is it about?
questions.a: The child correctly states the culture and meaning of the chosen song.

days.guide: The child writes a reflection: 2 things that went well and 1 to practice next time.

questions.q: What makes a useful reflection?
questions.a: Specific details about what went well and a clear plan for what to practice.

weeks.assessment_key: Folk song performance and reflection rubric: 4 = sings the song with accurate words and melody, steady fitting accompaniment, introduces its origin and meaning correctly, and writes a reflection with 2 specific strengths and 1 practice goal; 3 = minor errors; 2 = needs support to sing or reflection vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Air-dry clay (about 1 lb per child), a fork or toothpick for scoring, a small cup of water for slip (or make slip by mixing clay and water to a paste), a placemat, household texture tools (fork, bottle caps, lace, buttons). Pots dry 2–3 days.
misconceptions: Pressing two clay pieces together without scoring. Joints crack as clay dries; scratch both surfaces (score), add slip, press and smooth.
Making the bottom too thick and walls too thin. Aim for even walls about as thick as a finger.

days.guide: Draw a circle on paper and hold a clay ball. Explain shape (flat, 2D: length and width) vs. form (3D: length, width and depth). Roll a sphere, cylinder and cube.

questions.q: What is the difference between shape and form?
questions.a: A shape is flat (2D); a form is three-dimensional with height, width and depth.

questions.q: What form matches a ball? a can?
questions.a: A ball is a sphere; a can is a cylinder.

days.guide: Roll a ball about the size of an orange. Press the thumb into the center and pinch while turning the ball, working from the bottom up, keeping walls even.

questions.q: How do you keep a pinch pot's walls even?
questions.a: Pinch gently and evenly while turning the pot a little each time, working from the bottom up.

days.guide: Make a flat base. Roll coils like snakes, about pencil-thick. Score and slip each layer, then smooth coils together on the inside.

questions.q: What do score and slip mean?
questions.a: Score = scratch lines into both clay surfaces; slip = clay mixed with water used like glue to join them.

questions.q: Why smooth coils on the inside?
questions.a: It blends the coils together so the pot is strong and doesn't fall apart.

days.guide: Press or carve textures into both pots with household tools.

questions.q: Name a tool you used and the texture it made.
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., 'A fork made parallel lines like grass.'

days.guide: When dry, evaluate both pots: even walls, secure joins (no cracks), stable base, texture.

questions.q: If your coil pot cracked between coils, what went wrong?
questions.a: The coils were not scored, slipped and smoothed well enough (or dried too fast).

weeks.assessment_key: Pinch and coil pots rubric: 4 = pinch pot with even walls and smooth rim; coil pot with scored-and-slipped coils smoothed inside, no cracks, stable base; both have intentional texture; child evaluates using criteria; 3 = minor unevenness or a small crack; 2 = walls very uneven or pot collapsing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Images of Louise Nevelson's wall assemblages (e.g., 'Sky Cathedral,' MoMA). Recycled materials: boxes, tubes, lids, bottle caps, egg cartons; masking tape, strong glue or hot glue (adult only); one color of tempera or spray paint (adult applies spray outdoors).
misconceptions: Thinking sculpture must be carved from stone or wood. Assemblage builds a sculpture by joining found objects.
Building tall without a wide base. Put the heaviest, widest pieces at the bottom so the sculpture balances.

days.guide: Look at Nevelson's assemblages: found wooden objects arranged in boxes and painted all one color (often black). Ask how one color changes what we notice.

questions.q: Why did Nevelson paint her sculptures all one color?
questions.a: It unifies the different objects so we see them as one artwork and focus on shapes, shadows and patterns instead of what each object was.

questions.q: What is an assemblage?
questions.a: An artwork made by putting together found or recycled objects.

days.guide: Collect materials and sketch a plan from at least 2 views (front and side) for a free-standing sculpture.

questions.q: What does free-standing mean?
questions.a: It stands up on its own and can be seen from all sides.

days.guide: Build the sculpture, testing balance after each piece. Tape first, then glue.

questions.q: How do you make a tall sculpture stable?
questions.a: Use a wide, heavy base and place lighter pieces higher up; balance weight on both sides.

days.guide: Paint the whole sculpture one color, covering every surface.

questions.q: What does painting it one color do to the bottle caps and boxes?
questions.a: They blend together, so you notice the shapes, patterns, light and shadow.

days.guide: Turn the sculpture slowly as family views it from all sides. The child describes their favorite view and how they balanced it.

questions.q: Why should a sculpture be viewed from all sides?
questions.a: It is 3D, so it looks different from each angle.

weeks.assessment_key: Assemblage sculpture rubric: 4 = free-standing sculpture of 8+ recycled objects, stable without support, painted completely in one color, interesting from all sides; child explains unity and balance; 3 = stands with minor wobble or a few unpainted spots; 2 = needs support or few objects; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Cardboard (cereal boxes, a shoebox for the base), paper, glue, tape, markers, small bits of clay. Graph or plain paper for the map.
misconceptions: Drawing a map from the side. A bird's-eye view shows what you see from directly above (tops of tables, beds as rectangles).
Ignoring size relationships. Big things should be bigger in the model than small things (scale).

days.guide: The child picks a familiar place and lists its important features and where they are.

questions.q: Why list features before building?
questions.a: So you remember the important parts and their locations.

days.guide: Draw a bird's-eye-view map with symbols and a key (e.g., rectangle = bed, circle = rug).

questions.q: What is a map key?
questions.a: A box that explains what the symbols on a map mean.

questions.q: What does a table look like from a bird's-eye view?
questions.a: A rectangle or circle (its top).

days.guide: Build a 3D model in a box or on a cardboard base following the map. Fold paper into forms for furniture.

questions.q: How do you turn a flat paper rectangle into a table form?
questions.a: Fold or attach legs (or fold the edges down) so it stands with height.

days.guide: Add small details from paper and clay (lamps, trees, signs, books).

questions.q: Name 2 details that make the model look like the real place.
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., a rug pattern and a lamp on the desk.

days.guide: Evaluate with criteria (accurate to the map, detailed, sturdy) and give a tour.

questions.q: Rate your model on 'sturdy' and give evidence.
questions.a: E.g., '3 out of 4 — everything is glued, but the bookcase wobbles.'

weeks.assessment_key: Place model criteria: Accurate (layout matches the bird's-eye map and real place), Detailed (at least 6 recognizable features plus small details), Sturdy (holds together when moved). 4 = strong in all 3 plus a clear tour; 3 = strong in 2; 2 = strong in 1; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Xylophone or a keyboard/piano app, a drum or a metronome/drum-loop app for a steady beat, and a phone to record. Prepare 3 short story scenes (storm, sneaking, celebration).
misconceptions: Thinking improvising means playing randomly. Improvising is making up music on the spot while following a beat, a scale or an idea.
Thinking a mistake ruins an improvisation. Keep going; a 'wrong' note can become a new idea.

days.guide: Play a 4-beat melodic 'question' on the keyboard (ending on a note that feels unfinished, like re or sol). The child answers with a 4-beat phrase that ends on do (C). Repeat 8–10 times.

questions.q: Which note makes an answer sound finished?
questions.a: Do (the home note, C if playing in C).

questions.q: How long should the answer be?
questions.a: The same length as the question — 4 beats.

days.guide: Start a steady drum beat. The child improvises freely using only the black keys (a pentatonic scale), which always sound good together.

questions.q: Why do the black keys sound good together?
questions.a: They form a pentatonic (5-note) scale with no clashing half steps.

days.guide: For each scene, improvise music: storm (low, loud, fast, crashing), sneaking (soft, short, detached, maybe low), celebration (high, bright, fast, bouncy).

questions.q: How would you make 'sneaking' music?
questions.a: Soft (piano), short separate notes, slow or tiptoe tempo, maybe low pitches.

questions.q: What musical elements show a storm?
questions.a: Loud dynamics, low and rumbling pitches, fast tempo, sudden crashes.

days.guide: Record the 3 best improvisations and label each.

questions.q: Why record improvisations?
questions.a: So you can remember good ideas and develop them later.

days.guide: Listen back and choose a favorite idea (a short motive) to develop into a song next week. The child plays the motive and explains why they like it.

questions.q: What is a motive?
questions.a: A short musical idea that can be repeated and developed.

weeks.assessment_key: Improvisation recordings rubric: 4 = 3 labeled recordings that keep a steady beat; question-answer phrases end on do; scene music clearly uses dynamics, tempo and pitch to match the story; a favorite idea is chosen and explained; 3 = recordings complete, one scene unclear; 2 = beat unsteady or fewer than 3 recordings; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Staff paper or plain paper, pencil, Chrome Music Lab Song Maker (set to Major, C, 4 beats per bar). The favorite improvisation idea from week 28.
misconceptions: Putting the strong word syllables on weak beats. Say the words aloud and line up stressed syllables on beat 1 or strong beats.
Ending a melody on a random note. Ending on do (C) gives a finished feeling.

days.guide: The child writes 4 lines of lyrics on a topic they care about (pet, season, family). Each line should have about the same number of syllables; rhyming is optional.

questions.q: Why should lines have similar syllable counts?
questions.a: So each line fits the same rhythm pattern and the song feels balanced.

days.guide: Speak the lyrics rhythmically and write rhythms above the words using ta, ti-ti and ta-a (one syllable per note). Check each measure has 4 beats.

questions.q: Rhythm for 'I love my dog' (4 syllables) written ti-ti ta ta-a: how many beats?
questions.a: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 beats — one full measure of 4/4, with one note per syllable.

days.guide: Enter the rhythm into Song Maker and create a melody that moves mostly by steps, has one leap, and ends on do.

questions.q: Why end on do?
questions.a: It is the home note, so the song sounds finished.

questions.q: What is a step vs. a leap?
questions.a: A step moves to the next note up or down (C to D); a leap skips one or more notes (C to G).

days.guide: Write the song in standard notation on the staff (or iconic notation: dashes high/low with rhythm marks), with lyrics under the notes.

questions.q: Where do lyrics go in written music?
questions.a: Under the notes, one syllable lined up under each note.

days.guide: Share the draft and explain how the music fits the words (e.g., high notes for an exciting word, a long note for an important word).

questions.q: Give one example of how your melody matches a word.
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., 'I put "sky" on the highest note.'

weeks.assessment_key: Song draft rubric: 4 = 4 lines of original lyrics, rhythms that fit natural speech with 4 beats per measure, melody that ends on do, written in notation with lyrics aligned, and an explanation of how music fits words; 3 = one measure miscounted or notation incomplete; 2 = melody or rhythm missing; 1 = lyrics only.

weeks.prep: The song draft, Song Maker file, a family listener, a 'glow and grow' sheet, and simple percussion (shaker, drum, pot).
misconceptions: Thinking revising means starting over. Revising means improving parts of the song based on feedback.
Accepting all feedback without thinking. Composers decide which suggestions make the song better.

days.guide: Play or sing the song for a family member. They give 2 'glows' (what works) and 1 'grow' (a suggestion). Write them down.

questions.q: What is a 'grow'?
questions.a: A specific, kind suggestion for something to improve.

days.guide: Revise one rhythm or melody part based on the feedback. Write a 'change note' (what changed and why).

questions.q: Example of a change note?
questions.a: E.g., 'I changed measure 3 from all quarter notes to ti-ti ta ta so the words fit better.'

days.guide: Practice the revised song with a steady tempo, using a drum or metronome app.

questions.q: Why practice with a metronome?
questions.a: It keeps the tempo steady so you don't rush or slow down.

days.guide: Add a 1- or 2-measure percussion ostinato that repeats under the whole song.

questions.q: What makes a good ostinato accompaniment?
questions.a: A short, simple, repeating pattern that fits the beat and doesn't cover the melody.

days.guide: Compare the original and revised versions (recordings or notation) and explain which is better and why.

questions.q: Why might the revised version be better?
questions.a: Answers vary but should name the specific change and its effect, e.g., 'The words fit the rhythm now, so it is easier to sing.'

weeks.assessment_key: Revised composition rubric: 4 = feedback recorded (2 glows, 1 grow), at least one clear revision documented in change notes, steady-tempo performance with a fitting ostinato, and a reasoned comparison; 3 = revision made, notes brief; 2 = little revision; 1 = no revision.

weeks.prep: Final song and ostinato, a phone or tablet to record, paper for program notes, chairs for the 'audience.' Review concert etiquette from week 17.
misconceptions: Thinking program notes retell every note. Program notes briefly tell the audience what the piece is about and how it was made.
Only judging whether the performance was 'good.' Evaluate with specific criteria: steady beat, accurate pitch, expression.

days.guide: Rehearse 3 times with accompaniment, focusing on starting together, steady tempo and a clear ending.

questions.q: How do you start a performance together?
questions.a: Count off (e.g., '1, 2, 3, 4') in the tempo of the song.

days.guide: Write 3–5 sentences of program notes: song title, what it is about, how you composed it, and something to listen for.

questions.q: What should program notes include?
questions.a: The title, what the song is about, how it was made, and something to listen for.

days.guide: Premiere: read the program notes, perform, and bow. Record the performance.

questions.q: What does 'premiere' mean?
questions.a: The very first public performance of a new piece.

days.guide: Watch the recording and score it 1–4 on steady beat, accurate pitch, and expression with evidence.

questions.q: What evidence shows a steady beat?
questions.a: The tempo didn't speed up or slow down and the accompaniment stayed together with the voice.

days.guide: Write a reflection on the whole process (improvise → draft → revise → perform): what was hardest, what you're proud of, what you'd do next time.

questions.q: Name the steps you used to compose your song.
questions.a: Improvise ideas, write lyrics, set rhythms, create a melody, notate, get feedback, revise, add accompaniment, rehearse, perform.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance and reflection rubric: Performance (steady beat, accurate pitch, expression) each scored 1–4; Reflection: 4 = describes each stage of the process with specific examples, names a challenge and a success and a next step; 3 = most stages with some detail; 2 = brief; 1 = missing. Proficient = 3+ average.

weeks.prep: Images of a Diego Rivera mural (e.g., the 'Detroit Industry Murals,' 1932–33, Detroit Institute of Arts; or 'Pan American Unity,' San Francisco). Chumash rock art images from Calisphere or Chumash Painted Cave State Historic Park. Pencils, sketch paper.
misconceptions: Thinking we know exactly what Chumash rock paintings mean. Their meanings are connected to Chumash beliefs and ceremonies and are not fully known to outsiders; we should not guess as if certain.
Thinking it's harmless to touch ancient rock art. Oils from hands, chalk, graffiti and rubbing damage it permanently; look but don't touch.

days.guide: Show the Detroit Industry murals. Ask: What are the workers doing? What machines do you see? What story does the mural tell about workers and industry?

questions.q: What story does Rivera's Detroit Industry mural tell?
questions.a: It shows factory workers building cars and working together with huge machines, honoring workers and industry.

questions.q: Where was Diego Rivera from?
questions.a: Mexico.

days.guide: View Chumash rock paintings (red, black and white circles, figures, sun-like designs). Explain the Chumash are a California Indian people of the Central and Southern Coast whose ancestors made these paintings; they are sacred and still important to Chumash people today. Discuss why they must be protected.

questions.q: Why must rock art be protected?
questions.a: It is irreplaceable and sacred to the Chumash people; touching, graffiti and pollution can destroy it.

questions.q: Where did the Chumash live?
questions.a: Along the central and southern California coast (around Santa Barbara, Ventura, San Luis Obispo) and the Channel Islands.

days.guide: Discuss how context (when and where art was made, by whom and why) changes our response. Compare viewing the mural knowing it was painted during the Great Depression about Detroit factories.

questions.q: Why does knowing the context of an artwork matter?
questions.a: It helps us understand why it was made and what it meant to the people of that time and place.

days.guide: Sketch a mural plan showing important people and places in your community (library, park, farmers market, neighbors, helpers).

questions.q: What story will your mural tell?
questions.a: Answers vary; should name a clear community story or theme.

days.guide: Share the sketch with family and ask for feedback; note 1 change.

questions.q: What feedback did you get, and what will you change?
questions.a: Answers vary; the child names a specific change.

weeks.assessment_key: Mural sketch rubric: 4 = sketch tells a clear community story with at least 3 important people/places, uses the whole page with a planned composition (foreground/background), and the child explains its message and one change from feedback; 3 = clear story, less detail; 2 = unclear story; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Butcher paper (about 3 × 5 feet), pencil, ruler or yardstick, tempera paints in many colors plus white and black, large and small brushes, drop cloth. The week 32 sketch.
misconceptions: Drawing the large version freehand without guides. A grid lets you copy each small square onto a big square so proportions stay right.
Painting details first. Paint large background areas first, then middle shapes, then fine details on top.

days.guide: Draw a grid on the sketch (e.g., 2-inch squares) and the same number of squares on the butcher paper (e.g., 1-foot squares). Number rows and columns on both.

questions.q: If the sketch grid has 4 rows × 6 columns, how many squares should the big paper have?
questions.a: The same: 4 × 6 = 24 squares.

days.guide: Copy the drawing square by square, lightly in pencil, looking at what crosses each square's edges.

questions.q: Why draw lightly?
questions.a: So lines can be erased or covered by paint.

days.guide: Paint sky, land and large background shapes with big brushes.

questions.q: Why paint the background first?
questions.a: Big areas are easier first, and details can be painted on top without being covered.

days.guide: Paint people, buildings and details with small brushes, using tints and shades for form.

questions.q: How can you use shades on a building?
questions.a: Paint the side away from the sun a darker shade of the same color to make it look 3D.

days.guide: Step back with family, evaluate (clear story, color, details) and add finishing touches such as outlines.

questions.q: Why step back to look at a mural?
questions.a: Murals are meant to be seen from a distance; stepping back shows what is clear and what needs fixing.

weeks.assessment_key: Community mural rubric: 4 = design scaled up accurately with the grid, background fully painted, details use tints and shades, clear community story, neat finishing touches; 3 = small proportion issues or unfinished details; 2 = story unclear or large areas unpainted; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: The year's portfolio, construction paper slightly larger than each artwork, glue stick, index cards for labels, a slideshow app if doing a digital gallery.
misconceptions: Choosing only favorite subjects. Choose works that show different media and skills (drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture) and growth.
Artist statements that only say 'I like it.' A statement tells what the work is, how it was made and what the artist wanted to show.

days.guide: Review the whole portfolio and select 6 best works showing different media. Explain each choice.

questions.q: Why include different kinds of art?
questions.a: To show the range of skills and media learned during the year.

days.guide: Mount each work on a construction-paper mat with an even border, centered.

questions.q: Why use a mat?
questions.a: It frames the art, separates it from the wall and makes it look finished.

days.guide: Write a 3-sentence artist statement for each: what it is, how it was made (media/technique), what you wanted to show or what you learned.

questions.q: Write an example artist statement sentence about technique.
questions.a: E.g., 'I used tints and shades of red to make the flower petals look curved.'

days.guide: Compare a hallway wall gallery and a digital slideshow: pros and cons (real size and texture vs. easy to share with far-away family). Choose one or both.

questions.q: Name one advantage of a digital gallery.
questions.a: Family far away can see it; it can include music or narration; art isn't damaged.

days.guide: Arrange the layout (eye level, even spacing, group by theme or media) and make labels: title, artist, medium, date.

questions.q: What goes on a museum label?
questions.a: Title, artist's name, medium (materials) and date (year).

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibit preparation checklist: 6 works selected showing at least 3 different media (1 pt), all mounted neatly (1), 6 artist statements with what/how/why (2), exhibit space chosen with a reason (1), layout planned with labels including title, artist, medium, date (1). 6 = exemplary; 5 = proficient; 3–4 = developing; below 3 = beginning.

weeks.prep: List of songs from the year (unit 4 and 6 songs, the original song), accompaniment instruments, paper or a computer for designing a program.
misconceptions: Thinking the program order doesn't matter. Concerts usually open strong, vary tempos and moods, and end with a highlight (often the original piece).
Skipping the dress rehearsal. A full run-through in order shows transitions and timing problems.

days.guide: Choose 4 songs (including the original) and decide the order. Explain the reasons (contrast, energy, ending strong).

questions.q: Why vary fast and slow songs in a concert?
questions.a: Contrast keeps the audience interested and lets the performer rest their voice.

days.guide: Rehearse the songs from units 4 and 6, reviewing words, pitch and expression markings.

questions.q: What expression will you use in your folk song?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., soft dynamics for a gentle song, crescendo toward the end.

days.guide: Rehearse the original song with its ostinato accompaniment, focusing on a confident start and ending.

questions.q: How will you start together with your accompanist?
questions.a: Count off in tempo (e.g., '1, 2, ready, go').

days.guide: Dress rehearsal: run the whole program in order with spoken introductions and bows, without stopping.

questions.q: What do you do if you make a mistake in a performance?
questions.a: Keep going without stopping, as if nothing happened.

days.guide: Design and print a concert program: title, date, performer, song titles in order with composer/origin (e.g., 'Sakura' — traditional Japanese; your song — by you).

questions.q: What information goes in a concert program?
questions.a: Concert title, date, performer(s), the songs in order with composers or origins, and optional program notes.

weeks.assessment_key: Concert program check: 4 = program lists 4 songs in a planned order with composer/origin for each (traditional songs labeled 'traditional' with culture, original song credited to the child), title, date and performer, attractively designed; dress rehearsal run without stopping; 3 = one missing element; 2 = several missing; 1 = no program.

weeks.prep: Hanging supplies (painter's tape), the matted art and labels, chairs and a performance area, concert programs, recording device. Invite family or friends.
misconceptions: Thinking critique means finding what's wrong. A critique describes, analyzes, interprets and judges using criteria, including strengths.
Thinking growth is only about 'talent.' Growth comes from practice, feedback and revision.

days.guide: Hang the exhibit at eye level with even spacing and labels; set up the performance area.

questions.q: Why hang art at eye level?
questions.a: So viewers can see it comfortably and clearly.

days.guide: The child leads a gallery walk, explaining each work using their artist statements.

questions.q: Choose one work: what technique did you use?
questions.a: The child correctly names the media and technique, e.g., foam-plate printmaking or score-and-slip clay.

days.guide: Perform the concert program with introductions, using etiquette.

questions.q: What do you do at the end of each piece?
questions.a: Pause and bow while the audience applauds.

days.guide: Critique one artwork and one song using criteria from the year (art: line, shape, color, value, texture, craftsmanship; music: steady beat, pitch, expression).

questions.q: What are the steps of a critique?
questions.a: Describe what you see/hear, analyze how it's made, interpret its meaning or mood, and judge it with criteria.

days.guide: Write about growth as an artist and musician: compare a fall work to a spring work and name skills learned.

questions.q: Give an example comparing early and late work.
questions.a: E.g., 'In September I drew symbols, but by spring I drew from observation with shading.'

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibit and concert rubric: 4 = exhibit hung neatly with labels, gallery walk explains each work with art vocabulary, concert performed with etiquette, critique uses criteria for one artwork and one song, reflection compares early and late work with specific skills; 3 = all parts with less detail; 2 = some parts missing; 1 = minimal participation.
